def print_troubleshooting_guide():
    """
    Comprehensive troubleshooting guide for join issues
    """
    guide = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                    JOIN TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE                          ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 1: Join Takes Too Long                                           │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • Join stage runs for hours                                          │
    │   • Tasks are stuck or slow                                            │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Diagnosis:                                                              │
    │   result.explain(mode="formatted")  # Check join strategy              │
    │   df.rdd.getNumPartitions()  # Check partition count                   │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Enable broadcast for small tables:                                │
    │      result = df1.join(broadcast(df2), "key")                          │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Increase parallelism:                                             │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "400")             │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Pre-partition data:                                               │
    │      df1.repartition(200, "join_key")                                  │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Enable AQE:                                                       │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")              │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 2: Out of Memory Errors                                          │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • java.lang.OutOfMemoryError                                         │
    │   • Container killed by YARN                                           │
    │   • GC overhead limit exceeded                                         │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Diagnosis:                                                              │
    │   # Check broadcast size                                               │
    │   df.cache().count()                                                   │
    │   print(spark.catalog.cacheTable("table_name").sizeInBytes)            │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Reduce broadcast threshold:                                       │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1")      │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Increase executor memory:                                         │
    │      --executor-memory 8g --executor-memoryOverhead 2g                 │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Increase partitions:                                              │
    │      df.repartition(500)                                               │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Use disk-based shuffle:                                           │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.shuffle.spill.compress", "true")            │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 3: Data Skew (Some Tasks Much Slower)                            │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • Few tasks take 10x longer than others                              │
    │   • Uneven data distribution                                           │
    │   • Some executors idle while others busy                              │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Diagnosis:                                                              │
    │   # Check partition sizes                                              │
    │   df.groupBy("join_key").count().orderBy(desc("count")).show()         │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Enable AQE skew join:                                             │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")     │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Use salting technique:                                            │
    │      df.withColumn("salt", (rand() * 10).cast("int"))                  │
    │        .withColumn("salted_key", concat(col("key"), col("salt")))      │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Filter before join:                                               │
    │      df.filter(col("key").isNotNull())                                 │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Repartition by range:                                             │
    │      df.repartitionByRange(200, "join_key")                            │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 4: Incorrect Results / Missing Data                              │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • Expected rows missing from result                                  │
    │   • Duplicate rows in output                                           │
    │   • NULL values where unexpected                                       │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Diagnosis:                                                              │
    │   # Check join type and keys                                           │
    │   df1.join(df2, "key", "left").show()  # vs "inner"                    │
    │   df1.select("key").distinct().count()  # Check for duplicates         │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Verify join type:                                                 │
    │      - inner: Only matching rows                                       │
    │      - left: All from left + matching from right                       │
    │      - right: All from right + matching from left                      │
    │      - outer: All rows from both                                       │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Check for NULL keys:                                              │
    │      df.filter(col("key").isNull()).count()                            │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Handle duplicate keys:                                            │
    │      df.dropDuplicates(["key"])                                        │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Use explicit column names:                                        │
    │      df1.join(df2, df1.id == df2.id)  # Instead of "id"                │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 5: Shuffle Spill to Disk                                         │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • "Spill (Memory)" and "Spill (Disk)" in Spark UI                    │
    │   • Slow performance due to disk I/O                                   │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Diagnosis:                                                              │
    │   # Check Spark UI -> Stages -> Shuffle Read/Write                     │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Increase executor memory:                                         │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.executor.memory", "8g")                     │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Increase shuffle memory fraction:                                 │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.memory.fraction", "0.8")                    │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Reduce partition size:                                            │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes", "64MB")       │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Use broadcast for smaller table:                                  │
    │      df1.join(broadcast(df2), "key")                                   │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ ISSUE 6: Broadcast Timeout                                             │
    ├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
    │ Symptoms:                                                               │
    │   • "Could not execute broadcast"                                      │
    │   • "Timeout waiting for broadcast"                                    │
    │                                                                         │
    │ Solutions:                                                              │
    │   1. Increase broadcast timeout:                                       │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.broadcastTimeout", "600")  # 10 min     │
    │                                                                         │
    │   2. Reduce broadcast table size:                                      │
    │      df.select("id", "name")  # Only needed columns                    │
    │                                                                         │
    │   3. Disable broadcast:                                                │
    │      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1")      │
    │                                                                         │
    │   4. Use sort-merge join instead:                                      │
    │      df1.join(df2.hint("merge"), "key")                                │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    """
    print(guide)

def export_metrics_to_csv(spark, df, output_path="join_metrics.csv"):
    """
    Export join performance metrics to CSV
    """
    print(f"\nExporting metrics to {output_path}...")
    
    metrics = df.groupBy("join_type") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("row_count"),
            avg("execution_time").alias("avg_time"),
            max("execution_time").alias("max_time"),
            min("execution_time").alias("min_time")
        )
    
    metrics.coalesce(1).write.mode("overwrite").csv(output_path, header=True)
    print(f"✓ Metrics exported to {output_path}")


def generate_join_performance_report(spark):
    """
    Generate comprehensive performance report
    """
    report = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║              JOIN PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS REPORT                          ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    Report Generated: {timestamp}
    Spark Version: {spark_version}
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ CONFIGURATION SUMMARY                                                   │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    Broadcast Threshold:        {broadcast_threshold}
    Shuffle Partitions:         {shuffle_partitions}
    Adaptive Execution:         {adaptive_enabled}
    Skew Join Optimization:     {skew_join_enabled}
    Default Parallelism:        {parallelism}
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ RECOMMENDATIONS                                                         │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    Based on current configuration:
    
    1. For small dimension tables (< {broadcast_mb} MB):
       ✓ Use broadcast joins
       ✓ Cache frequently used dimensions
    
    2. For large-to-large joins:
       ✓ Enable adaptive query execution
       ✓ Use {shuffle_partitions} shuffle partitions
       ✓ Consider bucketing for repeated joins
    
    3. For skewed data:
       ✓ Skew join optimization is {skew_status}
       ✓ Consider salting technique for extreme skew
    
    4. Memory optimization:
       ✓ Monitor GC time in Spark UI
       ✓ Adjust spark.memory.fraction if needed
       ✓ Consider spill metrics
    
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    """
    
    import datetime
    
    # Get current configuration
    broadcast_threshold = spark.conf.get("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760")
    broadcast_mb = int(broadcast_threshold) / (1024 * 1024)
    shuffle_partitions = spark.conf.get("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
    adaptive_enabled = spark.conf.get("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")
    
    try:
        skew_join_enabled = spark.conf.get("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "false")
    except:
        skew_join_enabled = "false"
    
    parallelism = spark.conf.get("spark.default.parallelism", "N/A")
    
    skew_status = "ENABLED ✓" if skew_join_enabled == "true" else "DISABLED ✗"
    
    formatted_report = report.format(
        timestamp=datetime.datetime.now().strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"),
        spark_version=spark.version,
        broadcast_threshold=broadcast_threshold,
        broadcast_mb=f"{broadcast_mb:.1f}",
        shuffle_partitions=shuffle_partitions,
        adaptive_enabled=adaptive_enabled.upper(),
        skew_join_enabled=skew_join_enabled.upper(),
        parallelism=parallelism,
        skew_status=skew_status
    )
    
    print(formatted_report)
    return formatted_report


def create_sample_datasets_for_testing(spark, size="small"):
    """
    Create sample datasets for testing join patterns
    
    Parameters:
    - size: "small", "medium", "large"
    """
    print(f"\nCreating {size} sample datasets for testing...")
    
    if size == "small":
        num_orders = 10000
        num_customers = 1000
        num_products = 500
    elif size == "medium":
        num_orders = 100000
        num_customers = 10000
        num_products = 5000
    else:  # large
        num_orders = 1000000
        num_customers = 100000
        num_products = 50000
    
    # Orders (Fact table)
    orders = spark.range(num_orders).toDF("order_id") \
        .withColumn("customer_id", (col("order_id") % num_customers).cast("int")) \
        .withColumn("product_id", (col("order_id") % num_products).cast("int")) \
        .withColumn("quantity", (col("order_id") % 10 + 1).cast("int")) \
        .withColumn("price", (col("order_id") % 100 + 10.0)) \
        .withColumn("order_date", 
                   expr(f"date_add('2024-01-01', cast(order_id % 365 as int))"))
    
    # Customers (Dimension table)
    customers = spark.range(num_customers).toDF("customer_id") \
        .withColumn("customer_name", concat(lit("Customer_"), col("customer_id"))) \
        .withColumn("segment", concat(lit("Segment_"), (col("customer_id") % 5).cast("string"))) \
        .withColumn("city", concat(lit("City_"), (col("customer_id") % 100).cast("string")))
    
    # Products (Dimension table)
    products = spark.range(num_products).toDF("product_id") \
        .withColumn("product_name", concat(lit("Product_"), col("product_id"))) \
        .withColumn("category", concat(lit("Category_"), (col("product_id") % 20).cast("string"))) \
        .withColumn("brand", concat(lit("Brand_"), (col("product_id") % 50).cast("string")))
    
    print(f"✓ Created {size} datasets:")
    print(f"  Orders:    {orders.count():,} rows")
    print(f"  Customers: {customers.count():,} rows")
    print(f"  Products:  {products.count():,} rows")
    
    return orders, customers, products


def benchmark_all_join_types(spark):
    """
    Benchmark all join types and compare performance
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE JOIN BENCHMARK")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create test data
    orders, customers, products = create_sample_datasets_for_testing(spark, "medium")
    
    results = []
    
    # Benchmark 1: Broadcast Join
    print("\n[1/5] Benchmarking Broadcast Join...")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "104857600")  # 100MB
    start = time.time()
    broadcast_result = orders.join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
    broadcast_count = broadcast_result.count()
    broadcast_time = time.time() - start
    results.append(("Broadcast Join", broadcast_time, broadcast_count))
    print(f"    Time: {broadcast_time:.2f}s, Rows: {broadcast_count:,}")
    
    # Benchmark 2: Sort-Merge Join
    print("\n[2/5] Benchmarking Sort-Merge Join...")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "-1")
    orders_part = orders.repartition(20, "customer_id")
    customers_part = customers.repartition(20, "customer_id")
    start = time.time()
    sortmerge_result = orders_part.join(customers_part, "customer_id")
    sortmerge_count = sortmerge_result.count()
    sortmerge_time = time.time() - start
    results.append(("Sort-Merge Join", sortmerge_time, sortmerge_count))
    print(f"    Time: {sortmerge_time:.2f}s, Rows: {sortmerge_count:,}")
    
    # Benchmark 3: Shuffle Hash Join
    print("\n[3/5] Benchmarking Shuffle Hash Join...")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin", "false")
    start = time.time()
    shuffle_result = orders.join(customers.hint("shuffle_hash"), "customer_id")
    shuffle_count = shuffle_result.count()
    shuffle_time = time.time() - start
    results.append(("Shuffle Hash Join", shuffle_time, shuffle_count))
    print(f"    Time: {shuffle_time:.2f}s, Rows: {shuffle_count:,}")
    
    # Benchmark 4: Star Schema Join
    print("\n[4/5] Benchmarking Star Schema Join...")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "104857600")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.join.preferSortMergeJoin", "true")
    start = time.time()
    star_result = orders \
        .join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id") \
        .join(broadcast(products), "product_id")
    star_count = star_result.count()
    star_time = time.time() - start
    results.append(("Star Schema Join", star_time, star_count))
    print(f"    Time: {star_time:.2f}s, Rows: {star_count:,}")
    
    # Benchmark 5: Semi Join
    print("\n[5/5] Benchmarking Semi Join...")
    vip_customers = customers.filter(col("customer_id") < 1000)
    start = time.time()
    semi_result = orders.join(vip_customers, "customer_id", "left_semi")
    semi_count = semi_result.count()
    semi_time = time.time() - start
    results.append(("Semi Join", semi_time, semi_count))
    print(f"    Time: {semi_time:.2f}s, Rows: {semi_count:,}")
    
    # Print summary
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("BENCHMARK SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 80)
    print(f"{'Join Type':<25} {'Time (s)':<15} {'Rows':<15} {'Rows/sec':<15}")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    for join_type, exec_time, row_count in results:
        throughput = row_count / exec_time if exec_time > 0 else 0
        print(f"{join_type:<25} {exec_time:<15.2f} {row_count:<15,} {throughput:<15,.0f}")
    
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Find fastest
    fastest = min(results, key=lambda x: x[1])
    print(f"\n✓ Fastest: {fastest[0]} ({fastest[1]:.2f}s)")
    
    return results

def quick_start_examples():
    """
    Quick start examples for common scenarios
    """
    examples = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                        QUICK START EXAMPLES                            ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    # Initialize Spark
    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
    from pyspark.sql.functions import *
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \\
        .appName("QuickStart") \\
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") \\
        .getOrCreate()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 1: Join sales data with customer lookup table
    # ========================================================================
    
    sales = spark.read.parquet("sales.parquet")
    customers = spark.read.parquet("customers.parquet")
    
    # Use broadcast for small customer table
    result = sales.join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
    result.write.parquet("output/sales_with_customers.parquet")
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 2: Join two large datasets
    # ========================================================================
    
    orders = spark.read.parquet("orders.parquet")
    order_items = spark.read.parquet("order_items.parquet")
    
    # Pre-partition for efficient sort-merge join
    orders_part = orders.repartition(200, "order_id")
    items_part = order_items.repartition(200, "order_id")
    
    result = orders_part.join(items_part, "order_id")
    result.write.parquet("output/complete_orders.parquet")
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 3: Data warehouse star schema query
    # ========================================================================
    
    fact_sales = spark.read.parquet("fact_sales.parquet")
    dim_product = spark.read.parquet("dim_product.parquet")
    dim_store = spark.read.parquet("dim_store.parquet")
    dim_date = spark.read.parquet("dim_date.parquet")
    
    # Broadcast all dimensions
    result = fact_sales \\
        .join(broadcast(dim_product), "product_id") \\
        .join(broadcast(dim_store), "store_id") \\
        .join(broadcast(dim_date), "date_id") \\
        .groupBy("category", "region", "month") \\
        .agg(sum("amount").alias("total_sales"))
    
    result.show()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 4: Filter with semi-join (find matching records)
    # ========================================================================
    
    all_customers = spark.read.parquet("all_customers.parquet")
    active_customers = spark.read.parquet("active_customers.parquet")
    
    # Get only customers who are active
    result = all_customers.join(
        active_customers,
        "customer_id",
        "left_semi"  # Returns only left table columns
    )
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 5: Handle data skew
    # ========================================================================
    
    # Enable automatic skew handling
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
    
    skewed_data = spark.read.parquet("skewed_data.parquet")
    lookup = spark.read.parquet("lookup.parquet")
    
    result = skewed_data.join(lookup, "key")
    
    # Or use manual salting for extreme skew
    salt_factor = 10
    
    skewed_salted = skewed_data \\
        .withColumn("salt", (rand() * salt_factor).cast("int")) \\
        .withColumn("salted_key", concat(col("key"), lit("_"), col("salt")))
    
    lookup_salted = lookup \\
        .crossJoin(spark.range(salt_factor).toDF("salt")) \\
        .withColumn("salted_key", concat(col("key"), lit("_"), col("salt")))
    
    result = skewed_salted.join(lookup_salted, "salted_key")
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SCENARIO 6: Time-based range join
    # ========================================================================
    
    events = spark.read.parquet("events.parquet")
    campaigns = spark.read.parquet("campaigns.parquet")
    
    # Add date bucketing to reduce cartesian product
    events_dated = events.withColumn("event_date", to_date("event_time"))
    campaigns_dated = campaigns.withColumn("campaign_date", to_date("start_time"))
    
    # Join on date bucket first, then apply time range
    result = events_dated.join(
        campaigns_dated,
        events_dated.event_date == campaigns_dated.campaign_date
    ).filter(
        (col("event_time") >= col("start_time")) &
        (col("event_time") <= col("end_time"))
    )
    
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    """
    print(examples)

def print_optimization_checklist():
    """
    Print performance optimization checklist
    """
    checklist = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║              JOIN PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION CHECKLIST                   ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    BEFORE RUNNING JOINS:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Analyze data sizes and cardinality
    □ Check for NULL values in join keys
    □ Identify small tables suitable for broadcast
    □ Review data distribution and check for skew
    □ Choose appropriate file format (Parquet recommended)
    □ Partition data by frequently used join keys
    □ Collect table statistics for CBO
    
    CONFIGURATION:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Enable Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
    
    □ Set appropriate broadcast threshold
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760")
    
    □ Configure shuffle partitions based on data size
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
    
    □ Enable skew join optimization
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
    
    □ Disable cartesian joins for safety
      spark.conf.set("spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled", "false")
    
    JOIN STRATEGY SELECTION:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Use broadcast join for small tables (< 10MB)
      df1.join(broadcast(df2), "key")
    
    □ Use sort-merge join for large-to-large joins
      df1.repartition("key").join(df2.repartition("key"), "key")
    
    □ Use semi/anti join for filtering
      df1.join(df2, "key", "left_semi")
    
    □ Avoid cartesian joins - always specify join conditions
    
    □ Use appropriate join type (inner, left, right, outer)
    
    OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Filter data before joins (predicate pushdown)
      df.filter(condition).join(...)
    
    □ Select only required columns
      df.select("col1", "col2").join(...)
    
    □ Cache frequently reused tables
      df.cache() or df.persist()
    
    □ Repartition by join key for large datasets
      df.repartition(num_partitions, "join_key")
    
    □ Use bucketing for repeated joins
      df.write.bucketBy(num_buckets, "key").saveAsTable("table")
    
    □ Handle NULL values explicitly
      df.filter(col("key").isNotNull())
    
    □ Remove duplicate keys if not needed
      df.dropDuplicates(["key"])
    
    HANDLING DATA SKEW:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Enable AQE skew join optimization
    
    □ Use salting technique for extreme skew
      - Add random salt to skewed keys
      - Replicate small table with all salt values
    
    □ Use range partitioning instead of hash partitioning
      df.repartitionByRange("key")
    
    □ Split skewed keys and process separately
    
    MONITORING AND VALIDATION:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Check execution plan with explain()
      df.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    □ Verify join strategy in Spark UI
      - Check for BroadcastHashJoin, SortMergeJoin, etc.
    
    □ Monitor shuffle read/write metrics
    
    □ Check for spill to disk
    
    □ Verify result count matches expectations
    
    □ Look for long-running tasks (indicator of skew)
    
    □ Monitor memory usage and GC time
    
    POST-EXECUTION:
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    □ Validate results for correctness
    
    □ Check for duplicate or missing records
    
    □ Review execution time and identify bottlenecks
    
    □ Analyze partition sizes for balance
      df.groupBy(spark_partition_id()).count().show()
    
    □ Document optimization decisions
    
    □ Clear cache if no longer needed
      spark.catalog.clearCache()
    
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    """
    print(checklist)

# ============================================================================

def streaming_join_example(spark):
    """
    Example of stream-to-static and stream-to-stream joins
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: STREAMING JOIN PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Static dimension table
    dim_products = spark.read.parquet("products.parquet")
    
    # Streaming fact data
    streaming_sales = spark \
        .readStream \
        .format("kafka") \
        .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092") \
        .option("subscribe", "sales") \
        .load()
    
    # Stream-to-static join (broadcast recommended)
    enriched_sales = streaming_sales.join(
        broadcast(dim_products),
        "product_id"
    )
    
    # Write stream
    query = enriched_sales \
        .writeStream \
        .format("parquet") \
        .option("path", "output/enriched_sales") \
        .option("checkpointLocation", "checkpoint/sales") \
        .start()
    
    print("✓ Streaming join started")
    return query

def delta_lake_join_optimization(spark):
    """
    Join optimizations specific to Delta Lake
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: DELTA LAKE JOIN OPTIMIZATIONS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Enable Delta Lake optimizations
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.properties.defaults.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.properties.defaults.autoOptimize.autoCompact", "true")
    
    # Read Delta tables
    orders = spark.read.format("delta").load("delta/orders")
    customers = spark.read.format("delta").load("delta/customers")
    
    # Use Z-ordering for frequently joined columns
    # spark.sql("OPTIMIZE delta.orders ZORDER BY (customer_id)")
    # spark.sql("OPTIMIZE delta.customers ZORDER BY (customer_id)")
    
    # Perform join
    result = orders.join(broadcast(customers), "customer_id")
    
    # Write with optimization
    result.write \
        .format("delta") \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .option("overwriteSchema", "true") \
        .save("delta/orders_enriched")
    
    print("✓ Delta Lake join completed with optimizations")
    return result

def sql_join_examples(spark):
    """
    SQL-based join examples with hints
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: SQL JOIN EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create temp views
    spark.sql("""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW sales AS
        SELECT * FROM parquet.`data/sales.parquet`
    """)
    
    spark.sql("""
        CREATE OR REPLACE TEMP VIEW customers AS
        SELECT * FROM parquet.`data/customers.parquet`
    """)
    
    # Example 1: Broadcast hint in SQL
    result1 = spark.sql("""
        SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(c) */
            s.sale_id,
            s.amount,
            c.customer_name,
            c.segment
        FROM sales s
        INNER JOIN customers c ON s.customer_id = c.customer_id
        WHERE s.amount > 100
    """)
    
    print("\n1. Broadcast Join with SQL:")
    result1.explain(mode="simple")
    result1.show(5)
    
    # Example 2: Sort-merge hint
    result2 = spark.sql("""
        SELECT /*+ MERGE(s, o) */
            s.sale_id,
            o.order_id
        FROM sales s
        INNER JOIN orders o ON s.sale_id = o.sale_id
    """)
    
    print("\n2. Sort-Merge Join with SQL:")
    result2.explain(mode="simple")
    
    # Example 3: Semi join in SQL
    result3 = spark.sql("""
        SELECT *
        FROM sales s
        WHERE EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 
            FROM vip_customers v 
            WHERE v.customer_id = s.customer_id
        )
    """)
    
    print("\n3. Semi Join (EXISTS) with SQL:")
    result3.explain(mode="simple")
    
    return result1, result2, result3

def collect_and_use_statistics(spark):
    """
    Collect statistics for Cost-Based Optimizer
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: COST-BASED OPTIMIZER STATISTICS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create and register tables
    df = spark.range(1000000).toDF("id") \
        .withColumn("value", col("id") * 2)
    
    df.write.mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("test_table")
    
    # Collect table statistics
    spark.sql("ANALYZE TABLE test_table COMPUTE STATISTICS")
    
    # Collect column statistics
    spark.sql("ANALYZE TABLE test_table COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS id, value")
    
    # View statistics
    stats = spark.sql("DESCRIBE EXTENDED test_table").collect()
    
    print("\nTable Statistics:")
    for row in stats:
        if "Statistics" in str(row):
            print(f"  {row}")
    
    # CBO will now use these statistics for better join planning
    print("\n✓ Statistics collected - CBO will use for join optimization")
    
    return stats

def custom_partitioner_example(spark):
    """
    Use custom partitioner for optimal join performance
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("BONUS: CUSTOM PARTITIONER")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark import RDD
    from pyspark.rdd import portable_hash
    
    # Create sample data
    data1 = [(i, f"value_{i}") for i in range(10000)]
    data2 = [(i, f"detail_{i}") for i in range(10000)]
    
    rdd1 = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(data1)
    rdd2 = spark.sparkContext.parallelize(data2)
    
    # Custom hash partitioner
    num_partitions = 10
    
    def custom_partition_func(key):
        # Custom logic for partitioning
        return portable_hash(key) % num_partitions
    
    # Partition both RDDs with same partitioner
    rdd1_partitioned = rdd1.partitionBy(num_partitions, custom_partition_func)
    rdd2_partitioned = rdd2.partitionBy(num_partitions, custom_partition_func)
    
    # Join will be more efficient as co-located data
    result_rdd = rdd1_partitioned.join(rdd2_partitioned)
    
    print(f"✓ Custom partitioner applied with {num_partitions} partitions")
    print(f"  Result partitions: {result_rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    print(f"  Sample results: {result_rdd.take(3)}")
    
    return result_rdd

# PATTERN 1: NATURAL ORDER PATTERN

def natural_order_pattern(df):
    """
    Natural Order Pattern: Data is returned in the order it was inserted/stored
    without any explicit ordering. This is the default behavior.
    
    Use Case: When order doesn't matter or for initial data exploration
    Performance: Fastest - no sorting overhead
    """
    print("=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 1: NATURAL ORDER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Basic natural order (no ordering specified)
    print("\n1. Basic Natural Order (as stored in partitions):")
    natural_df = df.select("emp_id", "name", "department", "salary")
    natural_df.show()
    
    # Example 2: Natural order with filter
    print("\n2. Natural Order with Filter:")
    filtered_df = df.filter(col("salary") > 80000) \
        .select("emp_id", "name", "salary")
    filtered_df.show()
    
    # Example 3: Natural order with monotonically increasing ID
    # Note: This adds a unique ID but doesn't guarantee order
    print("\n3. Natural Order with Monotonic ID:")
    with_id_df = df.select(
        monotonically_increasing_id().alias("unique_id"),
        "emp_id", "name", "department"
    )
    with_id_df.show()
    
    # Example 4: Demonstrating partition-dependent natural order
    print("\n4. Natural Order across partitions (may vary):")
    repartitioned_df = df.repartition(3).select("emp_id", "name", "department")
    print(f"Number of partitions: {repartitioned_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    repartitioned_df.show()
    
    return natural_df

def sorted_order_pattern(df):
    """
    Sorted Order Pattern: Explicitly sort data by one or more columns
    
    Use Case: When specific ordering is required for output or processing
    Performance: Moderate - requires full data shuffle and sort
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 2: SORTED ORDER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Single column ascending sort
    print("\n1. Single Column Ascending Sort (by salary):")
    sorted_asc_df = df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary") \
        .orderBy("salary")
    sorted_asc_df.show()
    
    # Example 2: Single column descending sort
    print("\n2. Single Column Descending Sort (by salary):")
    sorted_desc_df = df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary") \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    sorted_desc_df.show()
    
    # Example 3: Multi-column sort
    print("\n3. Multi-Column Sort (department ASC, salary DESC):")
    multi_sorted_df = df.select("emp_id", "name", "department", "salary") \
        .orderBy(col("department").asc(), col("salary").desc())
    multi_sorted_df.show()
    
    # Example 4: Sort with null handling
    print("\n4. Sort with Null Handling:")
    # Add some null values for demonstration
    df_with_nulls = df.withColumn(
        "bonus",
        when(col("emp_id") % 3 == 0, None).otherwise(col("salary") * 0.1)
    )
    
    # Nulls first
    print("   a) Nulls First:")
    df_with_nulls.select("emp_id", "name", "bonus") \
        .orderBy(col("bonus").asc_nulls_first()) \
        .show()
    
    # Nulls last
    print("   b) Nulls Last:")
    df_with_nulls.select("emp_id", "name", "bonus") \
        .orderBy(col("bonus").asc_nulls_last()) \
        .show()
    
    # Example 5: Sort with expression
    print("\n5. Sort by Expression (total compensation):")
    sorted_expr_df = df.withColumn("total_comp", col("salary") * 1.15) \
        .select("emp_id", "name", "salary", "total_comp") \
        .orderBy(col("total_comp").desc())
    sorted_expr_df.show()
    
    # Example 6: Sort with limit (Top-N pattern)
    print("\n6. Sort with Limit (Top 5 Salaries):")
    top_n_df = df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary") \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc()) \
        .limit(5)
    top_n_df.show()
    
    return sorted_desc_df

# PATTERN 3: PARTITIONED ORDER PATTERN
# ============================================================================
def partitioned_order_pattern(df):
    """
    Partitioned Order Pattern: Order data within partitions/groups
    Uses Window functions for ordering within partitions
    
    Use Case: Ranking, top-N per group, running totals
    Performance: Better than global sort for grouped operations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 3: PARTITIONED ORDER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Row number within partition
    print("\n1. Row Number within Department (ordered by salary):")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    partitioned_df = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("salary_rank")
    )
    partitioned_df.orderBy("department", "salary_rank").show()
    
    # Example 2: Rank and Dense Rank within partition
    print("\n2. Rank vs Dense Rank within Department:")
    rank_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    rank_df = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary",
        rank().over(rank_window).alias("rank"),
        dense_rank().over(rank_window).alias("dense_rank")
    )
    rank_df.orderBy("department", "rank").show()
    
    # Example 3: Top N per partition
    print("\n3. Top 2 Earners per Department:")
    top_per_dept = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("rank")
    ).filter(col("rank") <= 2) \
     .orderBy("department", "rank")
    top_per_dept.show()
    
    # Example 4: Ntile (quartiles) within partition
    print("\n4. Salary Quartiles within Department:")
    ntile_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary"))
    
    quartile_df = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary",
        ntile(4).over(ntile_window).alias("salary_quartile")
    )
    quartile_df.orderBy("department", "salary_quartile", "salary").show()
    
    # Example 5: Multiple partition columns
    print("\n5. Ranking by Multiple Partitions (Department + Level):")
    multi_partition_window = Window.partitionBy("department", "level") \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    multi_partition_df = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "level", "salary",
        row_number().over(multi_partition_window).alias("rank_in_group")
    )
    multi_partition_df.orderBy("department", "level", "rank_in_group").show()
    
    # Example 6: Cumulative operations within partition
    print("\n6. Running Total Salary by Department:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum
    
    running_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("hire_date") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    running_total_df = df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "hire_date", "salary",
        spark_sum("salary").over(running_window).alias("running_total")
    )
    running_total_df.orderBy("department", "hire_date").show()
    
    return partitioned_df

def clustered_order_pattern(df):

    # Sales: order by hire_date asc
    # Marketing: order by level priority
    
    eng_df = df.filter(col("department") == "Engineering") \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    sales_df = df.filter(col("department") == "Sales") \
        .orderBy("hire_date")
    
    marketing_df = df.filter(col("department") == "Marketing") \
        .withColumn(
            "level_priority",
            when(col("level") == "Manager", 1)
            .when(col("level") == "Senior", 2)
            .otherwise(3)
        ).orderBy("level_priority")
    
    conditional_ordered = eng_df.union(sales_df).union(
        marketing_df.drop("level_priority")
    ).select("emp_id", "name", "department", "level", "salary", "hire_date")
    
    conditional_ordered.show()
    
    # Example 6: Custom ordering with UDF
    print("\n6. Custom Ordering using UDF:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
    from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
    
    # Define a complex custom ordering function
    def custom_rank_logic(dept, level, salary):
        """
        Custom ranking logic:
        - Engineering gets bonus points
        - Managers get multiplier
        - Salary contributes to score
        """
        score = salary / 1000
        
        if dept == "Engineering":
            score *= 1.2
        elif dept == "Sales":
            score *= 1.1
        
        if level == "Manager":
            score *= 1.5
        elif level == "Senior":
            score *= 1.2
        
        return int(score)
    
    custom_rank_udf = udf(custom_rank_logic, IntegerType())
    
    udf_ordered_df = df.withColumn(
        "custom_rank",
        custom_rank_udf(col("department"), col("level"), col("salary"))
    ).select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "level", 
        "salary", "custom_rank"
    ).orderBy(col("custom_rank").desc())
    
    udf_ordered_df.show()
    
    # Example 7: Bucketing for custom grouping
    print("\n7. Custom Bucketing Order:")
    # Create salary buckets and order within buckets
    bucket_df = df.withColumn(
        "salary_bucket",
        when(col("salary") >= 100000, "High")
        .when(col("salary") >= 80000, "Medium-High")
        .when(col("salary") >= 60000, "Medium")
        .otherwise("Low")
    ).withColumn(
        "bucket_order",
        when(col("salary_bucket") == "High", 1)
        .when(col("salary_bucket") == "Medium-High", 2)
        .when(col("salary_bucket") == "Medium", 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    ).select(
        "emp_id", "name", "salary", "salary_bucket", "bucket_order"
    ).orderBy("bucket_order", col("salary").desc())
    
    bucket_df.show()
    
    # Example 8: Fuzzy/approximate ordering
    print("\n8. Approximate Ordering (Salary ranges):")
    # Round salary to nearest 5000 for approximate ordering
    from pyspark.sql.functions import round as spark_round
    
    approx_df = df.withColumn(
        "salary_rounded",
        spark_round(col("salary") / 5000) * 5000
    ).select(
        "emp_id", "name", "salary", "salary_rounded"
    ).orderBy(col("salary_rounded").desc(), "name")
    
    approx_df.show()
    
    return weighted_df

# ADVANCED PATTERNS AND COMBINATIONS
# ============================================================================
def advanced_ordering_patterns(sales_df):
    """
    Advanced ordering patterns combining multiple techniques
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED ORDERING PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Partition + Custom Order
    print("\n1. Partitioned with Custom Order (Revenue ranking per category):")
    revenue_df = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    )
    
    category_window = Window.partitionBy("category") \
        .orderBy(col("revenue").desc())
    
    partition_custom = revenue_df.select(
        "sale_id", "category", "product", "revenue",
        row_number().over(category_window).alias("revenue_rank"),
        dense_rank().over(category_window).alias("revenue_dense_rank")
    ).orderBy("category", "revenue_rank")
    
    partition_custom.show()
    
    # Example 2: Clustered + Sorted Pattern
    print("\n2. Clustered by Category, Sorted within Partitions:")
    clustered_sorted = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).repartition("category") \
     .sortWithinPartitions(col("revenue").desc()) \
     .select("sale_id", "category", "product", "revenue")
    
    clustered_sorted.show()
    
    # Example 3: Multi-level aggregation with ordering
    print("\n3. Multi-level Aggregation with Custom Order:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum, avg, count
    
    agg_ordered = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).groupBy("category") \
     .agg(
         spark_sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
         avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
         count("*").alias("num_sales")
     ).withColumn(
         "revenue_tier",
         when(col("total_revenue") >= 2000, "Tier 1")
         .when(col("total_revenue") >= 1000, "Tier 2")
         .otherwise("Tier 3")
     ).orderBy(col("total_revenue").desc())
    
    agg_ordered.show()
    
    # Example 4: Time-based custom ordering
    print("\n4. Time-based Custom Ordering (Recent first, then by revenue):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import to_date
    
    time_ordered = sales_df.withColumn(
        "sale_date_typed",
        to_date(col("sale_date"))
    ).withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).withColumn(
        "days_ago",
        datediff(current_date(), col("sale_date_typed"))
    ).select(
        "sale_id", "sale_date", "product", "revenue", "days_ago"
    ).orderBy("days_ago", col("revenue").desc())
    
    time_ordered.show()
    
    # Example 5: Percentile-based ordering
    print("\n5. Percentile-based Custom Ordering:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import percent_rank
    
    percentile_window = Window.orderBy(col("price"))
    
    percentile_df = sales_df.select(
        "sale_id", "product", "price",
        percent_rank().over(percentile_window).alias("price_percentile")
    ).withColumn(
        "price_category",
        when(col("price_percentile") >= 0.75, "Premium")
        .when(col("price_percentile") >= 0.50, "Mid-range")
        .when(col("price_percentile") >= 0.25, "Budget")
        .otherwise("Economy")
    ).orderBy(col("price_percentile").desc())
    
    percentile_df.show()
    
    return partition_custom

def performance_comparison(df):
    """
    Compare performance characteristics of different ordering patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE COMPARISON")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    import time
    
    # Create a larger dataset for meaningful comparison
    large_df = df.union(df).union(df).union(df).union(df)
    large_df.cache()
    large_df.count()  # Force caching
    
    print(f"\nDataset size: {large_df.count()} records")
    print(f"Number of partitions: {large_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # Test 1: Natural order
    print("\n1. Natural Order Performance:")
    start = time.time()
    natural_result = large_df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary").count()
    natural_time = time.time() - start
    print(f"   Time: {natural_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    # Test 2: Global sort
    print("\n2. Global Sort Performance:")
    start = time.time()
    sorted_result = large_df.orderBy("salary").count()
    sorted_time = time.time() - start
    print(f"   Time: {sorted_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"   Overhead vs Natural: {((sorted_time/natural_time - 1) * 100):.2f}%")
    
    # Test 3: Partitioned order
    print("\n3. Partitioned Order Performance:")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    start = time.time()
    partitioned_result = large_df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("rank")
    ).count()
    partitioned_time = time.time() - start
    print(f"   Time: {partitioned_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"   Overhead vs Natural: {((partitioned_time/natural_time - 1) * 100):.2f}%")
    
    # Test 4: Clustered order
    print("\n4. Clustered Order Performance:")
    start = time.time()
```python
    clustered_result = large_df.repartition("department") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("salary") \
        .count()
    clustered_time = time.time() - start
    print(f"   Time: {clustered_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"   Overhead vs Natural: {((clustered_time/natural_time - 1) * 100):.2f}%")
    
    # Test 5: Custom order with UDF
    print("\n5. Custom Order (with expressions) Performance:")
    start = time.time()
    custom_result = large_df.withColumn(
        "priority",
        when(col("level") == "Manager", 1)
        .when(col("level") == "Senior", 2)
        .otherwise(3)
    ).orderBy("priority", col("salary").desc()).count()
    custom_time = time.time() - start
    print(f"   Time: {custom_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"   Overhead vs Natural: {((custom_time/natural_time - 1) * 100):.2f}%")
    
    # Summary
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 80)
    results = [
        ("Natural Order", natural_time, 1.0),
        ("Global Sort", sorted_time, sorted_time/natural_time),
        ("Partitioned Order", partitioned_time, partitioned_time/natural_time),
        ("Clustered Order", clustered_time, clustered_time/natural_time),
        ("Custom Order", custom_time, custom_time/natural_time)
    ]
    
    print(f"\n{'Pattern':<20} {'Time (s)':<12} {'Relative Speed':<15}")
    print("-" * 50)
    for pattern, time_taken, relative in results:
        print(f"{pattern:<20} {time_taken:<12.4f} {relative:<15.2f}x")
    
    large_df.unpersist()

def best_practices_demo(df):
    """
    Demonstrate best practices for ordering patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("BEST PRACTICES AND RECOMMENDATIONS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Practice 1: Avoid unnecessary sorting
    print("\n1. Avoid Unnecessary Sorting:")
    print("   BAD: Sorting when order doesn't matter")
    print("   df.orderBy('emp_id').filter(col('salary') > 80000)")
    print("\n   GOOD: Filter first, sort only if needed")
    print("   df.filter(col('salary') > 80000)  # No sorting needed")
    
    # Practice 2: Use sortWithinPartitions when possible
    print("\n2. Use sortWithinPartitions for Better Performance:")
    print("   BAD: Global sort when partition-level is sufficient")
    bad_example = df.repartition("department").orderBy("salary")
    
    print("\n   GOOD: Sort within partitions")
    good_example = df.repartition("department").sortWithinPartitions("salary")
    print("   This avoids a full shuffle!")
    
    # Practice 3: Combine operations efficiently
    print("\n3. Combine Filtering and Sorting Efficiently:")
    print("   BAD: Sort then filter")
    print("   df.orderBy('salary').filter(col('salary') > 80000)")
    
    print("\n   GOOD: Filter then sort (smaller dataset to sort)")
    efficient_df = df.filter(col("salary") > 80000).orderBy("salary")
    efficient_df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary").show(5)
    
    # Practice 4: Limit early when possible
    print("\n4. Apply Limit Early (Top-N optimization):")
    print("   GOOD: Use limit with orderBy for Top-N queries")
    top_n = df.orderBy(col("salary").desc()).limit(3)
    print("   Spark optimizes this to avoid sorting all data")
    top_n.select("emp_id", "name", "salary").show()
    
    # Practice 5: Choose appropriate partition count
    print("\n5. Optimize Partition Count for Sorting:")
    print(f"   Current partitions: {df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    print("   For sorting, use partitions = cores * 2-3")
    optimized_df = df.repartition(4).orderBy("salary")
    print(f"   Optimized partitions: {optimized_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # Practice 6: Cache before multiple sorts
    print("\n6. Cache Data Before Multiple Ordering Operations:")
    print("   If you need multiple different orderings:")
    cached_df = df.cache()
    cached_df.count()  # Materialize cache
    
    # Multiple orderings on cached data
    by_salary = cached_df.orderBy("salary").limit(3)
    by_name = cached_df.orderBy("name").limit(3)
    
    print("   First ordering (by salary):")
    by_salary.select("name", "salary").show()
    print("   Second ordering (by name):")
    by_name.select("name", "salary").show()
    
    cached_df.unpersist()
    
    # Practice 7: Use appropriate window frame
    print("\n7. Use Appropriate Window Frames:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum
    
    # Efficient: rows between for running totals
    efficient_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("hire_date") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    running_total = df.withColumn(
        "running_salary_total",
        spark_sum("salary").over(efficient_window)
    ).select("department", "hire_date", "salary", "running_salary_total")
    
    print("   Running total with optimized window frame:")
    running_total.orderBy("department", "hire_date").show(5)

def real_world_use_cases(employees_df, sales_df):
    """
    Demonstrate real-world applications of ordering patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("REAL-WORLD USE CASES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Use Case 1: Employee Performance Dashboard
    print("\n1. Employee Performance Dashboard (Top Performers by Department):")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    performance_dashboard = employees_df.select(
        "name",
        "department",
        "level",
        "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("dept_rank"),
        percent_rank().over(window_spec).alias("percentile")
    ).withColumn(
        "performance_tier",
        when(col("percentile") <= 0.2, "Top 20%")
        .when(col("percentile") <= 0.5, "Top 50%")
        .otherwise("Bottom 50%")
    ).filter(col("dept_rank") <= 3) \
     .orderBy("department", "dept_rank")
    
    performance_dashboard.show()
    
    # Use Case 2: Sales Leaderboard
    print("\n2. Sales Leaderboard (Daily Top Products):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum
    
    sales_leaderboard = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).groupBy("sale_date", "product", "category") \
     .agg(spark_sum("revenue").alias("daily_revenue")) \
     .withColumn(
         "daily_rank",
         row_number().over(
             Window.partitionBy("sale_date").orderBy(col("daily_revenue").desc())
         )
     ).filter(col("daily_rank") <= 5) \
     .orderBy("sale_date", "daily_rank")
    
    sales_leaderboard.show()
    
    # Use Case 3: Inventory Reorder Priority
    print("\n3. Inventory Reorder Priority (Custom Priority Logic):")
    inventory_priority = sales_df.groupBy("category", "product") \
        .agg(
            spark_sum("quantity").alias("total_sold"),
            avg("price").alias("avg_price")
        ).withColumn(
            "revenue_potential",
            col("total_sold") * col("avg_price")
        ).withColumn(
            "category_priority",
            when(col("category") == "Electronics", 1)
            .when(col("category") == "Clothing", 2)
            .otherwise(3)
        ).withColumn(
            "reorder_priority",
            col("category_priority") * 1000 - col("revenue_potential")
        ).select(
            "category",
            "product",
            "total_sold",
            "revenue_potential",
            "reorder_priority"
        ).orderBy("reorder_priority")
    
    inventory_priority.show()
    
    # Use Case 4: Salary Band Analysis
    print("\n4. Salary Band Analysis (Quartiles by Department):")
    salary_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy("salary")
    
    salary_bands = employees_df.select(
        "name",
        "department",
        "level",
        "salary",
        ntile(4).over(salary_window).alias("salary_quartile")
    ).withColumn(
        "band_description",
        when(col("salary_quartile") == 4, "High Earner")
        .when(col("salary_quartile") == 3, "Above Average")
        .when(col("salary_quartile") == 2, "Average")
        .otherwise("Below Average")
    ).orderBy("department", "salary_quartile", col("salary").desc())
    
    salary_bands.show()
    
    # Use Case 5: Time-series Analysis
    print("\n5. Time-series Analysis (Cumulative Sales by Category):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import to_date
    
    time_series = sales_df.withColumn(
        "sale_date_typed",
        to_date(col("sale_date"))
    ).withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).groupBy("sale_date_typed", "category") \
     .agg(spark_sum("revenue").alias("daily_revenue")) \
     .withColumn(
         "cumulative_revenue",
         spark_sum("daily_revenue").over(
             Window.partitionBy("category")
             .orderBy("sale_date_typed")
             .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
         )
     ).orderBy("category", "sale_date_typed")
    
    time_series.show()
    
    # Use Case 6: ABC Analysis (Pareto Principle)
    print("\n6. ABC Analysis (80-20 Rule for Products):")
    abc_analysis = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).groupBy("product") \
     .agg(spark_sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue")) \
     .orderBy(col("total_revenue").desc()) \
     .withColumn(
         "cumulative_revenue",
         spark_sum("total_revenue").over(
             Window.orderBy(col("total_revenue").desc())
             .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
         )
     )
    
    total_revenue = abc_analysis.agg(spark_sum("total_revenue")).collect()[0][0]
    
    abc_final = abc_analysis.withColumn(
        "cumulative_percentage",
        (col("cumulative_revenue") / total_revenue) * 100
    ).withColumn(
        "abc_category",
        when(col("cumulative_percentage") <= 80, "A - High Value")
        .when(col("cumulative_percentage") <= 95, "B - Medium Value")
        .otherwise("C - Low Value")
    ).select("product", "total_revenue", "cumulative_percentage", "abc_category")
    
    abc_final.show()

# OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES
# ============================================================================
def optimization_techniques(df):
    """
    Advanced optimization techniques for ordering operations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Technique 1: Sampling for approximate results
    print("\n1. Sampling for Approximate Top-N:")
    print("   Use sampling when exact order isn't critical")
    sampled_top = df.sample(False, 0.5, seed=42) \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc()) \
        .limit(5)
    
    print("   Approximate top 5 (from 50% sample):")
    sampled_top.select("name", "salary").show()
    
    # Technique 2: Broadcast for small dimension tables
    print("\n2. Broadcast Join with Ordering:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Create a small lookup table
    dept_priority = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("Engineering", 1),
        ("Sales", 2),
        ("Marketing", 3)
    ], ["department", "priority"])
    
    # Broadcast join and order
    broadcast_ordered = df.join(
        broadcast(dept_priority),
        "department"
    ).select(
        "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary", "priority"
    ).orderBy("priority", col("salary").desc())
    
    print("   Ordered with broadcast join:")
    broadcast_ordered.show()
    
    # Technique 3: Predicate pushdown with ordering
    print("\n3. Predicate Pushdown Optimization:")
    # Filter early, then order
    optimized_query = df.filter(
        (col("salary") > 70000) & (col("department") == "Engineering")
    ).orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    print("   Filtered and ordered efficiently:")
    optimized_query.select("name", "department", "salary").show()
    
    # Technique 4: Columnar pruning
    print("\n4. Column Pruning with Ordering:")
    # Select only needed columns before ordering
    pruned_ordered = df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary") \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    print("   Only necessary columns selected:")
    pruned_ordered.show(5)
    
    # Technique 5: Avoid multiple shuffles
    print("\n5. Minimize Shuffles:")
    print("   BAD: Multiple operations causing shuffles")
    print("   df.repartition(4).orderBy('salary').repartition('department')")
    
    print("\n   GOOD: Combine operations to minimize shuffles")
    minimized_shuffle = df.repartition(4, "department") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("salary")
    
    print("   Single shuffle with partition + sort:")
    minimized_shuffle.select("department", "name", "salary").show(5)
    
    # Technique 6: Use explain() to understand execution
    print("\n6. Understanding Execution Plan:")
    print("   Use explain() to see physical plan:")
    print("\n   Physical plan for orderBy:")
    df.orderBy("salary").select("name", "salary").explain()

def print_summary():
    """
    Print comprehensive summary and recommendations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    summary = """
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                    ORDERING PATTERNS COMPARISON                            ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    1. NATURAL ORDER PATTERN
       ├─ Use Case: Data exploration, when order doesn't matter
       ├─ Performance: ★★★★★ (Fastest - no overhead)
       ├─ Complexity: ★☆☆☆☆ (Simplest)
       └─ Recommendation: Default choice when ordering is not required
    
    2. SORTED ORDER PATTERN
       ├─ Use Case: Reports, exports, user-facing results
       ├─ Performance: ★★☆☆☆ (Requires full shuffle)
       ├─ Complexity: ★★☆☆☆ (Simple API)
       ├─ Methods: orderBy(), sort(), asc(), desc()
       └─ Recommendation: Use only when global ordering is necessary
    
    3. PARTITIONED ORDER PATTERN
       ├─ Use Case: Rankings, top-N per group, running totals
       ├─ Performance: ★★★★☆ (Better than global sort)
       ├─ Complexity: ★★★☆☆ (Requires window functions)
       ├─ Methods: Window.partitionBy(), row_number(), rank()
       └─ Recommendation: Preferred for group-wise operations
    
    4. CLUSTERED ORDER PATTERN
       ├─ Use Case: Optimize for repeated queries on same keys
       ├─ Performance: ★★★★☆ (Good for subsequent operations)
       ├─ Complexity: ★★★☆☆ (Requires understanding of partitioning)
       ├─ Methods: repartition(), coalesce(), sortWithinPartitions()
       └─ Recommendation: Use for data organization and query optimization
    
    5. CUSTOM ORDER PATTERN
       ├─ Use Case: Complex business logic, priority-based ordering
       ├─ Performance: ★★★☆☆ (Depends on complexity)
       ├─ Complexity: ★★★★☆ (Most complex)
       ├─ Methods: when(), UDFs, custom expressions
       └─ Recommendation: Use when standard ordering isn't sufficient
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                        DECISION TREE                                       ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    Does order matter?
    │
    ├─ NO → Use NATURAL ORDER (fastest)
    │
    └─ YES → Need ordering within groups?
           │
           ├─ YES → Use PARTITIONED ORDER (Window functions)
           │        Example: Top 5 per department
           │
           └─ NO → Need global ordering?
                  │
                  ├─ YES → Simple sort criteria?
                  │        │
                  │        ├─ YES → Use SORTED ORDER (orderBy)
                  │        │
                  │        └─ NO → Use CUSTOM ORDER (complex logic)
                  │
                  └─ NO → Optimizing for queries?
                          │
                          └─ Use CLUSTERED ORDER (repartition)
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                     PERFORMANCE TIPS                                       ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ✓ Filter before sorting (reduce data volume)
    ✓ Use sortWithinPartitions instead of orderBy when possible
    ✓ Apply limit() with orderBy() for Top-N queries
    ✓ Cache data if multiple different orderings are needed
    ✓ Use appropriate partition count (cores × 2-3)
    ✓ Avoid sorting in loops or repeated operations
    ✓ Consider sampling for approximate results
    ✓ Use columnar pruning (select only needed columns)
    ✓ Leverage predicate pushdown
    ✓ Monitor shuffle operations with explain()
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                     COMMON PITFALLS                                        ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ✗ Sorting large datasets unnecessarily
    ✗ Multiple orderBy() calls (only last one applies)
    ✗ Sorting before filtering (sort smaller datasets)
    ✗ Using UDFs in order expressions (performance hit)
    ✗ Ignoring partition count (too many or too few)
    ✗ Not caching when doing multiple orderings
    ✗ Sorting in the middle of transformation chains
    ✗ Over-partitioning small datasets
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                  PATTERN SELECTION GUIDE                                   ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    Scenario                              | Recommended Pattern
    ─────────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────
    Data exploration                      | Natural Order
    Generating reports                    | Sorted Order
    Top N per category                    | Partitioned Order (Window)
    Running totals by group               | Partitioned Order (Window)
    Leaderboards                          | Partitioned Order + Custom
    Data organization for queries         | Clustered Order
    Priority-based processing             | Custom Order
    Time-series analysis                  | Sorted/Partitioned Order
    Percentile calculations               | Partitioned Order (Window)
    ABC analysis                          | Sorted Order + Window
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                     CODE EXAMPLES RECAP                                    ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    # Natural Order
    df.select("col1", "col2")
    
    # Sorted Order
    df.orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    df.orderBy("dept", col("salary").desc())
    
    # Partitioned Order
    window = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window))
    
    # Clustered Order
    df.repartition("dept").sortWithinPartitions("salary")
    
    # Custom Order
    df.withColumn("priority", 
        when(col("level") == "Manager", 1).otherwise(2)
    ).orderBy("priority", col("salary").desc())
    
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                     ADDITIONAL RESOURCES                                   ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    • PySpark SQL Functions: pyspark.sql.functions
    • Window Functions: pyspark.sql.window.Window
    • DataFrame API: pyspark.sql.DataFrame
    • Performance Tuning: spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-performance-tuning.html
    • Best Practices: databricks.com/blog/best-practices
    
    """
    
    print(summary)

def create_visualization_data(df):
    """
    Create data suitable for visualization of ordering patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("VISUALIZATION DATA EXPORT")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Export different orderings for visualization
    viz_data = {
        "natural_order": df.select("emp_id", "name", "salary").limit(10),
        "sorted_order": df.orderBy(col("salary").desc()).select("emp_id", "name", "salary").limit(10),
        "partitioned_order": df.select(
            "emp_id", "name", "department", "salary",
            row_number().over(
                Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
            ).alias("rank")
        ).filter(col("rank") <= 3)
    }
    
    print("\nVisualization datasets created:")
    for name, data in viz_data.items():
        print(f"  - {name}: {data.count()} records")
    
    return viz_data

def export_results(df, path, format="parquet"):
    """
    Export ordered results to file system
    """
    try:
        if format == "parquet":
            df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(path)
        elif format == "csv":
            df.write.mode("overwrite").option("header", "true").csv(path)
        elif format == "json":
            df.write.mode("overwrite").json(path)
        
        print(f"Results exported to {path} in {format} format")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Export failed: {str(e)}")

def analyze_ordering_impact(df):
    """
    Analyze the impact of different ordering strategies
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING IMPACT ANALYSIS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Analyze partition distribution
    print("\n1. Partition Distribution Analysis:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import spark_partition_id
    
    partition_stats = df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .groupBy("partition_id") \
        .count() \
        .orderBy("partition_id")
    
    print("   Records per partition (before repartitioning):")
    partition_stats.show()
    
    # Analyze after clustering
    clustered = df.repartition(3, "department") \
        .withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id())
    
    clustered_stats = clustered.groupBy("partition_id", "department") \
        .count() \
        .orderBy("partition_id", "department")
    
    print("\n   Records per partition after clustering by department:")
    clustered_stats.show()
    
    # Analyze data skew
    print("\n2. Data Skew Analysis:")
    dept_counts = df.groupBy("department").count().orderBy("department")
    print("   Records per department:")
    dept_counts.show()
    
    # Calculate skew factor
    from pyspark.sql.functions import max as spark_max, min as spark_min
    skew_stats = dept_counts.agg(
        spark_max("count").alias("max_count"),
        spark_min("count").alias("min_count")
    ).collect()[0]
    
    skew_factor = skew_stats["max_count"] / skew_stats["min_count"] if skew_stats["min_count"] > 0 else 0
    print(f"\n   Skew Factor: {skew_factor:.2f}")
    print(f"   (1.0 = perfectly balanced, >2.0 = significant skew)")
