# TESTING AND VALIDATION
# ============================================================================
def validate_ordering_patterns(df):
    """
    Validate that ordering patterns work correctly
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING PATTERN VALIDATION")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Test 1: Verify sorted order
    print("\n1. Validating Sorted Order:")
    sorted_df = df.orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    salaries = [row.salary for row in sorted_df.select("salary").collect()]
    is_sorted = all(salaries[i] >= salaries[i+1] for i in range(len(salaries)-1))
    print(f"   Descending order verified: {is_sorted} ✓" if is_sorted else "   Descending order verified: {is_sorted} ✗")
    
    # Test 2: Verify partitioned order
    print("\n2. Validating Partitioned Order:")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    partitioned_df = df.select(
        "department", "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("rank")
    ).collect()
    
    # Group by department and check ordering
    from itertools import groupby
    partitioned_df.sort(key=lambda x: (x.department, x.rank))
    
    valid_partition_order = True
    for dept, group in groupby(partitioned_df, key=lambda x: x.department):
        salaries = [row.salary for row in group]
        if not all(salaries[i] >= salaries[i+1] for i in range(len(salaries)-1)):
            valid_partition_order = False
            break
    
    print(f"   Partitioned order verified: {valid_partition_order} ✓" if valid_partition_order else "   Partitioned order verified: {valid_partition_order} ✗")
    
    # Test 3: Verify rank consistency
    print("\n3. Validating Rank Functions:")
    rank_df = df.select(
        "salary",
        rank().over(Window.orderBy(col("salary").desc())).alias("rank"),
        dense_rank().over(Window.orderBy(col("salary").desc())).alias("dense_rank"),
        row_number().over(Window.orderBy(col("salary").desc())).alias("row_num")
    ).collect()
    
    # Verify row_number is sequential
    row_nums = [row.row_num for row in rank_df]
    is_sequential = row_nums == list(range(1, len(row_nums) + 1))
    print(f"   Row numbers sequential: {is_sequential} ✓" if is_sequential else "   Row numbers sequential: {is_sequential} ✗")
    
    # Test 4: Verify custom order logic
    print("\n4. Validating Custom Order:")
    custom_df = df.withColumn(
        "priority",
        when(col("level") == "Manager", 1)
        .when(col("level") == "Senior", 2)
        .when(col("level") == "Junior", 3)
        .otherwise(4)
    ).orderBy("priority").collect()
    
    priorities = [row.priority for row in custom_df]
    is_custom_sorted = all(priorities[i] <= priorities[i+1] for i in range(len(priorities)-1))
    print(f"   Custom priority order verified: {is_custom_sorted} ✓" if is_custom_sorted else "   Custom priority order verified: {is_custom_sorted} ✗")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("VALIDATION COMPLETE")
    print("=" * 80)

def advanced_window_examples(df):
    """
    Advanced window function examples with ordering
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED WINDOW FUNCTION EXAMPLES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Example 1: Lead and Lag
    print("\n1. Lead and Lag Functions (Salary Comparison):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lead, lag
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy("salary")
    
    lead_lag_df = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        lag("salary", 1).over(window_spec).alias("prev_salary"),
        lead("salary", 1).over(window_spec).alias("next_salary")
    ).withColumn(
        "diff_from_prev",
        when(col("prev_salary").isNotNull(), 
             col("salary") - col("prev_salary")).otherwise(None)
    ).orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    lead_lag_df.show()
    
    # Example 2: Moving Average
    print("\n2. Moving Average (3-person salary window):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import avg
    
    moving_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("salary") \
        .rowsBetween(-1, 1)  # Previous, current, and next row
    
    moving_avg_df = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        avg("salary").over(moving_window).alias("moving_avg_salary")
    ).withColumn(
        "moving_avg_salary",
        col("moving_avg_salary").cast("int")
    ).orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    moving_avg_df.show()
    
    # Example 3: First and Last Value
    print("\n3. First and Last Value in Partition:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import first, last
    
    first_last_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("salary") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.unboundedFollowing)
    
    first_last_df = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        first("salary").over(first_last_window).alias("min_dept_salary"),
        last("salary").over(first_last_window).alias("max_dept_salary")
    ).withColumn(
        "salary_range",
        col("max_dept_salary") - col("min_dept_salary")
    ).orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    first_last_df.show()
    
    # Example 4: Cumulative Distribution
    print("\n4. Cumulative Distribution Function:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import cume_dist
    
    cume_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy("salary")
    
    cume_dist_df = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        cume_dist().over(cume_window).alias("cumulative_dist"),
        percent_rank().over(cume_window).alias("percent_rank")
    ).withColumn(
        "cumulative_dist",
        (col("cumulative_dist") * 100).cast("int")
    ).withColumn(
        "percent_rank",
        (col("percent_rank") * 100).cast("int")
    ).orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    cume_dist_df.show()
    
    # Example 5: Range Between (Salary Range)
    print("\n5. Range Between (Employees within $10k salary range):")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import count
    
    range_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("salary") \
        .rangeBetween(-10000, 10000)
    
    range_df = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        count("*").over(range_window).alias("peers_in_range")
    ).orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    range_df.show()

def edge_cases_and_special_scenarios(spark):
    """
    Handle edge cases and special scenarios in ordering
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("EDGE CASES AND SPECIAL SCENARIOS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Edge Case 1: Empty DataFrame
    print("\n1. Ordering Empty DataFrame:")
    empty_schema = StructType([
        StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("value", StringType(), True)
    ])
    empty_df = spark.createDataFrame([], empty_schema)
    ordered_empty = empty_df.orderBy("id")
    print(f"   Empty DataFrame count after ordering: {ordered_empty.count()}")
    
    # Edge Case 2: All Null Values
    print("\n2. Ordering with All Null Values:")
    null_data = [(1, None), (2, None), (3, None)]
    null_df = spark.createDataFrame(null_data, ["id", "value"])
    
    print("   Nulls First:")
    null_df.orderBy(col("value").asc_nulls_first(), "id").show()
    
    print("   Nulls Last:")
    null_df.orderBy(col("value").asc_nulls_last(), "id").show()
    
    # Edge Case 3: Duplicate Values
    print("\n3. Ordering with Many Duplicates:")
    duplicate_data = [
        (1, "A", 100),
        (2, "A", 100),
        (3, "A", 100),
        (4, "B", 200),
        (5, "B", 200),
    ]
    dup_df = spark.createDataFrame(duplicate_data, ["id", "category", "value"])
    
    print("   Using rank (gaps in sequence):")
    dup_df.select(
        "id", "category", "value",
        rank().over(Window.orderBy("value")).alias("rank")
    ).show()
    
    print("   Using dense_rank (no gaps):")
    dup_df.select(
        "id", "category", "value",
        dense_rank().over(Window.orderBy("value")).alias("dense_rank")
    ).show()
    
    # Edge Case 4: Very Large Number of Partitions
    print("\n4. Handling Many Partitions:")
    large_partition_df = dup_df.repartition(100)
    print(f"   Partitions before coalesce: {large_partition_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    coalesced = large_partition_df.coalesce(4)
    print(f"   Partitions after coalesce: {coalesced.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # Edge Case 5: Mixed Data Types (Strings with Numbers)
    print("\n5. Ordering Mixed String/Numeric Data:")
    mixed_data = [
        (1, "10"),
        (2, "2"),
        (3, "100"),
        (4, "20"),
        (5, "3"),
    ]
    mixed_df = spark.createDataFrame(mixed_data, ["id", "str_value"])
    
    print("   String ordering (lexicographic):")
    mixed_df.orderBy("str_value").show()
    
    print("   Numeric ordering (cast to int):")
    mixed_df.orderBy(col("str_value").cast("int")).show()
    
    # Edge Case 6: Unicode and Special Characters
    print("\n6. Ordering with Unicode Characters:")
    unicode_data = [
        (1, "Zebra"),
        (2, "Äpfel"),
        (3, "Banana"),
        (4, "Ñoño"),
        (5, "Apple"),
    ]
    unicode_df = spark.createDataFrame(unicode_data, ["id", "name"])
    
    print("   Default ordering:")
    unicode_df.orderBy("name").show()
    
    print("   Case-insensitive ordering:")
    unicode_df.orderBy(lower(col("name"))).show()

# COMPARISON WITH SQL
# ============================================================================
def sql_vs_dataframe_ordering(spark, df):
    """
    Compare SQL and DataFrame API for ordering
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("SQL vs DATAFRAME API COMPARISON")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Register DataFrame as temp view
    df.createOrReplaceTempView("employees")
    
    # Example 1: Simple ORDER BY
    print("\n1. Simple ORDER BY:")
    print("\n   SQL:")
    print("   SELECT name, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC")
    sql_result1 = spark.sql("""
        SELECT name, salary 
        FROM employees 
        ORDER BY salary DESC
    """)
    sql_result1.show(5)
    
    print("\n   DataFrame API:")
    print("   df.select('name', 'salary').orderBy(col('salary').desc())")
    df_result1 = df.select("name", "salary").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    df_result1.show(5)
    
    # Example 2: Window Functions
    print("\n2. Window Functions (Rank):")
    print("\n   SQL:")
    sql_query = """
        SELECT name, department, salary,
               RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) as rank
        FROM employees
    """
    print(f"   {sql_query}")
    sql_result2 = spark.sql(sql_query)
    sql_result2.orderBy("department", "rank").show()
    
    print("\n   DataFrame API:")
    print("   df.withColumn('rank', rank().over(Window.partitionBy('department').orderBy(col('salary').desc())))")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    df_result2 = df.select(
        "name", "department", "salary",
        rank().over(window_spec).alias("rank")
    )
    df_result2.orderBy("department", "rank").show()
    
    # Example 3: Complex ORDER BY
    print("\n3. Multi-Column Ordering:")
    print("\n   SQL:")
    sql_query3 = """
        SELECT name, department, level, salary
        FROM employees
        ORDER BY department ASC, level DESC, salary DESC
    """
    print(f"   {sql_query3}")
    sql_result3 = spark.sql(sql_query3)
    sql_result3.show()
    
    print("\n   DataFrame API:")
    print("   df.orderBy('department', col('level').desc(), col('salary').desc())")
    df_result3 = df.select("name", "department", "level", "salary") \
        .orderBy("department", col("level").desc(), col("salary").desc())
    df_result3.show()

    print(f"Partitions: {large_df.rd
```python
    print(f"Partitions: {large_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    benchmarks = []

    benchmarks.append(("Multi-Column Sort", time3, time3/time1))
    print(f"   Time: {time3:.4f}s (Overhead: {((time3/time1-1)*100):.2f}%)")
    
    # Benchmark 4: Window function (partitioned)
    print("\n4. Window Function (Partitioned):")
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    start = time.time()
    result4 = large_df.select(
        "emp_id", "name", "salary",
        row_number().over(window_spec).alias("rank")
    ).count()
    time4 = time.time() - start
    benchmarks.append(("Window Function", time4, time4/time1))
    print(f"   Time: {time4:.4f}s (Overhead: {((time4/time1-1)*100):.2f}%)")
    
    # Benchmark 5: Repartition + sort within partitions
    print("\n5. Repartition + Sort Within Partitions:")
    start = time.time()
    result5 = large_df.repartition("department") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("salary") \
        .count()
    time5 = time.time() - start
    benchmarks.append(("Repartition + Sort Within", time5, time5/time1))
    print(f"   Time: {time5:.4f}s (Overhead: {((time5/time1-1)*100):.2f}%)")
    
    # Benchmark 6: Filter then sort (optimized)
    print("\n6. Filter Then Sort (Optimized):")
    start = time.time()
    result6 = large_df.filter(col("salary") > 80000) \
        .orderBy(col("salary").desc()) \
        .count()
    time6 = time.time() - start
    benchmarks.append(("Filter Then Sort", time6, time6/time1))
    print(f"   Time: {time6:.4f}s (Overhead: {((time6/time1-1)*100):.2f}%)")
    
    # Benchmark 7: Sort with limit (Top-N)
    print("\n7. Sort with Limit (Top 100):")
    start = time.time()
    result7 = large_df.orderBy(col("salary").desc()).limit(100).count()
    time7 = time.time() - start
    benchmarks.append(("Sort with Limit", time7, time7/time1))
    print(f"   Time: {time7:.4f}s (Overhead: {((time7/time1-1)*100):.2f}%)")
    
    # Print summary table
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("BENCHMARK SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 80)
    print(f"\n{'Operation':<30} {'Time (s)':<12} {'Relative':<12} {'Overhead':<12}")
    print("-" * 80)
    for name, time_taken, relative in benchmarks:
        overhead = f"{((relative-1)*100):.2f}%" if relative > 1 else "N/A"
        print(f"{name:<30} {time_taken:<12.4f} {relative:<12.2f}x {overhead:<12}")
    
    large_df.unpersist()
    
    return benchmarks

# FINAL COMPREHENSIVE EXAMPLE
# ============================================================================
def comprehensive_example(employees_df, sales_df):
    """
    Comprehensive example combining multiple ordering patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE")
    print("Employee Performance & Sales Analysis Dashboard")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import sum as spark_sum, avg, count, max as spark_max
    
    # Step 1: Calculate employee metrics with partitioned ordering
    print("\n1. Employee Performance Metrics:")
    emp_window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    
    emp_metrics = employees_df.select(
        "emp_id",
        "name",
        "department",
        "level",
        "salary",
        "hire_date",
        row_number().over(emp_window).alias("dept_rank"),
        percent_rank().over(emp_window).alias("salary_percentile"),
        ntile(4).over(emp_window).alias("salary_quartile")
    ).withColumn(
        "performance_tier",
        when(col("salary_percentile") <= 0.25, "Top Performer")
        .when(col("salary_percentile") <= 0.50, "High Performer")
        .when(col("salary_percentile") <= 0.75, "Average Performer")
        .otherwise("Needs Improvement")
    )
    
    print("\n   Top 2 performers per department:")
    emp_metrics.filter(col("dept_rank") <= 2) \
        .orderBy("department", "dept_rank") \
        .select("name", "department", "salary", "dept_rank", "performance_tier") \
        .show()
    
    # Step 2: Sales analysis with custom ordering
    print("\n2. Sales Performance Analysis:")
    sales_metrics = sales_df.withColumn(
        "revenue",
        col("price") * col("quantity")
    ).groupBy("category", "product") \
     .agg(
         spark_sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
         spark_sum("quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
         avg("price").alias("avg_price"),
         count("*").alias("num_transactions")
     ).withColumn(
         "category_priority",
         when(col("category") == "Electronics", 1)
         .when(col("category") == "Clothing", 2)
         .otherwise(3)
     )
    
    # Rank products within categories
    category_window = Window.partitionBy("category") \
        .orderBy(col("total_revenue").desc())
    
    sales_ranked = sales_metrics.select(
        "category",
        "product",
        "total_revenue",
        "total_quantity",
        "num_transactions",
        row_number().over(category_window).alias("category_rank")
    )
    
    print("\n   Top product per category:")
    sales_ranked.filter(col("category_rank") == 1) \
        .orderBy("category") \
        .show()
    
    # Step 3: Combined analysis with multiple ordering patterns
    print("\n3. Combined Department Performance:")
    
    # Department aggregations
    dept_performance = employees_df.groupBy("department") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("emp_count"),
            avg("salary").alias("avg_salary"),
            spark_max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
            spark_sum("salary").alias("total_payroll")
        ).withColumn(
            "avg_salary_rounded",
            col("avg_salary").cast("int")
        )
    
    # Custom ordering by multiple criteria
    dept_ordered = dept_performance.withColumn(
        "priority_score",
        col("emp_count") * 10 + col("avg_salary") / 1000
    ).select(
        "department",
        "emp_count",
        "avg_salary_rounded",
        "max_salary",
        "total_payroll",
        "priority_score"
    ).orderBy(col("priority_score").desc())
    
    print("\n   Department rankings by priority score:")
    dept_ordered.show()
    
    # Step 4: Time-based analysis with clustered ordering
    print("\n4. Tenure-based Analysis:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import datediff, current_date, to_date
    
    tenure_analysis = employees_df.withColumn(
        "hire_date_typed",
        to_date(col("hire_date"))
    ).withColumn(
        "days_tenure",
        datediff(current_date(), col("hire_date_typed"))
    ).withColumn(
        "years_tenure",
        (col("days_tenure") / 365).cast("int")
    ).withColumn(
        "tenure_band",
        when(col("years_tenure") >= 5, "Veteran (5+ years)")
        .when(col("years_tenure") >= 3, "Experienced (3-5 years)")
        .when(col("years_tenure") >= 1, "Intermediate (1-3 years)")
        .otherwise("New (<1 year)")
    )
    
    # Cluster by tenure band and sort within
    tenure_ordered = tenure_analysis.repartition("tenure_band") \
        .sortWithinPartitions(col("years_tenure").desc()) \
        .select(
            "name",
            "department",
            "years_tenure",
            "tenure_band",
            "salary"
        )
    
    print("\n   Employees by tenure:")
    tenure_ordered.orderBy(col("years_tenure").desc()).show()
    
    # Step 5: Final comprehensive report
    print("\n5. Executive Summary Report:")
    
    # Combine all metrics
    exec_summary = employees_df.join(
        dept_performance,
        "department"
    ).select(
        "name",
        "department",
        "level",
        "salary",
        "emp_count",
        "avg_salary_rounded"
    ).withColumn(
        "salary_vs_dept_avg",
        ((col("salary") / col("avg_salary_rounded") - 1) * 100).cast("int")
    ).withColumn(
        "level_priority",
        when(col("level") == "Manager", 1)
        .when(col("level") == "Senior", 2)
        .otherwise(3)
    ).orderBy(
        "department",
        "level_priority",
        col("salary").desc()
    )
    
    print("\n   Complete employee ranking:")
    exec_summary.select(
        "name",
        "department",
        "level",
        "salary",
        "salary_vs_dept_avg"
    ).show(15)
    
    return emp_metrics, sales_ranked, dept_ordered

def safe_execute(func, *args, **kwargs):
    """

    """
    try:
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"\n❌ Error in {func.__name__}: {str(e)}")
        import traceback
        traceback.print_exc()
        return None

This comprehensive PySpark program demonstrates all 5 query result ordering patterns with:

## **Key Features:**

1. **Natural Order Pattern** - Default ordering without explicit sorting
2. **Sorted Order Pattern** - Global ordering with `orderBy(
```python
)`
3. **Partitioned Order Pattern** - Window functions for group-wise ordering
4. **Clustered Order Pattern** - Physical data organization with `repartition()`
5. **Custom Order Pattern** - Complex business logic ordering

## **Quick Reference Guide:**

```python
# ============================================================================
# QUICK REFERENCE - COPY & PASTE EXAMPLES
# ============================================================================

# 1. NATURAL ORDER (No sorting - fastest)
df.select("col1", "col2", "col3")

# 2. SORTED ORDER (Global sort)
# Single column ascending
df.orderBy("salary")

# Single column descending
df.orderBy(col("salary").desc())

# Multiple columns
df.orderBy("department", col("salary").desc())

# With null handling
df.orderBy(col("salary").asc_nulls_last())

# 3. PARTITIONED ORDER (Window functions)
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Rank within partition
window = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window))

# Top N per group
df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window)) \
  .filter(col("rank") <= 3)

# Running total
window_running = Window.partitionBy("dept") \
    .orderBy("date") \
    .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
df.withColumn("running_total", sum("amount").over(window_running))

# 4. CLUSTERED ORDER (Physical organization)
# Cluster by column
df.repartition("department")

# Cluster and sort within partitions
df.repartition("department").sortWithinPartitions("salary")

# Range partitioning
df.repartitionByRange(10, "salary")

# Reduce partitions (maintains locality)
df.repartition(100, "key").coalesce(10)

# 5. CUSTOM ORDER (Complex logic)
# Priority-based ordering
df.withColumn("priority",
    when(col("level") == "Manager", 1)
    .when(col("level") == "Senior", 2)
    .otherwise(3)
).orderBy("priority", col("salary").desc())

# Weighted score
df.withColumn("score",
    col("metric1") * 0.4 + col("metric2") * 0.6
).orderBy(col("score").desc())

# Conditional ordering per group
high_priority = df.filter(col("priority") == "high").orderBy("date")
low_priority = df.filter(col("priority") == "low").orderBy("amount")
result = high_priority.union(low_priority)
```

## **Pattern Selection Decision Tree:**

```python
def select_ordering_pattern(requirements):
    """
    Helper function to select appropriate ordering pattern
    
    Usage:
        pattern = select_ordering_pattern({
            'needs_order': True,
            'grouped': True,
            'complex_logic': False,
            'optimize_queries': False
        })
    """
    if not requirements.get('needs_order', False):
        return "NATURAL_ORDER"
    
    if requirements.get('grouped', False):
        return "PARTITIONED_ORDER"
    
    if requirements.get('optimize_queries', False):
        return "CLUSTERED_ORDER"
    
    if requirements.get('complex_logic', False):
        return "CUSTOM_ORDER"
    
    return "SORTED_ORDER"

# Example usage
pattern = select_ordering_pattern({
    'needs_order': True,
    'grouped': True,
    'complex_logic': False,
    'optimize_queries': False
})
print(f"Recommended pattern: {pattern}")
# Output: Recommended pattern: PARTITIONED_ORDER
```

## **Common Pitfalls to Avoid:**

```python
# ============================================================================
# ANTI-PATTERNS (DON'T DO THIS)
# ============================================================================

# ❌ BAD: Multiple orderBy calls (only last one applies)
df.orderBy("col1").orderBy("col2")  # Only col2 ordering applies!

# ✓ GOOD: Single orderBy with multiple columns
df.orderBy("col1", "col2")

# ❌ BAD: Sorting before filtering
df.orderBy("salary").filter(col("salary") > 80000)

# ✓ GOOD: Filter first, then sort
df.filter(col("salary") > 80000).orderBy("salary")

# ❌ BAD: Global sort when partition sort is sufficient
df.orderBy("category", "amount")  # Full shuffle

# ✓ GOOD: Partition and sort within
df.repartition("category").sortWithinPartitions("amount")

# ❌ BAD: Sorting in loops
for category in categories:
    df.filter(col("category") == category).orderBy("amount").show()

# ✓ GOOD: Use window functions
window = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy("amount")
df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window)).show()

# ❌ BAD: Not caching when doing multiple sorts
df.orderBy("col1").show()
df.orderBy("col2").show()
df.orderBy("col3").show()

# ✓ GOOD: Cache first
df.cache()
df.orderBy("col1").show()
df.orderBy("col2").show()
df.orderBy("col3").show()
df.unpersist()

# ❌ BAD: UDF in order expression (slow)
custom_sort_udf = udf(lambda x: complex_logic(x), IntegerType())
df.orderBy(custom_sort_udf("col"))

# ✓ GOOD: Use built-in functions
df.withColumn("sort_key", 
    when(col("col") == "A", 1).otherwise(2)
).orderBy("sort_key")
```

## **Performance Tips:**

```python
# ============================================================================
# PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION TIPS
# ============================================================================

# TIP 1: Use limit with orderBy for Top-N
# Spark optimizes this to avoid sorting all data
top_10 = df.orderBy(col("revenue").desc()).limit(10)

# TIP 2: Partition count should match cluster resources
# Rule of thumb: partitions = cores × 2 or 3
df.repartition(spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism * 2)

# TIP 3: Use broadcast for small dimension tables
from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
large_df.join(broadcast(small_df), "key")

# TIP 4: Coalesce instead of repartition when reducing partitions
df.repartition(100).coalesce(10)  # No shuffle for coalesce

# TIP 5: Use explain() to understand execution plan
df.orderBy("col").explain()
df.orderBy("col").explain("formatted")  # More detailed

# TIP 6: Monitor shuffle operations
df.orderBy("col").explain()  # Look for "Exchange" operations

# TIP 7: Cache strategically
expensive_df = df.join(other_df, "key").filter(complex_condition)
expensive_df.cache()
expensive_df.count()  # Materialize cache

# Use multiple times
result1 = expensive_df.orderBy("col1")
result2 = expensive_df.orderBy("col2")

expensive_df.unpersist()

# TIP 8: Use sampling for approximate results
# 10% sample for quick analysis
df.sample(False, 0.1).orderBy("col").show()

# TIP 9: Predicate pushdown with Parquet/ORC
# Filter is pushed to storage layer
df.read.parquet("path").filter(col("date") == "2023-01-01").orderBy("time")

# TIP 10: Avoid wide transformations before narrow ones
# Wide transformation (shuffle): orderBy, groupBy, join
# Narrow transformation (no shuffle): select, filter, withColumn

# ✓ GOOD: Narrow then wide
df.filter(condition).select(cols).orderBy("col")

# ❌ BAD: Wide then narrow (sorts more data)
df.orderBy("col").filter(condition).select(cols)
```

## **Testing and Validation:**

```python
# ============================================================================
# UNIT TESTS FOR ORDERING PATTERNS
# ============================================================================

def test_ordering_patterns():
    """
    Unit tests for validating ordering patterns
    """
    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("OrderingTests").getOrCreate()
    
    # Test data
    test_data = [
        (1, "A", 100),
        (2, "B", 200),
        (3, "A", 150),
        (4, "B", 250),
        (5, "A", 120),
    ]
    df = spark.createDataFrame(test_data, ["id", "category", "value"])
    
    # Test 1: Sorted order
    sorted_df = df.orderBy(col("value").desc())
    sorted_values = [row.value for row in sorted_df.collect()]
    assert sorted_values == [250, 200, 150, 120, 100], "Sort order incorrect"
    print("✓ Test 1 passed: Sorted order")
    
    # Test 2: Partitioned order
    window = Window.partitionBy("category").orderBy(col("value").desc())
    partitioned_df = df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window))
    
    category_a = partitioned_df.filter(col("category") == "A") \
        .orderBy("rank").select("value").collect()
    assert [r.value for r in category_a] == [150, 120, 100], "Partition order incorrect"
    print("✓ Test 2 passed: Partitioned order")
    
    # Test 3: Custom order
    custom_df = df.withColumn("priority",
        when(col("category") == "A", 1).otherwise(2)
    ).orderBy("priority", col("value").desc())
    
    first_row = custom_df.first()
    assert first_row.category == "A", "Custom order incorrect"
    print("✓ Test 3 passed: Custom order")
    
    # Test 4: Null handling
    null_data = [(1, None), (2, 100), (3, None), (4, 200)]
    null_df = spark.createDataFrame(null_data, ["id", "value"])
    
    nulls_last = null_df.orderBy(col("value").asc_nulls_last()).collect()
    assert nulls_last[-1].value is None, "Nulls last failed"
    print("✓ Test 4 passed: Null handling")
    
    print("\n✓ All tests passed!")
    
    spark.stop()

# Run tests
# test_ordering_patterns()
```

    customer_segments.show()
    
    # 4. Daily trends (Clustered Order)
    print("\n4. DAILY SALES TRENDS:")
    daily_sales = orders_df.repartition("order_date") \
        .groupBy("order_date") \
        .agg(
            spark_sum("amount").alias("daily_revenue"),
            count("*").alias("
```python
            count("*").alias("num_orders")

        .withColumn("cumulative_revenue",
            spark_sum("daily_revenue").over(
                Window.orderBy("order_date")
                .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
            )

    daily_sales.show()
    
    # 5. Shipping method analysis (Multi-pattern combination)
    print("\n5. SHIPPING METHOD PERFORMANCE:")
    shipping_window = Window.partitionBy("shipping") \
        .orderBy(col("amount").desc())
    
    shipping_analysis = orders_df.select(
        "order_id",
        "shipping",
        "amount",
        "category",
        row_number().over(shipping_window).alias("rank_in_shipping")
    ).withColumn("shipping_priority",
        when(col("shipping") == "Express", 1)
        .when(col("shipping") == "Premium", 2)
        .otherwise(3)
    ).orderBy("shipping_priority", "rank_in_shipping")
    
    shipping_analysis.filter(col("rank_in_shipping") <= 2).show()
    
    # 6. Revenue contribution analysis (Pareto/ABC)
    print("\n6. REVENUE CONTRIBUTION (ABC ANALYSIS):")
    product_revenue = orders_df.groupBy("category") \
        .agg(spark_sum("amount").alias("category_revenue")) \
        .orderBy(col("category_revenue").desc()) \
        .withColumn("cumulative_revenue",
            spark_sum("category_revenue").over(
                Window.orderBy(col("category_revenue").desc())
                .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
            )
        )
    
    total_rev = product_revenue.agg(spark_sum("category_revenue")).collect()[0][0]
    
    abc_analysis = product_revenue.withColumn(
        "revenue_percentage",
        (col("category_revenue") / total_rev * 100).cast("decimal(5,2)")
    ).withColumn(
        "cumulative_percentage",
        (col("cumulative_revenue") / total_rev * 100).cast("decimal(5,2)")
    ).withColumn("abc_class",
        when(col("cumulative_percentage") <= 80, "A")
        .when(col("cumulative_percentage") <= 95, "B")
        .otherwise("C")
    )
    
    abc_analysis.show()
    
    # 7. Customer purchase patterns (Advanced window)
    print("\n7. CUSTOMER PURCHASE PATTERNS:")
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lag, lead, datediff, to_date
    
    customer_window = Window.partitionBy("customer_id") \
        .orderBy("order_date")
    
    purchase_patterns = orders_df.withColumn("order_date_typed", 
        to_date(col("order_date"))
    ).select(
        "customer_id",
        "order_date",
        "amount",
        lag("order_date").over(customer_window).alias("prev_order_date"),
        lead("order_date").over(customer_window).alias("next_order_date"),
        lag("amount").over(customer_window).alias("prev_amount")
    ).withColumn("order_frequency",
        when(col("prev_order_date").isNotNull(),
            datediff(to_date(col("order_date")), 
                    to_date(col("prev_order_date")))
        ).otherwise(None)
    ).withColumn("amount_change",
        when(col("prev_amount").isNotNull(),
            ((col("amount") - col("prev_amount")) / col("prev_amount") * 100)
            .cast("decimal(5,2)")
        ).otherwise(None)
    ).orderBy("customer_id", "order_date")
    
    purchase_patterns.show()
    
    return {
        'top_customers': top_customers,
        'category_leaders': category_leaders,
        'customer_segments': customer_segments,
        'abc_analysis': abc_analysis
    }

def get_optimized_spark_config():
    """
    Recommended Spark configurations for ordering operations
    """
    config = {
        # Shuffle partitions (adjust based on data size)
        "spark.sql.shuffle.partitions": "200",  # Default: 200
        # For small datasets: 4-8
        # For medium datasets: 50-100
        # For large datasets: 200-500
        
        # Adaptive Query Execution (Spark 3.0+)
        "spark.sql.adaptive.enabled": "true",
        "spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled": "true",
        "spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled": "true",
        
        # Memory management
        "spark.executor.memory": "4g",
        "spark.driver.memory": "2g",
        "spark.memory.fraction": "0.8",
        
        # Serialization
        "spark.serializer": "org.apache.spark.serializer.KryoSerializer",
        
        # Compression
        "spark.sql.inMemoryColumnarStorage.compressed": "true",
        "spark.sql.inMemoryColumnarStorage.batchSize": "10000",
        
        # Optimization
        "spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold": "10485760",  # 10MB
        "spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes": "134217728",  # 128MB
        
        # Debugging
        "spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.enabled": "true",
        "spark.sql.execution.arrow.pyspark.fallback.enabled": "true",
    }
    
    return config

def create_optimized_spark_session():
    """
    Create Spark session with optimized settings
    """
    from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
    
    config = get_optimized_spark_config()
    
    builder = SparkSession.builder.appName("OrderingPatterns")
    
    for key, value in config.items():
        builder = builder.config(key, value)
    
    spark = builder.getOrCreate()
    
    # Set log level
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
    
    return spark

```python
# ============================================================================
# MONITORING AND DEBUGGING UTILITIES
# ============================================================================

def analyze_query_plan(df, query_name="Query"):
    """
    Analyze and print query execution plan
    """
    print(f"\n{'='*80}")
    print(f"QUERY PLAN ANALYSIS: {query_name}")
    print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    print("\n1. LOGICAL PLAN:")
    print("-" * 80)
    df.explain(mode="simple")
    
    print("\n2. PHYSICAL PLAN:")
    print("-" * 80)
    df.explain(mode="extended")
    
    print("\n3. FORMATTED PLAN:")
    print("-" * 80)
    df.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    print("\n4. COST ANALYSIS:")
    print("-" * 80)
    df.explain(mode="cost")

def monitor_shuffle_operations(df):
    """
    Monitor shuffle operations in query
    """
    plan = df._jdf.queryExecution().executedPlan().toString()
    
    shuffle_count = plan.count("Exchange")
    sort_count = plan.count("Sort")
    
    print(f"\nShuffle Operations: {shuffle_count}")
    print(f"Sort Operations: {sort_count}")
    
    if shuffle_count > 2:
        print("⚠️  Warning: High number of shuffle operations detected")
        print("   Consider optimizing query plan")
    
    return {
        'shuffles': shuffle_count,
        'sorts': sort_count
    }

def profile_ordering_operation(df, operation_name="Operation"):
    """
    Profile ordering operation performance
    """
    import time
    
    print(f"\nProfiling: {operation_name}")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    # Measure planning time
    start = time.time()
    plan = df.explain(mode="simple")
    planning_time = time.time() - start
    
    # Measure execution time
    start = time.time()
    count = df.count()
    execution_time = time.time() - start
    
    # Get partition info
    num_partitions = df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
    
    print(f"Planning Time: {planning_time:.4f}s")
    print(f"Execution Time: {execution_time:.4f}s")
    print(f"Total Time: {(planning_time + execution_time):.4f}s")
    print(f"Record Count: {count:,}")
    print(f"Partitions: {num_partitions}")
    print(f"Records/Partition: {count/num_partitions:.2f}")
    
    return {
        'planning_time': planning_time,
        'execution_time': execution_time,
        'total_time': planning_time + execution_time,
        'count': count,
        'partitions': num_partitions
    }

## **Export and Persistence:**

```python
# ============================================================================
# EXPORT AND PERSISTENCE UTILITIES
# ============================================================================

def export_ordered_results(df, output_path, format="parquet", 
                          partition_by=None, mode="overwrite"):
    """
    Export ordered results with various options
    """
    writer = df.write.mode(mode)
    
    if partition_by:
        writer = writer.partitionBy(partition_by)
    
    if format == "parquet":
        writer.option("compression", "snappy").parquet(output_path)
    elif format == "csv":
        writer.option("header", "true").csv(output_path)
    elif format == "json":
        writer.json(output_path)
    elif format == "orc":
        writer.orc(output_path)
    elif format == "delta":  # Requires Delta Lake
        writer.format("delta").save(output_path)
    
    print(f"✓ Results exported to {output_path} as {format}")

def save_ordered_table(df, table_name, database="default", 
                       partition_cols=None, sort_cols=None):
    """
    Save ordered results as Hive table
    """
    # Create database if not exists
    spark.sql(f"CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS {database}")
    
    # Write table
    writer = df.write.mode("overwrite")
    
    if partition_cols:
        writer = writer.partitionBy(*partition_cols)
    
    if sort_cols:
        # Sort before writing
        df = df.orderBy(*sort_cols)
    
    writer.saveAsTable(f"{database}.{table_name}")
    
    print(f"✓ Table saved: {database}.{table_name}")
    
    # Optimize table (if using Delta)
    try:
        spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE {database}.{table_name}")
        print(f"✓ Table optimized")
    except:
        pass

def checkpoint_ordered_data(df, checkpoint_path):
    """
    Checkpoint ordered data for fault tolerance
    """
    df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(checkpoint_path)
    checkpointed_df = spark.read.parquet(checkpoint_path)
    
    print(f"✓ Data checkpointed to {checkpoint_path}")
    return checkpointed_df

# ============================================================================
# ADDITIONAL ADVANCED PATTERNS AND TECHNIQUES
# ============================================================================

def streaming_ordering_patterns(spark):
    """
    Ordering patterns for Spark Structured Streaming
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("STREAMING ORDERING PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    print("""
    Note: In streaming, ordering is handled differently:
    
    1. WATERMARKING for event-time ordering
    2. WINDOW OPERATIONS for time-based ordering
    3. STATE MANAGEMENT for stateful ordering
    """)
    
    # Example: Streaming with watermark and ordering
    print("\n1. Streaming with Watermark (Pseudo-code):")
    print("""
    # Read stream
    stream_df = spark.readStream \\
        .format("kafka") \\
        .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "localhost:9092") \\
        .option("subscribe", "orders") \\
        .load()
    
    # Parse and order with watermark
    ordered_stream = stream_df \\
        .withWatermark("timestamp", "10 minutes") \\
        .groupBy(
            window("timestamp", "5 minutes"),
            "category"
        ) \\
        .agg(sum("amount").alias("total")) \\
        .orderBy("window")
    
    # Write stream
    query = ordered_stream.writeStream \\
        .outputMode("complete") \\
        .format("console") \\
        .start()
    """)
    
    # Example: Windowed aggregation with ordering
    print("\n2. Windowed Aggregation Pattern:")
    print("""
    from pyspark.sql.functions import window
    
    windowed_df = stream_df \\
        .groupBy(
            window("event_time", "1 hour", "30 minutes"),
            "product_id"
        ) \\
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("event_count"),
            sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue")
        ) \\
        .orderBy("window.start")
    """)
    
    # Example: State-based ordering
    print("\n3. Stateful Ordering Pattern:")
    print("""
    # Use mapGroupsWithState for complex stateful operations
    from pyspark.sql.streaming import GroupState
    
    def update_state(key, values, state):
        # Maintain sorted state per key
        if state.exists:
            old_values = state.get
        else:
            old_values = []
        
        new_values = sorted(old_values + list(values), 
                          key=lambda x: x.timestamp)
        state.update(new_values)
        
        return new_values
    
    stateful_stream = stream_df \\
        .groupByKey(lambda x: x.key) \\
        .mapGroupsWithState(update_state)
    """)

def distributed_sorting_algorithms(df):
    """
    Demonstrate different distributed sorting algorithms
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("DISTRIBUTED SORTING ALGORITHMS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # 1. Sort-Merge (Default in Spark)
    print("\n1. SORT-MERGE ALGORITHM (Default):")
    print("   - Partitions data by hash/range")
    print("   - Sorts within each partition")
    print("   - Merges sorted partitions")
    
    sort_merge_df = df.orderBy("salary")
    print("\n   Execution plan:")
    sort_merge_df.explain()
    
    # 2. Range Partitioning
    print("\n2. RANGE PARTITIONING ALGORITHM:")
    print("   - Samples data to determine ranges")
    print("   - Partitions by value ranges")
    print("   - Each partition contains sorted range")
    
    range_sorted_df = df.repartitionByRange(4, "salary")
    print("\n   Partition distribution:")
    range_sorted_df.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .groupBy("partition_id") \
        .agg(
            spark_min("salary").alias("min_salary"),
            spark_max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
            count("*").alias("count")
        ).orderBy("partition_id").show()
    
    # 3. External Sort (for very large datasets)
    print("\n3. EXTERNAL SORT (Spill to Disk):")
    print("   - Used when data doesn't fit in memory")
    print("   - Sorts chunks that fit in memory")
    print("   - Merges sorted chunks from disk")
    print("   - Controlled by: spark.memory.fraction")
    
    # 4. Sampling-based Sort
    print("\n4. SAMPLING-BASED SORT:")
    print("   - Sample data to estimate distribution")
    print("   - Use sample to optimize partitioning")
    
    # Sample and analyze
    sample_df = df.sample(False, 0.3, seed=42)
    sample_stats = sample_df.agg(
        spark_min("salary").alias("min"),
        spark_max("salary").alias("max"),
        avg("salary").alias("avg")
    ).collect()[0]
    
    print(f"\n   Sample statistics:")
    print(f"   Min: {sample_stats['min']}")
    print(f"   Max: {sample_stats['max']}")
    print(f"   Avg: {sample_stats['avg']:.2f}")

def advanced_window_patterns(df):
    """
    Advanced window function patterns
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED WINDOW FUNCTION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Pattern 1: Session Windows
    print("\n1. SESSION WINDOW PATTERN:")
    print("   Identify sessions based on time gaps")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import lag, when, sum as spark_sum
    
    # Add session boundaries
    time_window = Window.partitionBy("emp_id").orderBy("hire_date")
    
    sessions_df = df.withColumn("prev_date", 
        lag("hire_date").over(time_window)
    ).withColumn("new_session",
        when(col("prev_date").isNull(), 1)
        .when(datediff(to_date(col("hire_date")), 
                      to_date(col("prev_date"))) > 30, 1)
        .otherwise(0)
    ).withColumn("session_id",
        spark_sum("new_session").over(
            Window.partitionBy("emp_id")
            .orderBy("hire_date")
            .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
        )
    )
    
    print("\n   Sessions identified:")
    sessions_df.select("emp_id", "name", "hire_date", "session_id") \
        .orderBy("emp_id", "hire_date").show()
    
    # Pattern 2: Gaps and Islands
    print("\n2. GAPS AND ISLANDS PATTERN:")
    print("   Find consecutive sequences")
    
    gaps_islands = df.withColumn("row_num",
        row_number().over(Window.orderBy("emp_id"))
    ).withColumn("island_id",
        col("emp_id") - col("row_num")
    ).groupBy("island_id") \
     .agg(
         spark_min("emp_id").alias("island_start"),
         spark_max("emp_id").alias("island_end"),
         count("*").alias("island_size")
     ).orderBy("island_start")
    
    print("\n   Islands found:")
    gaps_islands.show()
    
    # Pattern 3: Running Difference
    print("\n3. RUNNING DIFFERENCE PATTERN:")
    
    running_diff = df.select(
        "name", "salary",
        lag("salary").over(Window.orderBy("salary")).alias("prev_salary")
    ).withColumn("salary_diff",
        when(col("prev_salary").isNotNull(),
             col("salary") - col("prev_salary"))
        .otherwise(0)
    ).orderBy("salary")
    
    print("\n   Salary differences:")
    running_diff.show()
    
    # Pattern 4: Conditional Aggregation in Window
    print("\n4. CONDITIONAL WINDOW AGGREGATION:")
    
    conditional_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("salary") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    conditional_agg = df.withColumn("high_earners_count",
        spark_sum(when(col("salary") > 90000, 1).otherwise(0))
        .over(conditional_window)
    ).select("name", "department", "salary", "high_earners_count") \
     .orderBy("department", "salary")
    
    print("\n   Conditional aggregation:")
    conditional_agg.show()
    
    # Pattern 5: Expanding Window
    print("\n5. EXPANDING WINDOW PATTERN:")
    
    expanding_window = Window.partitionBy("department") \
        .orderBy("hire_date") \
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    
    expanding_metrics = df.select(
        "name", "department", "hire_date", "salary",
        avg("salary").over(expanding_window).alias("expanding_avg"),
        spark_max("salary").over(expanding_window).alias("expanding_max"),
        count("*").over(expanding_window).alias("team_size")
    ).orderBy("department", "hire_date")
    
    print("\n   Expanding window metrics:")
    expanding_metrics.show()

def partition_skew_handling(df):
    """
    Handle data skew in ordering operations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("HANDLING DATA SKEW IN ORDERING")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Detect skew
    print("\n1. DETECTING DATA SKEW:")
    
    skew_analysis = df.groupBy("department").count() \
        .withColumn("skew_ratio",
            col("count") / avg("count").over(Window.partitionBy())
        ).orderBy(col("count").desc())
    
    print("\n   Department distribution:")
    skew_analysis.show()
    
    # Technique 1: Salting
    print("\n2. SALTING TECHNIQUE (for skewed keys):")
    
    import random
    from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
    from pyspark.sql.types import IntegerType
    
    # Add salt to skewed key
    salt_udf = udf(lambda: random.randint(0, 3), IntegerType())
    
    salted_df = df.withColumn("salt", salt_udf()) \
        .withColumn("salted_key", 
                   concat(col("department"), lit("_"), col("salt")))
    
    # Process with salted key
    salted_result = salted_df.repartition("salted_key") \
        .sortWithinPartitions("salary") \
        .drop("salt", "salted_key")
    
    print("\n   Salted partition distribution:")
    salted_df.groupBy("salted_key").count().show()
    
    # Technique 2: Adaptive partitioning
    print("\n3. ADAPTIVE PARTITIONING:")
    
    # Use AQE (Adaptive Query Execution) in Spark 3.0+
    print("""
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")
    """)
    
    # Technique 3: Broadcast for small skewed dimensions
    print("\n4. BROADCAST SMALL TABLES:")
    
    # Create small lookup table
    dept_info = spark.createDataFrame([
        ("Engineering", "Tech", 1),
        ("Sales", "Business", 2),
        ("Marketing", "Business", 3)
    ], ["department", "division", "priority"])
    
    # Broadcast join to avoid shuffle
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    broadcast_result = df.join(
        broadcast(dept_info),
        "department"
    ).orderBy("priority", col("salary").desc())
    
    print("\n   Broadcast join result:")
    broadcast_result.select("name", "department", "division", "salary") \
        .show(5)
    
    # Technique 4: Custom partitioner
    print("\n5. CUSTOM PARTITIONING STRATEGY:")
    
    # Repartition based on data distribution
    small_depts = ["Marketing"]
    large_depts = ["Engineering", "Sales"]
    
    custom_partitioned = df.withColumn("partition_group",
        when(col("department").isin(small_depts), "small")
        .otherwise("large")
    ).repartition(2, "partition_group", "department") \
     .drop("partition_group")
    
    print("\n   Custom partition distribution:")
    custom_partitioned.withColumn("partition_id", spark_partition_id()) \
        .groupBy("partition_id", "department").count() \
        .orderBy("partition_id").show()

def memory_optimization_patterns(df):
    """
    Memory optimization for ordering operations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("MEMORY OPTIMIZATION PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Pattern 1: Column Pruning
    print("\n1. COLUMN PRUNING:")
    print("   Select only necessary columns before ordering")
    
    # Bad: Select all columns
    print("\n   ❌ BAD:")
    print("   df.orderBy('salary').select('name', 'salary')")
    
    # Good: Prune first
    print("\n   ✓ GOOD:")
    print("   df.select('name', 'salary').orderBy('salary')")
    
    pruned_df = df.select("name", "salary").orderBy("salary")
    
    # Pattern 2: Incremental Processing
    print("\n2. INCREMENTAL PROCESSING:")
    print("   Process data in chunks")
    
    # Process by partition
    for dept in ["Engineering", "Sales", "Marketing"]:
        chunk = df.filter(col("department") == dept) \
            .orderBy("salary") \
            .select("name", "department", "salary")
        
        print(f"\n   Processing {dept}:")
        chunk.show(3)
    
    # Pattern 3: Caching Strategy
    print("\n3. SMART CACHING STRATEGY:")
    
    # Cache only filtered/aggregated results
    filtered_df = df.filter(col("salary") > 80000)
    filtered_df.cache()
    filtered_df.count()  # Materialize
    
    # Multiple orderings on cached data
    by_salary = filtered_df.orderBy("salary")
    by_name = filtered_df.orderBy("name")
    
    print("\n   Cached and reused for multiple orderings")
    
    filtered_df.unpersist()
    
    # Pattern 4: Compression
    print("\n4. ENABLE COMPRESSION:")
    print("""
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.inMemoryColumnarStorage.compressed", "true")
    spark.conf.set("spark.sql.inMemoryColumnarStorage.batchSize", "10000")
    """)
    
    # Pattern 5: Spill Management
    print("\n5. SPILL
```python

    # Monitor and control disk spills
    spark.conf.set("spark.memory.fraction", "0.8")  # 80% for execution/storage

def complex_ordering_scenarios(df):
    """
    Complex real-world ordering scenarios
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("COMPLEX ORDERING SCENARIOS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Scenario 1: Multi-level Hierarchical Ordering
    print("\n1. HIERARCHICAL ORDERING (Organization Chart):")
    
    # Simulate hierarchical data
    hierarchy_data = [
        (1, None, "CEO", 200000, 1),
        (2, 1, "CTO", 180000, 2),
        (3, 1, "CFO", 180000, 2),
        (4, 2, "Eng Manager", 150000, 3),
        (5, 2, "Eng Manager", 150000, 3),
        (6, 3, "Finance Manager", 140000, 3),
        (7, 4, "Senior Dev", 120000, 4),
        (8, 4, "Senior Dev", 120000, 4),
        (9, 5, "Senior Dev", 120000, 4),
    ]
    
    hierarchy_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        hierarchy_data,
        ["emp_id", "manager_id", "title", "salary", "level"]
    )
    
    # Order by hierarchy level, then salary
    hierarchical_order = hierarchy_df.orderBy(
        "level",
        col("manager_id").asc_nulls_first(),
        col("salary").desc()
    )
    
    print("\n   Organization hierarchy:")
    hierarchical_order.select("emp_id", "manager_id", "title", "level", "salary").show()
    
    # Scenario 2: Circular/Cyclic Ordering
    print("\n2. CYCLIC ORDERING (Round-robin Assignment):")
    
    # Assign employees to teams in round-robin fashion
    cyclic_order = df.withColumn("row_num",
        row_number().over(Window.orderBy("emp_id"))
    ).withColumn("team_assignment",
        (col("row_num") % 3) + 1  # 3 teams
    ).orderBy("team_assignment", "salary")
    
    print("\n   Round-robin team assignment:")
    cyclic_order.select("name", "team_assignment", "salary").show()
    
    # Scenario 3: Conditional Multi-field Ordering
    print("\n3. CONDITIONAL MULTI-FIELD ORDERING:")
    
    # Different ordering logic per department
    conditional_order = df.withColumn("sort_key",
        when(col("department") == "Engineering", col("salary") * -1)  # Desc
        .when(col("department") == "Sales", col("salary"))  # Asc
        .otherwise(0)
    ).orderBy("department", "sort_key")
    
    print("\n   Conditional ordering (Eng: desc, Sales: asc):")
    conditional_order.select("name", "department", "salary", "sort_key").show()
    
    # Scenario 4: Fuzzy/Approximate Ordering
    print("\n4. FUZZY ORDERING (Tolerance-based):")
    
    # Group similar salaries together (within 5k tolerance)
    fuzzy_order = df.withColumn("salary_bucket",
        (col("salary") / 5000).cast("int") * 5000
    ).orderBy("salary_bucket", "name")
    
    print("\n   Fuzzy ordering (5k buckets):")
    fuzzy_order.select("name", "salary", "salary_bucket").show()
    
    # Scenario 5: Weighted Multi-criteria Ordering
    print("\n5. WEIGHTED MULTI-CRITERIA ORDERING:")
    
    # Score based on multiple factors
    weighted_order = df.withColumn("hire_date_typed", to_date(col("hire_date"))) \
        .withColumn("tenure_days", datediff(current_date(), col("hire_date_typed"))) \
        .withColumn("level_score",
            when(col("level") == "Manager", 100)
            .when(col("level") == "Senior", 70)
            .otherwise(40)
        ).withColumn("composite_score",
            (col("salary") / 1000 * 0.5) +  # 50% weight
            (col("tenure_days") / 365 * 0.3) +  # 30% weight
            (col("level_score") * 0.2)  # 20% weight
        ).orderBy(col("composite_score").desc())
    
    print("\n   Weighted multi-criteria score:")
    weighted_order.select("name", "salary", "tenure_days", "level", "composite_score") \
        .show()
    
    # Scenario 6: Stable Sort (Preserve Original Order)
    print("\n6. STABLE SORT (Preserve ties):")
    
    # Add original order tracking
    stable_sort = df.withColumn("original_order",
        monotonically_increasing_id()
    ).orderBy("salary", "original_order")
    
    print("\n   Stable sort (preserves original order for ties):")
    stable_sort.select("name", "salary", "original_order").show()

def ordering_with_joins(spark):
    """
    Ordering patterns with join operations
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING WITH JOIN OPERATIONS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Create sample datasets
    employees = spark.createDataFrame([
        (1, "Alice", "Engineering", 95000),
        (2, "Bob", "Sales", 85000),
        (3, "Charlie", "Engineering", 105000),
        (4, "Diana", "Marketing", 88000),
    ], ["emp_id", "name", "department", "salary"])
    
    projects = spark.createDataFrame([
        (101, "Project A", 1, 50),
        (102, "Project B", 2, 30),
        (103, "Project C", 1, 70),
        (104, "Project D", 3, 90),
        (105, "Project E", 2, 40),
    ], ["project_id", "project_name", "emp_id", "completion"])
    
    # Pattern 1: Order Before Join
    print("\n1. ORDER BEFORE JOIN (Pre-sorted join):")
    
    sorted_employees = employees.orderBy("emp_id")
    sorted_projects = projects.orderBy("emp_id")
    
    joined_presorted = sorted_employees.join(sorted_projects, "emp_id")
    
    print("\n   Pre-sorted join result:")
    joined_presorted.select("name", "project_name", "completion").show()
    
    # Pattern 2: Order After Join
    print("\n2. ORDER AFTER JOIN (Post-join ordering):")
    
    joined_postsorted = employees.join(projects, "emp_id") \
        .orderBy("name", col("completion").desc())
    
    print("\n   Post-join ordering:")
    joined_postsorted.select("name", "project_name", "completion").show()
    
    # Pattern 3: Window Functions Across Joins
    print("\n3. WINDOW FUNCTIONS ACROSS JOINS:")
    
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("emp_id").orderBy(col("completion").desc())
    
    joined_windowed = employees.join(projects, "emp_id") \
        .withColumn("project_rank",
            row_number().over(window_spec)
        ).orderBy("name", "project_rank")
    
    print("\n   Ranked projects per employee:")
    joined_windowed.select("name", "project_name", "completion", "project_rank").show()
    
    # Pattern 4: Sort-Merge Join Optimization
    print("\n4. SORT-MERGE JOIN OPTIMIZATION:")
    
    # Partition both datasets by join key
    partitioned_emp = employees.repartition("emp_id").sortWithinPartitions("emp_id")
    partitioned_proj = projects.repartition("emp_id").sortWithinPartitions("emp_id")
    
    # Join will use sort-merge join
    optimized_join = partitioned_emp.join(partitioned_proj, "emp_id")
    
    print("\n   Execution plan (note SortMergeJoin):")
    optimized_join.explain()
    
    # Pattern 5: Broadcast Join with Ordering
    print("\n5. BROADCAST JOIN WITH ORDERING:")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Small table broadcast
    broadcast_join = employees.join(
        broadcast(projects),
        "emp_id"
    ).orderBy("salary", col("completion").desc())
    
    print("\n   Broadcast join with ordering:")
    broadcast_join.select("name", "salary", "project_name", "completion").show()

def dynamic_ordering_patterns(df):
    """
    Dynamic ordering based on runtime conditions
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("DYNAMIC ORDERING PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Pattern 1: Parameterized Ordering
    print("\n1. PARAMETERIZED ORDERING:")
    
    def order_by_column(df, column_name, ascending=True):
        """Dynamic column ordering"""
        if ascending:
            return df.orderBy(col(column_name).asc())
        else:
            return df.orderBy(col(column_name).desc())
    
    # Use with different parameters
    print("\n   Order by salary (descending):")
    order_by_column(df, "salary", ascending=False) \
        .select("name", "salary").show(3)
    
    print("\n   Order by name (ascending):")
    order_by_column(df, "name", ascending=True) \
        .select("name", "salary").show(3)
    
    # Pattern 2: Multi-column Dynamic Ordering
    print("\n2. MULTI-COLUMN DYNAMIC ORDERING:")
    
    def dynamic_multi_order(df, order_specs):
        """
        order_specs: list of tuples (column, direction)
        Example: [("department", "asc"), ("salary", "desc")]
        """
        order_cols = []
        for col_name, direction in order_specs:
            if direction.lower() == "desc":
                order_cols.append(col(col_name).desc())
            else:
                order_cols.append(col(col_name).asc())
        
        return df.orderBy(*order_cols)
    
    # Dynamic ordering specification
    order_spec = [("department", "asc"), ("salary", "desc")]
    
    print(f"\n   Dynamic ordering: {order_spec}")
    dynamic_multi_order(df, order_spec) \
        .select("name", "department", "salary").show()
    
    # Pattern 3: Conditional Dynamic Ordering
    print("\n3. CONDITIONAL DYNAMIC ORDERING:")
    
    def conditional_order(df, condition_col, condition_val, 
                         order_col_if_true, order_col_if_false):
        """Order by different columns based on condition"""
        
        # Split data
        true_df = df.filter(col(condition_col) == condition_val) \
            .orderBy(order_col_if_true)
        
        false_df = df.filter(col(condition_col) != condition_val) \
            .orderBy(order_col_if_false)
        
        # Union results
        return true_df.union(false_df)
    
    print("\n   Engineering: order by salary, Others: order by name")
    conditional_order(df, "department", "Engineering", "salary", "name") \
        .select("name", "department", "salary").show()
    
    # Pattern 4: User-defined Ordering Function
    print("\n4. USER-DEFINED ORDERING FUNCTION:")
    
    def custom_sort_function(df, sort_logic):
        """
        Apply custom sorting logic
        sort_logic: lambda function returning sort key
        """
        # Add sort key column
        df_with_key = df.withColumn("_sort_key", sort_logic(df))
        
        # Order and remove key
        return df_with_key.orderBy("_sort_key").drop("_sort_key")
    
    # Example: Sort by salary quartile then name
    sort_logic = lambda df: ntile(4).over(Window.orderBy("salary"))
    
    print("\n   Custom sort by salary quartile:")
    custom_sorted = df.withColumn("quartile",
        ntile(4).over(Window.orderBy("salary"))
    ).orderBy("quartile", "name")
    
    custom_sorted.select("name", "salary", "quartile").show()
    
    # Pattern 5: Configuration-driven Ordering
    print("\n5. CONFIGURATION-DRIVEN ORDERING:")
    
    # Configuration dictionary
    sort_config = {
        "primary": {"column": "department", "direction": "asc"},
        "secondary": {"column": "salary", "direction": "desc"},
        "tertiary": {"column": "name", "direction": "asc"}
    }
    
    def config_driven_sort(df, config):
        """Sort based on configuration"""
        order_cols = []
        
        for level in ["primary", "secondary", "tertiary"]:
            if level in config:
                col_name = config[level]["column"]
                direction = config[level]["direction"]
                
                if direction == "desc":
                    order_cols.append(col(col_name).desc())
                else:
                    order_cols.append(col(col_name).asc())
        
        return df.orderBy(*order_cols)
    
    print(f"\n   Config-driven sort: {sort_config}")
    config_driven_sort(df, sort_config) \
        .select("name", "department", "salary").show()

def ordering_best_practices_checklist():
    """
    Print comprehensive best practices checklist
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING BEST PRACTICES CHECKLIST")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    checklist = """
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     PRE-ORDERING CHECKLIST                              │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    □ Do I really need ordering?
      ├─ For output/reports: YES
      ├─ For intermediate processing: Usually NO
      └─ For data exploration: MAYBE (use limit)
    
    □ What type of ordering do I need?
      
```python
      ├─ Global ordering: Use orderBy()
      ├─ Group-wise ordering: Use Window functions
      ├─ Physical organization: Use repartition()
      └─ Complex logic: Use custom expressions
    
    □ Have I optimized the query?
      ├─ Filter before ordering ✓
      ├─ Select only needed columns ✓
      ├─ Use limit() for Top-N ✓
      ├─ Cache if multiple orderings needed ✓
      └─ Check partition count ✓
    
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     DURING ORDERING CHECKLIST                           │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    □ Partition Management
      ├─ Appropriate partition count (cores × 2-3) ✓
      ├─ Avoid over-partitioning small datasets ✓
      ├─ Use coalesce() to reduce partitions ✓
      └─ Monitor partition skew ✓
    
    □ Memory Management
      ├─ Enable compression ✓
      ├─ Monitor spill metrics ✓
      ├─ Adjust memory fractions if needed ✓
      └─ Consider off-heap memory ✓
    
    □ Performance Optimization
      ├─ Use sortWithinPartitions when possible ✓
      ├─ Leverage broadcast for small tables ✓
      ├─ Enable Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) ✓
      ├─ Use sampling for approximate results ✓
      └─ Avoid UDFs in sort expressions ✓
    
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     POST-ORDERING CHECKLIST                             │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    □ Validation
      ├─ Verify sort order is correct ✓
      ├─ Check for null handling ✓
      ├─ Validate partition distribution ✓
      └─ Test with edge cases ✓
    
    □ Monitoring
      ├─ Review execution plan (explain()) ✓
      ├─ Check shuffle operations ✓
      ├─ Monitor execution time ✓
      ├─ Check Spark UI for spills ✓
      └─ Verify memory usage ✓
    
    □ Documentation
      ├─ Document ordering logic ✓
      ├─ Add comments for complex sorts ✓
      ├─ Note performance considerations ✓
      └─ Document edge cases handled ✓
    
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     COMMON MISTAKES TO AVOID                            │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    ✗ Multiple orderBy() calls (only last applies)
    ✗ Sorting before filtering
    ✗ Not using window functions for group operations
    ✗ Ignoring data skew
    ✗ Over-partitioning or under-partitioning
    ✗ Not caching for multiple sorts
    ✗ Using global sort when partition sort suffices
    ✗ Forgetting to handle nulls explicitly
    ✗ Not monitoring shuffle operations
    ✗ Ignoring memory pressure warnings
    
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     PERFORMANCE TARGETS                                 │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    Dataset Size          | Expected Sort Time  | Recommended Partitions
    ─────────────────────┼────────────────────┼──────────────────────
    < 1 GB               | < 10 seconds       | 4-8
    1-10 GB              | 10-60 seconds      | 50-100
    10-100 GB            | 1-10 minutes       | 200-500
    100-1000 GB          | 10-60 minutes      | 500-2000
    > 1 TB               | > 1 hour           | 2000+
    
    Note: Times vary based on cluster size and configuration
    
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE                               │
    └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    Problem: Slow ordering performance
    Solutions:
      1. Reduce data volume with filters
      2. Increase partition count
      3. Enable compression
      4. Use sampling for approximate results
      5. Check for data skew
    
    Problem: Out of memory errors
    Solutions:
      1. Increase executor memory
      2. Reduce partition size
      3. Enable spill to disk
      4. Use off-heap memory
      5. Process in smaller batches
    
    Problem: Data skew
    Solutions:
      1. Use salting technique
      2. Repartition with custom logic
      3. Enable AQE skew join handling
      4. Broadcast small skewed dimensions
      5. Use range partitioning
    
    Problem: Incorrect sort order
    Solutions:
      1. Check null handling (nulls_first/last)
      2. Verify data types (string vs numeric)
      3. Check for multiple orderBy() calls
      4. Validate custom sort expressions
      5. Test with sample data
    
    Problem: High shuffle overhead
    Solutions:
      1. Use sortWithinPartitions
      2. Reduce number of partitions
      3. Colocate related data
      4. Use broadcast joins
      5. Enable partition coalescing
    """
    
    print(checklist)

def generate_ordering_patterns_report(spark, df):
    """
    Generate comprehensive report on ordering patterns usage
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING PATTERNS USAGE REPORT")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    report = {
        "dataset_info": {},
        "pattern_examples": {},
        "performance_metrics": {},
        "recommendations": []
    }
    
    # Dataset Information
    print("\n1. DATASET INFORMATION")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    row_count = df.count()
    partition_count = df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
    column_count = len(df.columns)
    
    report["dataset_info"] = {
        "rows": row_count,
        "columns": column_count,
        "partitions": partition_count,
        "rows_per_partition": row_count / partition_count
    }
    
    print(f"Total Rows: {row_count:,}")
    print(f"Total Columns: {column_count}")
    print(f"Partitions: {partition_count}")
    print(f"Rows per Partition: {row_count/partition_count:.2f}")
    
    # Pattern Usage Examples
    print("\n2. PATTERN USAGE EXAMPLES")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    patterns_used = []
    
    # Check which patterns would be beneficial
    if row_count < 1000:
        patterns_used.append(("Natural Order", "Small dataset, ordering optional"))
        report["recommendations"].append("Dataset is small - ordering overhead minimal")
    
    if partition_count > row_count / 100:
        patterns_used.append(("Clustered Order", "Too many partitions, consider coalescing"))
        report["recommendations"].append(f"Reduce partitions from {partition_count} to ~{row_count//100}")
    
    # Check for skew
    dept_dist = df.groupBy("department").count().collect()
    max_count = max([r['count'] for r in dept_dist])
    min_count = min([r['count'] for r in dept_dist])
    skew_ratio = max_count / min_count if min_count > 0 else 0
    
    if skew_ratio > 2.0:
        patterns_used.append(("Custom Order", f"Data skew detected (ratio: {skew_ratio:.2f})"))
        report["recommendations"].append("Consider salting or custom partitioning for skewed data")
    
    for pattern, reason in patterns_used:
        print(f"  • {pattern}: {reason}")
    
    report["pattern_examples"] = patterns_used
    
    # Performance Metrics
    print("\n3. PERFORMANCE METRICS")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    import time
    
    # Benchmark different patterns
    metrics = []
    
    # Natural order
    start = time.time()
    df.select("emp_id", "name").count()
    natural_time = time.time() - start
    metrics.append(("Natural Order", natural_time))
    
    # Sorted order
    start = time.time()
    df.orderBy("salary").count()
    sorted_time = time.time() - start
    metrics.append(("Sorted Order", sorted_time))
    
    # Partitioned order
    start = time.time()
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy("salary")
    df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(window_spec)).count()
    partitioned_time = time.time() - start
    metrics.append(("Partitioned Order", partitioned_time))
    
    report["performance_metrics"] = metrics
    
    for pattern, exec_time in metrics:
        overhead = ((exec_time / natural_time - 1) * 100) if natural_time > 0 else 0
        print(f"  {pattern:<20} {exec_time:.4f}s  (Overhead: {overhead:+.1f}%)")
    
    # Recommendations
    print("\n4. RECOMMENDATIONS")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    # Add general recommendations
    if row_count > 1000000:
        report["recommendations"].append("Large dataset - enable AQE and compression")
    
    if partition_count < spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism:
        report["recommendations"].append(
            f"Increase partitions to {spark.sparkContext.defaultParallelism} for better parallelism"
        )
    
    for i, rec in enumerate(report["recommendations"], 1):
        print(f"  {i}. {rec}")
    
    # Summary
    print("\n5. SUMMARY")
    print("-" * 80)
    print(f"""
    Dataset Size: {row_count:,} rows
    Recommended Pattern: {"Partitioned Order" if row_count > 10000 else "Sorted Order"}
    Estimated Sort Time: {sorted_time * (row_count/df.count()):.2f}s (projected)
    Memory Requirement: {(row_count * column_count * 8 / 1024 / 1024):.2f} MB (estimated)
    """)
    
    return report

def create_ordering_patterns_cheatsheet():
    """
    Create a quick reference cheatsheet
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ORDERING PATTERNS QUICK REFERENCE CHEATSHEET")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    cheatsheet = """
    ╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
    ║                    QUICK REFERENCE CHEATSHEET                          ║
    ╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 1. NATURAL ORDER - No explicit ordering                               │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    df.select("col1", "col2")
    
    Use when: Order doesn't matter, fastest performance
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 2. SORTED ORDER - Global ordering                                     │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    # Single column
    df.orderBy("salary")                    # Ascending
    df.orderBy(col("salary").desc())        # Descending
    
    # Multiple columns
    df.orderBy("dept", col("salary").desc())
    
    # Null handling
    df.orderBy(col("salary").asc_nulls_last())
    
    # With limit (Top-N optimization)
    df.orderBy(col("salary").desc()).limit(10)
    
    Use when: Need globally sorted output
    
    ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ 3. PARTITIONED ORDER - Window functions                               │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    # Rank within groups
    w = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy(col("salary").desc())
    df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(w))
    
    # Top N per group
    df.withColumn("rank", row_number().over(w)) \\
      .filter(col("rank") <= 3)
    
    # Running total
    w = Window.partitionBy("dept").orderBy("date") \\
        .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
    df.withColumn("running_total", sum("amount").over(w))
    
    # Other window functions
    rank().over(w)              # Rank with gaps
    dense_rank().over(w)        # Rank without gaps
    ntile(4).over(w)           # Quartiles
    lag("col", 1).over(w)      # Previous value
    lead("col", 1).over(w)     # Next value
    percent_rank().over(w)     # Percentile
    
    Use when: Need ordering within groups, rankings, running calculations
