def create_troubleshooting_guide():
    """
    Display troubleshooting guide for common issues
    """
    troubleshooting = """
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE                                   ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                            ║
║  ISSUE 1: Late Events Being Dropped                                        ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║  Symptoms: Missing data in aggregations, gaps in results                   ║
║  Causes:                                                                   ║
║    • Watermark threshold too aggressive                                    ║
║    • Network delays or upstream processing issues                          ║
║    • Clock skew between systems                                            ║
║  Solutions:                                                                ║
║    1. Increase watermark threshold                                         ║
║    2. Monitor late event metrics                                           ║
║    3. Implement dead letter queue for late events                          ║
║    4. Use allowedLateness configuration if available                       ║
║                                                                            ║
║  ISSUE 2: Memory/OOM Errors                                                ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║  Symptoms: OutOfMemoryError, executor failures                             ║
║  Causes:                                                                   ║
║    • State size growing unbounded                                          ║
║    • Too many active windows                                               ║
║    • Watermark not configured (state never cleaned)                        ║
║  Solutions:                                                                ║
║    1. Configure watermark to clean up old state                            ║
║    2. Reduce window size or increase slide interval                        ║
║    3. Increase executor memory                                             ║
║    4. Use RocksDB state store for large state                              ║
║    5. Enable state compression                                             ║
║                                                                            ║
║  ISSUE 3: Slow Processing/Backpressure                                     ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║  Symptoms: Increasing lag, delayed results                                 ║
║  Causes:                                                                   ║
║    • Insufficient resources                                                ║
║    • Complex aggregations                                                  ║
║    • Too many shuffle operations                                           ║
║  Solutions:                                                                ║
║    1. Increase parallelism (more executors/cores)                          ║
║    2. Optimize query (reduce shuffles)                                     ║
║    3. Increase trigger interval                                            ║
║    4. Enable adaptive query execution                                      ║
║    5. Partition data appropriately                                         ║
║                                                                            ║
║  ISSUE 4: Incorrect Window Results                                         ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║  Symptoms: Wrong aggregation values, unexpected window boundaries          ║
║  Causes:                                                                   ║
║    • Using wrong timestamp column                                          ║
║    • Timezone issues                                                       ║
║    • Window configuration errors                                           ║
║  Solutions:                                                                ║
║    1. Verify timestamp column is correct                                   ║
║    2. Check timezone handling                                              ║
║    3. Validate window start/end times                                      ║
║    4. Test with known data patterns                                        ║
║                                                                            ║
║  ISSUE 5: Checkpoint Failures                                              ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║  Symptoms: Cannot recover from failure, checkpoint errors                  ║
║  Causes:                                                                   ║
║    • Checkpoint location not accessible                                    ║
║    • Schema changes without new checkpoint                                 ║
║    • Corrupted checkpoint files                                            ║
║  Solutions:                                                                ║
║    1. Ensure checkpoint location is reliable (HDFS/S3)                     ║
║    2. Use new checkpoint for schema changes                                ║
║    3. Implement checkpoint backup strategy                                 ║
║    4. Monitor checkpoint health                                            ║
║                                                                            ║
║  DEBUGGING COMMANDS                                                        ║
║  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────      ║
║                                                                            ║
║  # Check query status                                                      ║
║  query.status                                                              ║
║  query.lastProgress                                                        ║
║  query.recentProgress                                                      ║
║                                                                            ║
║  # Monitor metrics                                                         ║
║  query.lastProgress['numInputRows']                                        ║
║  query.lastProgress['processedRowsPerSecond']                              ║
║  query.lastProgress['stateOperators']                                      ║
║                                                                            ║
║  # Enable detailed logging                                                 ║
║  spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("DEBUG")                                   ║
║                                                                            ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
    """
    print(troubleshooting)


def create_complete_production_example():
    """
    Complete production-ready example with all best practices
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PRODUCTION-READY COMPLETE EXAMPLE")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("ProductionStreamTimeSemantics") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .config("spark.sql.streaming.schemaInference", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass", 
                "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN")
    
    print("\n✓ Production Spark Session Created with:")
    print("  - Adaptive Query Execution enabled")
    print("  - State store configured")
    print("  - Optimized for production workloads")
    
    # Create production-grade streaming source
    raw_stream = spark.readStream \
        .format("rate") \
        .option("rowsPerSecond", 100) \
        .option("numPartitions", 4) \
        .load()
    
    # Production event schema with all time dimensions
    production_events = raw_stream.selectExpr(
        "CONCAT('evt_', CAST(value AS STRING)) as event_id",
        "CONCAT('user_', CAST(value % 1000 AS STRING)) as user_id",
        "CAST(timestamp - INTERVAL 15 SECONDS as TIMESTAMP) as event_time",
        "timestamp as ingestion_time",
        "CASE WHEN value % 100 = 0 THEN 'critical' " +
        "     WHEN value % 10 = 0 
```python
        "     WHEN value % 10 = 0 THEN 'error' " +
        "     WHEN value % 5 = 0 THEN 'warning' " +
        "     ELSE 'info' END as severity",
        "CASE WHEN value % 7 = 0 THEN 'api' " +
        "     WHEN value % 7 = 1 THEN 'database' " +
        "     WHEN value % 7 = 2 THEN 'cache' " +
        "     WHEN value % 7 = 3 THEN 'queue' " +
        "     ELSE 'service' END as component",
        "CAST(50 + (value % 200) + RAND() * 100 AS DOUBLE) as response_time_ms",
        "CAST(value % 1000 AS INT) as request_count"
    ) \
    .withColumn("processing_time", current_timestamp()) \
    .withColumn("partition_date", expr("date_format(event_time, 'yyyy-MM-dd')"))
    
    # Calculate latency metrics
    enriched_events = production_events \
        .withColumn("ingestion_latency_ms",
            (unix_timestamp(col("ingestion_time")) - 
             unix_timestamp(col("event_time"))) * 1000) \
        .withColumn("processing_latency_ms",
            (unix_timestamp(col("processing_time")) - 
             unix_timestamp(col("ingestion_time"))) * 1000) \
        .withColumn("e2e_latency_ms",
            (unix_timestamp(col("processing_time")) - 
             unix_timestamp(col("event_time"))) * 1000)
    
    # Apply watermark with production settings
    watermarked_events = enriched_events \
        .withWatermark("event_time", "2 minutes")
    
    # Production aggregations with multiple windows
    
    # 1. Real-time metrics (1-minute tumbling window)
    realtime_metrics = watermarked_events \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("event_time"), "1 minute"),
            col("component"),
            col("severity")
        ) \
        .agg(
            expr("count(*) as event_count"),
            expr("sum(request_count) as total_requests"),
            expr("avg(response_time_ms) as avg_response_time"),
            expr("percentile_approx(response_time_ms, 0.95) as p95_response_time"),
            expr("percentile_approx(response_time_ms, 0.99) as p99_response_time"),
            expr("max(response_time_ms) as max_response_time"),
            expr("avg(e2e_latency_ms) as avg_e2e_latency"),
            expr("max(e2e_latency_ms) as max_e2e_latency"),
            expr("count(DISTINCT user_id) as unique_users"),
            expr("min(event_time) as window_earliest_event"),
            expr("max(event_time) as window_latest_event")
        ) \
        .select(
            col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
            col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
            col("component"),
            col("severity"),
            col("event_count"),
            col("total_requests"),
            col("avg_response_time"),
            col("p95_response_time"),
            col("p99_response_time"),
            col("max_response_time"),
            col("avg_e2e_latency"),
            col("max_e2e_latency"),
            col("unique_users"),
            col("window_earliest_event"),
            col("window_latest_event")
        ) \
        .withColumn("window_duration_seconds",
            unix_timestamp(col("window_end")) - unix_timestamp(col("window_start")))
    
    # 2. SLA monitoring (5-minute sliding window)
    sla_monitoring = watermarked_events \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("event_time"), "5 minutes", "1 minute"),
            col("component")
        ) \
        .agg(
            expr("count(*) as total_events"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN severity = 'critical' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as critical_count"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN severity = 'error' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as error_count"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN severity = 'warning' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as warning_count"),
            expr("avg(response_time_ms) as avg_response_time"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN response_time_ms > 1000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as slow_requests"),
            expr("avg(e2e_latency_ms) as avg_latency")
        ) \
        .select(
            col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
            col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
            col("component"),
            col("total_events"),
            col("critical_count"),
            col("error_count"),
            col("warning_count"),
            col("avg_response_time"),
            col("slow_requests"),
            col("avg_latency")
        ) \
        .withColumn("error_rate_pct",
            (col("critical_count") + col("error_count")) / col("total_events") * 100) \
        .withColumn("slow_request_rate_pct",
            col("slow_requests") / col("total_events") * 100) \
        .withColumn("sla_breach",
            (col("error_rate_pct") > 5) | (col("slow_request_rate_pct") > 10))
    
    # 3. Anomaly detection with statistical analysis
    anomaly_detection = watermarked_events \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("event_time"), "2 minutes"),
            col("component")
        ) \
        .agg(
            expr("count(*) as event_count"),
            expr("avg(response_time_ms) as avg_response_time"),
            expr("stddev(response_time_ms) as stddev_response_time"),
            expr("avg(e2e_latency_ms) as avg_latency"),
            expr("stddev(e2e_latency_ms) as stddev_latency"),
            expr("max(response_time_ms) as max_response_time"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN severity IN ('critical', 'error') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as error_count")
        ) \
        .select(
            col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
            col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
            col("component"),
            col("event_count"),
            col("avg_response_time"),
            col("stddev_response_time"),
            col("avg_latency"),
            col("stddev_latency"),
            col("max_response_time"),
            col("error_count")
        ) \
        .withColumn("response_time_anomaly",
            col("max_response_time") > (col("avg_response_time") + 3 * col("stddev_response_time"))) \
        .withColumn("latency_anomaly",
            col("avg_latency") > 5000) \
        .withColumn("error_spike",
            col("error_count") > 10) \
        .withColumn("anomaly_detected",
            col("response_time_anomaly") | col("latency_anomaly") | col("error_spike")) \
        .filter(col("anomaly_detected") == True) \
        .withColumn("anomaly_type",
            expr("""CASE 
                WHEN response_time_anomaly THEN 'response_time_spike'
                WHEN latency_anomaly THEN 'high_latency'
                WHEN error_spike THEN 'error_spike'
                ELSE 'multiple_anomalies' END"""))
    
    # 4. Data quality monitoring
    quality_metrics = enriched_events \
        .groupBy(
            window(col("event_time"), "1 minute")
        ) \
        .agg(
            expr("count(*) as total_records"),
            expr("count(DISTINCT event_id) as unique_events"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN event_id IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as null_event_ids"),
            expr("sum(CASE WHEN ingestion_latency_ms > 60000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as late_arrivals"),
            expr("avg(ingestion_latency_ms) as avg_ingestion_latency"),
            expr("max(ingestion_latency_ms) as max_ingestion_latency"),
            expr("percentile_approx(ingestion_latency_ms, 0.99) as p99_ingestion_latency")
        ) \
        .select(
            col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
            col("window.end").alias("window_end"),
            col("total_records"),
            col("unique_events"),
            col("null_event_ids"),
            col("late_arrivals"),
            col("avg_ingestion_latency"),
            col("max_ingestion_latency"),
            col("p99_ingestion_latency")
        ) \
        .withColumn("duplicate_rate_pct",
            ((col("total_records") - col("unique_events")) / col("total_records") * 100)) \
        .withColumn("late_arrival_rate_pct",
            (col("late_arrivals") / col("total_records") * 100)) \
        .withColumn("data_quality_issue",
            (col("duplicate_rate_pct") > 1) | (col("late_arrival_rate_pct") > 5))
    
    # Configure output paths
    checkpoint_base = "/tmp/production_streaming/checkpoint"
    output_base = "/tmp/production_streaming/output"
    
    # Start all queries with production configurations
    
    # Query 1: Real-time metrics
    query1 = realtime_metrics.writeStream \
        .outputMode("update") \
        .format("console") \
        .option("truncate", "false") \
        .option("numRows", 10) \
        .queryName("realtime_metrics") \
        .trigger(processingTime="10 seconds") \
        .option("checkpointLocation", f"{checkpoint_base}/realtime_metrics") \
        .start()
    
    # Query 2: SLA monitoring with alerts
    query2 = sla_monitoring.writeStream \
        .outputMode("update") \
        .format("console") \
        .option("truncate", "false") \
        .option("numRows", 10) \
        .queryName("sla_monitoring") \
        .trigger(processingTime="15 seconds") \
        .option("checkpointLocation", f"{checkpoint_base}/sla_monitoring") \
        .start()
    
    # Query 3: Anomaly detection alerts
    query3 = anomaly_detection.writeStream \
        .outputMode("append") \
        .format("console") \
        .option("truncate", "false") \
        .queryName("anomaly_detection") \
        .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds") \
        .option("checkpointLocation", f"{checkpoint_base}/anomaly_detection") \
        .start()
    
    # Query 4: Data quality monitoring
    query4 = quality_metrics.writeStream \
        .outputMode("update") \
        .format("console") \
        .option("truncate", "false") \
        .queryName("quality_monitoring") \
        .trigger(processingTime="20 seconds") \
        .option("checkpointLocation", f"{checkpoint_base}/quality_monitoring") \
        .start()
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("✓ PRODUCTION STREAMING PIPELINE STARTED")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("\nActive Queries:")
    print("  1. realtime_metrics      - 1-minute tumbling windows")
    print("  2. sla_monitoring        - 5-minute sliding windows with breach detection")
    print("  3. anomaly_detection     - Statistical anomaly detection")
    print("  4. quality_monitoring    - Data quality and latency tracking")
    print("\nFeatures Enabled:")
    print("  ✓ Event time semantics with 2-minute watermark")
    print("  ✓ Multiple time dimensions (event, ingestion, processing)")
    print("  ✓ SLA breach detection and alerting")
    print("  ✓ Anomaly detection with statistical thresholds")
    print("  ✓ Data quality monitoring")
    print("  ✓ Checkpoint-based fault tolerance")
    print("  ✓ Adaptive query execution")
    print("  ✓ Partitioning for scalability")
    print("\nMonitoring:")
    
    # Monitor query health
    import time
    start_time = time.time()
    duration = 40  # Run for 40 seconds
    
    while time.time() - start_time < duration:
        time.sleep(10)
        print(f"\n{'=' * 80}")
        print(f"Query Health Check (Running for {int(time.time() - start_time)}s)")
        print(f"{'=' * 80}")
        
        for i, query in enumerate([query1, query2, query3, query4], 1):
            if query.isActive:
                progress = query.lastProgress
                if progress:
                    print(f"\nQuery {i} ({query.name}):")
                    print(f"  Status: ACTIVE")
                    print(f"  Input Rows: {progress.get('numInputRows', 0)}")
                    print(f"  Processed Rows/sec: {progress.get('processedRowsPerSecond', 0):.2f}")
                    print(f"  Batch Duration: {progress.get('batchDuration', 0)}ms")
                    
                    # State store info
                    state_ops = progress.get('stateOperators', [])
                    if state_ops:
                        for state_op in state_ops:
                            print(f"  State Rows: {state_op.get('numRowsTotal', 0)}")
                            print(f"  State Memory: {state_op.get('memoryUsedBytes', 0) / 1024 / 1024:.2f} MB")
            else:
                print(f"\nQuery {i}: INACTIVE")
    
    print(f"\n{'=' * 80}")
    print("Stopping all queries gracefully...")
    print(f"{'=' * 80}")
    
    # Stop all queries
    query1.stop()
    query2.stop()
    query3.stop()
    query4.stop()
    
    print("\n✓ All queries stopped successfully")
    print(f"✓ Total runtime: {int(time.time() - start_time)} seconds")
    
    spark.stop()
    
    return "Production Example Completed Successfully"

# ============================================================================
# DOCUMENTATION AND EXAMPLES
# ============================================================================

"""
USAGE EXAMPLES:
===============

1. Run Interactive Mode:
   python stream_time_semantics.py

2. Run Specific Pattern:
   python stream_time_semantics.py event
   python stream_time_semantics.py hybrid
   python stream_time_semantics.py production

3. View Guides:
   python stream_time_semantics.py best-practices
   python stream_time_semantics.py troubleshooting

4. Integration Examples:
   python stream_time_semantics.py kafka
   python stream_time_semantics.py delta
   python stream_time_semantics.py monitoring


PATTERN DESCRIPTIONS:
=====================

EVENT TIME SEMANTICS:
- Most accurate for business logic
- Handles out-of-order events
- Requires watermarking
- Example: Financial transactions where event order matters

INGESTION TIME SEMANTICS:
- Timestamp when data enters the system
- Good balance of accuracy and simplicity
- Tracks pipeline performance
- Example: Log aggregation systems

PROCESSING TIME SEMANTICS:
- Uses current system time
- Simplest to implement
- No watermarking needed
- Example: Real-time dashboards

HYBRID TIME SEMANTICS:
- Combines multiple time dimensions
- Comprehensive analysis
- Most flexible
- Example: SLA tracking, audit systems

CUSTOM TIME SEMANTICS:
- Business-specific time logic
- Custom calendars and rules
- Domain-specific requirements
- Example: Trading hours, business days


CONFIGURATION REFERENCE:
========================

Watermark Settings:
-------------------
.withWatermark("timestamp_column", "threshold")

Threshold examples:
- "10 seconds"  - For low-latency systems
- "1 minute"    - For moderate latency
- "10 minutes"  - For high-latency or batch-like streaming
- "1 hour"      - For very delayed data

Window Types:
-------------
1. Tumbling (non-overlapping):
   window(col("timestamp"), "5 minutes")

2. Sliding (overlapping):
   window(col("timestamp"), "10 minutes", "2 minutes")
   
3. Session (gap-based, Spark 3.2+):
   session_window(col("timestamp"), "30 minutes")

Trigger Types:
--------------
.trigger(processingTime="10 seconds")  # Micro-batch every 10s
.trigger(once=True)                     # Process once and stop
.trigger(continuous="1 second")         # Continuous processing (experimental)

Output Modes:
-------------
.outputMode("append")    # Only new rows (for event time)
.outputMode("update")    # New and updated rows (for aggregations)
.outputMode("complete")  # All rows (for small results)


PERFORMANCE TUNING:
===================

Memory Optimization:
--------------------
spark.conf.set("spark.executor.memory", "4g")
spark.conf.set("spark.driver.memory", "2g")
spark.conf.set("spark.memory.fraction", "0.8")

Shuffle Optimization:
---------------------
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true")

State Store Optimization:
-------------------------
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.compactOnCommit", "true")

Checkpoint Configuration:
-------------------------
.option("checkpointLocation", "/path/to/checkpoint")
# Ensure this is on reliable storage (HDFS, S3, etc.)

ERROR HANDLING:
===============

Try-Catch Pattern:
------------------
try:
    query = df.writeStream \\
        .outputMode("update") \\
        .format("console") \\
        .start()
    
    query.awaitTermination()
    
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
    if 'query' in locals():
        query.stop()
finally:
    spark.stop()

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

def test_event_time_window():
    spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[2]").getOrCreate()
    
    # Create test data
    test_data = [
        ("2024-01-01 10:00:00", 100),
        ("2024-01-01 10:00:30", 200),
        ("2024-01-01 10:01:00", 300)
    ]
    
    df = spark.createDataFrame(test_data, ["timestamp", "value"])
    df = df.withColumn("timestamp", to_timestamp(col("timestamp")))
    
    # Apply windowing
    result = df.groupBy(window(col("timestamp"), "1 minute")) \\
        .agg(sum("value").alias("total"))
    
    # Assert results
    assert result.count() > 0
    
    spark.stop()

from datetime import date, timedelta
import random

def generate_sample_data(num_records=100000):
    """Generate sample data for demonstration"""
    data = []
    categories = ['Electronics', 'Clothing', 'Food', 'Books', 'Sports']
    regions = ['North', 'South', 'East', 'West', 'Central']
    
    start_date = date(2023, 1, 1)
    
    for i in range(num_records):
        data.append((
            random.randint(1, 10000),  # customer_id
            random.randint(1, 1000),   # product_id
            start_date + timedelta(days=random.randint(0, 365)),  # order_date
            round(random.uniform(10, 1000), 2),  # amount
            random.choice(categories),  # category
            random.choice(regions),     # region
            random.randint(1, 50)       # quantity
        ))
    
    return data

# Generate and create DataFrame

# =============================================================================
# PATTERN 1: EARLY FILTER PATTERN
# =============================================================================
# Description: Apply filters as early as possible in the transformation chain
# to reduce data volume before expensive operations
# Use Case: When you know specific criteria upfront and can eliminate data early

def early_filter_pattern():
    """
    Early Filter Pattern: Filter data BEFORE joins and aggregations
    Benefits:
    - Reduces data volume early in the pipeline
    - Minimizes shuffle operations
    - Improves overall query performance
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 1: EARLY FILTER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # BAD: Late filtering (filter after aggregation)
    result_bad = orders_df \
        .groupBy("category", "region") \
        .agg(
            _sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_amount"),
            count("*").alias("order_count")
        ) \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("region") == "North")
    
    bad_count = result_bad.count()
    bad_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nBAD APPROACH (Late Filter): {bad_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records processed: {bad_count}")
    
    # GOOD: Early filtering (filter before aggregation)
    start_time = time.time()
    
    result_good = orders_df \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("region") == "North") \
        .groupBy("category", "region") \
        .agg(
            _sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_amount"),
            count("*").alias("order_count")
        )
    
    good_count = result_good.count()
    good_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nGOOD APPROACH (Early Filter): {good_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records processed: {good_count}")
    
    result_good.show(10)
    
    # Performance comparison
    improvement = ((bad_time - good_time) / bad_time) * 100
    print(f"\nPerformance Improvement: {improvement:.2f}%")
    
    return result_good


# =============================================================================
# PATTERN 2: LATE FILTER PATTERN
# =============================================================================
# Description: Apply filters after aggregations or transformations
# Use Case: When filter conditions depend on aggregated results

def late_filter_pattern():
    """
    Late Filter Pattern: Filter data AFTER aggregations
    Benefits:
    - Filters based on computed/aggregated values
    - Useful for threshold-based filtering
    - Enables filtering on derived metrics
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 2: LATE FILTER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # Appropriate use of late filtering
    # Filter customers based on their aggregated spending
    result = orders_df \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("amount").alias("total_spent"),
            count("*").alias("order_count"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_order_value")
        ) \
        .filter(col("total_spent") > 5000) \
        .filter(col("order_count") >= 5) \
        .orderBy(col("total_spent").desc())
    
    elapsed_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nExecution Time: {elapsed_time:.4f} seconds")
    print("\nHigh-Value Customers (Total Spent > $5000 and >= 5 Orders):")
    result.show(10)
    
    # This is appropriate because we MUST aggregate first to calculate
    # total_spent and order_count before filtering
    print("\n✓ Late filtering is APPROPRIATE here because:")
    print("  - Filter conditions depend on aggregated values")
    print("  - Cannot filter on total_spent before calculating it")
    print("  - Used for identifying high-value customer segments")
    
    return result


# =============================================================================
# PATTERN 3: PUSHED-DOWN FILTER PATTERN
# =============================================================================
# Description: Leverage predicate pushdown to filter at the data source level
# Use Case: When reading from databases or partitioned file systems

def pushed_down_filter_pattern():
    """
    Pushed-Down Filter Pattern: Push filters to data source
    Benefits:
    - Reduces data transfer from source
    - Leverages database indexes
    - Minimizes network I/O
    - Reduces memory usage in Spark
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 3: PUSHED-DOWN FILTER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Save data partitioned by date for demonstration
    output_path = "/tmp/orders_partitioned"
    
    orders_df.write \
        .partitionBy("category", "region") \
        .mode("overwrite") \
        .parquet(output_path)
    
    print(f"\nData written to: {output_path}")
    print("Partitioned by: category, region")
    
    # BAD: Read all data then filter
    start_time = time.time()
    result_bad = spark.read.parquet(output_path) \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("region") == "North")
    
    bad_count = result_bad.count()
    bad_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nBAD APPROACH (No Pushdown): {bad_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records: {bad_count}")
    
    # GOOD: Use partition filters (predicate pushdown)
    start_time = time.time()
    result_good = spark.read.parquet(output_path) \
        .where("category = 'Electronics' AND region = 'North'")
    
    good_count = result_good.count()
    good_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nGOOD APPROACH (Partition Pushdown): {good_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records: {good_count}")
    
    result_good.show(10)
    
    # Demonstrate with database-style pushdown
    print("\n--- Database Pushdown Example ---")
    print("When reading from JDBC sources:")
    print("""
    # BAD: Load all data then filter
    df = spark.read.jdbc(url, table) \\
        .filter(col("date") >= "2023-01-01")
    
    # GOOD: Push filter to database
    df = spark.read.jdbc(
        url=url,
        table=table,
        predicates=["date >= '2023-01-01'", "category = 'Electronics'"]
    )
    
    # BETTER: Use pushDownPredicate option
    df = spark.read.format("jdbc") \\
        .option("url", url) \\
        .option("dbtable", table) \\
        .option("pushDownPredicate", True) \\
        .load() \\
        .filter(col("date") >= "2023-01-01")
    """)
    
    return result_good

def combined_filter_pattern():
    """
    Combined Filter Pattern: Efficiently combine multiple filter conditions
    Benefits:
    - Single pass through data
    - Optimized by Catalyst optimizer
    - Better than multiple separate filter operations
    - Cleaner code
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PATTERN 4: COMBINED FILTER PATTERN")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # BAD: Multiple separate filter calls
    start_time = time.time()
    result_bad = orders_df \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("amount") > 100) \
        .filter(col("quantity") >= 2) \
        .filter(col("region").isin(["North", "South"]))
    
    bad_count = result_bad.count()
    bad_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nBAD APPROACH (Multiple Filters): {bad_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records: {bad_count}")
    
    # GOOD: Combined filter with AND conditions
    start_time = time.time()
    result_good = orders_df.filter(
        (col("category") == "Electronics") &
        (col("amount") > 100) &
        (col("quantity") >= 2) &
        (col("region").isin(["North", "South"]))
    )
    
    good_count = result_good.count()
    good_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"\nGOOD APPROACH (Combined Filter): {good_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records: {good_count}")
    
    result_good.show(10)
    
    # Complex combined filters with OR conditions
    print("\n--- Complex Combined Filters ---")
    
    complex_result = orders_df.filter(

    print("  2. Filter by regions (North, East)")
    print("  3. Filter by amount threshold")
    print("  4. Join with customer lifetime value")
    print("  5. Filter by aggregated metrics")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    
    # STEP 1: Early Filter Pattern - Filter raw data first
    print("\n[STEP 1] Applying Early Filters...")
    electronics_orders = orders_df \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("region").isin(["North", "East"])) \
        .filter(col("amount") > 100)
    
    # Cache for reuse (Indexed Filter Pattern)
    electronics_orders.cache()
    initial_count = electronics_orders.count()
    print(f"  Filtered records: {initial_count}")
    
    # STEP 2: Calculate customer metrics
    print("\n[STEP 2] Calculating Customer Metrics...")
    customer_metrics = orders_df \
        .groupBy("customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("amount").alias("lifetime_value"),
            count("*").alias("total_orders"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_order_value")
        )
    
    # Cache customer metrics (Indexed Filter Pattern)
    customer_metrics.cache()
    customer_metrics.count()
    
    # STEP 3: Combined Filter Pattern - Complex conditions
    print("\n[STEP 3] Applying Combined Filters on Metrics...")
    high_value_customers = customer_metrics.filter(
        (col("lifetime_value") > 5000) &
        (col("total_orders") >= 5) &
        (col("avg_order_value") > 200)
    )
    
    hvc_count = high_value_customers.count()
    print(f"  High-value customers: {hvc_count}")
    
    # STEP 4: Join with early filtered data
    print("\n[STEP 4] Joining Filtered Datasets...")
    enriched_orders = electronics_orders \
        .join(high_value_customers, "customer_id", "inner")
    
    join_count = enriched_orders.count()
    print(f"  Enriched orders: {join_count}")
    
    # STEP 5: Late Filter Pattern - Filter on aggregated results
    print("\n[STEP 5] Applying Late Filters on Aggregated Data...")
    final_result = enriched_orders \
        .groupBy("region", "customer_id") \
        .agg(
            _sum("amount").alias("region_spend"),
            count("*").alias("region_orders"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_region_order")
        ) \
        .filter(col("region_spend") > 1000) \
        .orderBy(col("region_spend").desc())
    
    final_count = final_result.count()
    total_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"  Final results: {final_count}")
    print(f"\nTotal Execution Time: {total_time:.4f} seconds")
    
    print("\n--- Final Results ---")
    final_result.show(20)
    
    # Explain the query plan
    print("\n--- Query Execution Plan ---")
    final_result.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    # Cleanup
    electronics_orders.unpersist()
    customer_metrics.unpersist()
    
    return final_result

def performance_comparison_dashboard():
    """
    Compare all filtering patterns with metrics
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE COMPARISON DASHBOARD")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    results = {}
    
    # Test each pattern
    print("\nRunning performance tests...")
    
    # Pattern 1: Early vs Late Filter
    print("\n[1/5] Testing Early Filter Pattern...")
    start = time.time()
    early_result = orders_df \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .groupBy("region") \
        .agg(count("*").alias("count"))
    early_count = early_result.count()
    results['Early Filter'] = time.time() - start
    
    start = time.time()
    late_result = orders_df \
        .groupBy("region", "category") \
        .agg(count("*").alias("count")) \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics")
    late_count = late_result.count()
    results['Late Filter (Inappropriate)'] = time.time() - start
    
    # Pattern 2: Combined Filter
    print("[2/5] Testing Combined Filter Pattern...")
    start = time.time()
    combined_result = orders_df.filter(
        (col("category") == "Electronics") &
        (col("amount") > 100) &
        (col("region").isin(["North", "South"]))
    )
    combined_result.count()
    results['Combined Filter'] = time.time() - start
    
    start = time.time()
    separate_result = orders_df \
        .filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \
        .filter(col("amount") > 100) \
        .filter(col("region").isin(["North", "South"]))
    separate_result.count()
    results['Separate Filters'] = time.time() - start
    
    # Pattern 3: Cached vs Non-cached
    print("[3/5] Testing Indexed Filter Pattern...")
    
    # Non-cached
    start = time.time()
    for i in range(3):
        temp = orders_df.filter(col("amount") > 100).count()
    results['Without Cache (3 iterations)'] = time.time() - start
    
    # Cached
    cached_df = orders_df.filter(col("amount") > 100)
    cached_df.cache()
    cached_df.count()
    
    start = time.time()
    for i in range(3):
        temp = cached_df.count()
    results['With Cache (3 iterations)'] = time.time() - start
    
    cached_df.unpersist()
    
    # Display results
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE RESULTS")
    print("=" * 80)
    print(f"{'Pattern':<35} {'Time (seconds)':<15} {'Relative':<10}")
    print("-" * 80)
    
    baseline = results['Early Filter']
    for pattern, exec_time in sorted(results.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]):
        relative = exec_time / baseline
        print(f"{pattern:<35} {exec_time:>10.4f}      {relative:>6.2f}x")
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("KEY INSIGHTS")
    print("=" * 80)
    print("""
    1. Early Filter Pattern: 
       - Always filter before aggregations when possible
       - Reduces data volume early in the pipeline
    
    2. Combined Filter Pattern:
       - Use single filter with combined conditions
       - Catalyst optimizer handles optimization
    
    3. Pushed-Down Filter Pattern:
       - Leverage partition pruning
       - Push predicates to data sources
    
    4. Indexed Filter Pattern:
       - Cache frequently accessed filtered datasets
       - Use bucketing for repeated joins
    
    5. Late Filter Pattern:
       - Only use when filtering on aggregated values
       - Necessary for threshold-based filtering on metrics
    """)

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ 1. EARLY FILTER PATTERN                                                     ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

✓ DO:
  - Filter data as early as possible in the transformation chain
  - Apply filters before joins, aggregations, and window functions
  - Use partition filters when reading partitioned data
  - Filter before expensive operations like explode()

✗ DON'T:
  - Wait until after aggregations to filter on dimensions
  - Load entire datasets before filtering
  - Apply filters after costly transformations

Example:
  # Good
  df.filter(col("date") >= "2023-01-01").groupBy("category").count()
  
  # Bad
  df.groupBy("category", "date").count().filter(col("date") >= "2023-01-01")

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ 2. LATE FILTER PATTERN                                                      ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

✓ DO:
  - Use when filtering on aggregated/computed values
  - Apply for threshold-based filtering on metrics
  - Filter on window function results
  - Use for post-processing aggregated data

✗ DON'T:
  - Use for filtering on raw dimension columns
  - Apply when early filtering is possible

Example:
  # Appropriate use
  df.groupBy("customer_id") \\
    .agg(sum("amount").alias("total")) \\
    .filter(col("total") > 1000)  # Must aggregate first

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ 3. PUSHED-DOWN FILTER PATTERN                                               ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

✓ DO:
  - Use partition columns in filters for partition pruning
  - Leverage database indexes with JDBC predicates
  - Use file-level statistics (Parquet, ORC)
  - Enable predicate pushdown in configurations

✗ DON'T:
  - Use complex UDFs in partition filters
  - Ignore partitioning scheme when filtering
  - Disable predicate pushdown optimizations

Example:
  # Partition pruning
  spark.read.parquet("data") \\
    .filter(col("year") == 2023)  # Prunes partitions
  
  # JDBC pushdown
  spark.read.jdbc(url, table, predicates=["date >= '2023-01-01'"])

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ 4. COMBINED FILTER PATTERN                                                  ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

✓ DO:
  - Combine multiple conditions in a single filter
  - Use & (and) and | (or) operators appropriately
  - Group related conditions together
  - Use SQL-style where clause for complex logic

✗ DON'T:
```python
✗ DON'T:
  - Chain multiple separate filter() calls unnecessarily
  - Mix filter styles inconsistently
  - Create overly complex single-line conditions

Example:
  # Good
  df.filter((col("category") == "Electronics") & 
            (col("amount") > 100) & 
            (col("region").isin(["North", "South"])))
  
  # Also Good (for complex logic)
  df.filter("""
    (category = 'Electronics' AND amount > 100) OR
    (category = 'Clothing' AND amount > 200)
  """)
  
  # Bad
  df.filter(col("category") == "Electronics") \\
    .filter(col("amount") > 100) \\
    .filter(col("region").isin(["North", "South"]))

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ 5. INDEXED FILTER PATTERN                                                   ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

✓ DO:
  - Cache frequently filtered datasets
  - Use bucketing for repeated joins on same keys
  - Leverage Z-ordering for multi-dimensional queries (Delta Lake)
  - Create broadcast variables for small lookup tables
  - Use bloom filters for existence checks

✗ DON'T:
  - Cache everything (memory overhead)
  - Bucket on high-cardinality columns without analysis
  - Ignore statistics collection

Example:
  # Caching for repeated use
  filtered_df = df.filter(col("active") == True).cache()
  
  # Bucketing for joins
  df.write.bucketBy(10, "customer_id").saveAsTable("orders")
  
  # Z-ordering (Delta Lake)
  deltaTable.optimize().executeZOrderBy("category", "date")

╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ GENERAL FILTERING GUIDELINES                                                ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

1. Filter Selectivity:
   - Apply most selective filters first
   - Use statistics to estimate selectivity
   - Monitor data skew after filtering

2. Data Types:
   - Use appropriate data types for comparisons
   - Avoid implicit type conversions in filters
   - Use native Spark functions over UDFs

3. Null Handling:
   - Be explicit about null handling
   - Use isNull() / isNotNull() appropriately
   - Consider null behavior in complex conditions

4. Performance Monitoring:
   - Use explain() to verify filter pushdown
   - Monitor Spark UI for shuffle operations
   - Check partition pruning in query plans

5. Anti-Patterns to Avoid:
   - Filtering after collect()
   - Using UDFs when native functions available
   - Ignoring partition columns in filters
   - Over-caching without memory consideration

def analyze_filter_performance(df, filter_condition, description=""):
    """
    Utility function to analyze filter performance
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        filter_condition: Filter condition to apply
        description: Description of the filter
    
    Returns:
        Tuple of (filtered_df, execution_time, record_count)
    """
    print(f"\n--- Analyzing: {description} ---")
    
    start_time = time.time()
    filtered_df = df.filter(filter_condition)
    record_count = filtered_df.count()
    execution_time = time.time() - start_time
    
    print(f"Execution Time: {execution_time:.4f} seconds")
    print(f"Records: {record_count:,}")
    
    # Show query plan
    print("\nPhysical Plan:")
    filtered_df.explain()
    
    return filtered_df, execution_time, record_count


def compare_filter_strategies(df, strategies):
    """
    Compare multiple filtering strategies
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        strategies: Dict of {name: filter_function}
    
    Returns:
        Dict of results with timing information
    """
    results = {}
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("COMPARING FILTER STRATEGIES")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    for name, filter_func in strategies.items():
        print(f"\n[Testing] {name}...")
        start_time = time.time()
        
        result_df = filter_func(df)
        count = result_df.count()
        
        exec_time = time.time() - start_time
        results[name] = {
            'time': exec_time,
            'count': count,
            'df': result_df
        }
        
        print(f"  Time: {exec_time:.4f}s | Records: {count:,}")
    
    # Find best strategy
    best_strategy = min(results.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]['time'])
    
    print("\n" + "-" * 80)
    print(f"✓ Best Strategy: {best_strategy[0]}")
    print(f"  Time: {best_strategy[1]['time']:.4f}s")
    print(f"  Records: {best_strategy[1]['count']:,}")
    
    return results


def generate_filter_report(df, filter_columns):
    """
    Generate a comprehensive filter analysis report
    
    Args:
        df: Input DataFrame
        filter_columns: List of columns to analyze
    
    Returns:
        DataFrame with filter statistics
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("FILTER ANALYSIS REPORT")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import countDistinct, min as _min, max as _max
    
    for column in filter_columns:
        print(f"\n--- Column: {column} ---")
        
        stats = df.select(
            count(column).alias("count"),
            countDistinct(column).alias("distinct_count"),
            _min(column).alias("min_value"),
            _max(column).alias("max_value")
        ).collect()[0]
        
        print(f"Total Records: {stats['count']:,}")
        print(f"Distinct Values: {stats['distinct_count']:,}")
        print(f"Min Value: {stats['min_value']}")
        print(f"Max Value: {stats['max_value']}")
        
        # Calculate selectivity
        selectivity = stats['distinct_count'] / stats['count'] if stats['count'] > 0 else 0
        print(f"Selectivity: {selectivity:.4f}")
        
        # Recommendations
        if selectivity > 0.9:
            print("⚠ High cardinality - not ideal for filtering")
        elif selectivity < 0.1:
            print("✓ Low cardinality - good for filtering")
        else:
            print("ℹ Medium cardinality - moderate filtering efficiency")
        
        # Show value distribution for categorical columns
        if stats['distinct_count'] <= 20:
            print("\nValue Distribution:")
            df.groupBy(column).count().orderBy(col("count").desc()).show(10)

"""
PySpark Query Execution DAG Patterns
=====================================
This module demonstrates various DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) patterns
that emerge during Spark query execution and optimization.

# Initialize Spark Session with appropriate configurations
def create_spark_session(app_name):
    """
    Create and configure SparkSession with optimizations enabled
    
    Args:
        app_name (str): Name of the Spark application
    
    Returns:
        SparkSession: Configured Spark session
    """
    return SparkSession.builder \
        .appName(app_name) \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760") \
        .getOrCreate()


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 1: LINEAR DAG PATTERN
# ============================================================================
def linear_dag_pattern(spark):
    """
    Linear DAG Pattern: Sequential transformations forming a straight line
    
    Characteristics:
    - Each transformation depends only on the previous one
    - No branching or merging
    - Simple dependency chain: A -> B -> C -> D
    
    Use Case: ETL pipelines with sequential data cleaning steps
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 1: LINEAR DAG PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create sample sales data
    sales_data = [
        (1, "Product_A", 100.0, "2024-01-01", "Electronics"),
        (2, "Product_B", 150.0, "2024-01-02", "Clothing"),
        (3, "Product_C", 200.0, "2024-01-03", "Electronics"),
        (4, "Product_D", 75.0, "2024-01-04", "Food"),
        (5, "Product_E", 300.0, "2024-01-05", "Electronics"),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("product", StringType(), True),
        StructField("amount", DoubleType(), True),
        StructField("date", StringType(), True),
        StructField("category", StringType(), True)
    ])
    
    # Step 1: Load data
    df = spark.createDataFrame(sales_data, schema)
    print("\nStep 1: Initial DataFrame")
    df.show()
    
    # Step 2: Filter records (Linear transformation 1)
    df_filtered = df.filter(col("amount") > 80)
    print("\nStep 2: After filtering (amount > 80)")
    
    # Step 3: Add computed column (Linear transformation 2)
    df_with_tax = df_filtered.withColumn("tax", col("amount") * 0.1)
    print("\nStep 3: After adding tax column")
    
    # Step 4: Add total amount (Linear transformation 3)
    df_with_total = df_with_tax.withColumn("total", col("amount") + col("tax"))
    print("\nStep 4: After adding total column")
    
    # Step 5: Select and rename columns (Linear transformation 4)
    df_final = df_with_total.select(
        col("id"),
        col("product"),
        col("category"),
        round(col("total"), 2).alias("final_amount")
    )
    
    print("\nFinal Result:")
    df_final.show()
    
    # Explain the execution plan
    print("\n--- Execution Plan ---")
    df_final.explain(extended=True)
    
    return df_final


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 2: TREE DAG PATTERN
# ============================================================================
def tree_dag_pattern(spark):
    """
    Tree DAG Pattern: Single source branching into multiple independent paths
    
    Characteristics:
    - One root DataFrame branches into multiple transformations
    - No merging of branches
    - Pattern: A -> B, A -> C, A -> D (diverging)
    
    Use Case: Generating multiple reports from single data source
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 2: TREE DAG PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create sample employee data
    employee_data = [
        (1, "Alice", "Engineering", 95000, 5),
        (2, "Bob", "Sales", 75000, 3),
        (3, "Charlie", "Engineering", 105000, 7),
        (4, "Diana", "HR", 65000, 2),
        (5, "Eve", "Sales", 85000, 4),
        (6, "Frank", "Engineering", 98000, 6),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("emp_id", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("name", StringType(), True),
        StructField("department", StringType(), True),
        StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("years_exp", IntegerType(), True)
    ])
    
    # Root DataFrame
    df_employees = spark.createDataFrame(employee_data, schema)
    print("\nRoot DataFrame: Employee Data")
    df_employees.show()
    
    # Branch 1: Department-wise salary statistics
    print("\n--- Branch 1: Department Salary Statistics ---")
    df_dept_stats = df_employees.groupBy("department").agg(
        count("*").alias("employee_count"),
        avg("salary").alias("avg_salary"),
        max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
        min("salary").alias("min_salary")
    ).orderBy("department")
    df_dept_stats.show()
    
    # Branch 2: High performers (salary > 90k)
    print("\n--- Branch 2: High Performers ---")
    df_high_performers = df_employees.filter(col("salary") > 90000).select(
        "name",
        "department",
        "salary",
        (col("salary") * 1.1).alias("projected_salary")
    ).orderBy(desc("salary"))
    df_high_performers.show()
    
    # Branch 3: Experience-based categorization
    print("\n--- Branch 3: Experience Categories ---")
    df_experience_categories = df_employees.withColumn(
        "experience_level",
        when(col("years_exp") < 3, "Junior")
        .when((col("years_exp") >= 3) & (col("years_exp") < 6), "Mid-Level")
        .otherwise("Senior")
    ).groupBy("experience_level").agg(
        count("*").alias("count"),
        avg("salary").alias("avg_salary")
    ).orderBy("experience_level")
    df_experience_categories.show()
    
    # Branch 4: Department headcount
    print("\n--- Branch 4: Department Headcount ---")
    df_headcount = df_employees.groupBy("department").count().orderBy(desc("count"))
    df_headcount.show()
    
    print("\n--- Execution Plans for All Branches ---")
    print("\nBranch 1 Plan:")
    df_dept_stats.explain()
    print("\nBranch 2 Plan:")
    df_high_performers.explain()
    
    return {
        "dept_stats": df_dept_stats,
        "high_performers": df_high_performers,
        "experience_categories": df_experience_categories,
        "headcount": df_headcount
    }


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 3: DIAMOND DAG PATTERN
# ============================================================================
def diamond_dag_pattern(spark):
    """
    Diamond DAG Pattern: Branches that diverge and then converge
    
    Characteristics:
    - Single source splits into multiple paths
    - Multiple paths merge back together
    - Pattern: A -> B, A -> C, B+C -> D (diverge then converge)
    
    Use Case: Complex aggregations requiring multiple intermediate computations
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 3: DIAMOND DAG PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create sample order data
    order_data = [
        (1, "Customer_A", "Product_X", 100, 10.0),
        (2, "Customer_B", "Product_Y", 200, 15.0),
        (3, "Customer_A", "Product_Z", 150, 12.0),
        (4, "Customer_C", "Product_X", 300, 10.0),
        (5, "Customer_B", "Product_X", 250, 10.0),
        (6, "Customer_A", "Product_Y", 180, 15.0),
    ]
    
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("order_id", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("customer", StringType(), True),
        StructField("product", StringType(), True),
        StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("unit_price", DoubleType(), True)
    ])
    
    # Root: Original DataFrame
    df_orders = spark.createDataFrame(order_data, schema)
    df_orders = df_orders.withColumn("total_amount", col("quantity") * col("unit_price"))
    
    print("\nRoot DataFrame: Order Data")
    df_orders.show()
    
    # Left Branch: Customer-level aggregation
    print("\n--- Left Branch: Customer Aggregation ---")
    df_customer_agg = df_orders.groupBy("customer").agg(
        count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
        sum("total_amount").alias("total_spent")
    )
    print("Customer Aggregation:")
    df_customer_agg.show()
    
    # Right Branch: Product-level aggregation
    print("\n--- Right Branch: Product Aggregation ---")
    df_product_agg = df_orders.groupBy("product").agg(
        sum("quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
        avg("unit_price").alias("avg_price")
    )
    print("Product Aggregation:")
    df_product_agg.show()
    
    # Convergence: Join both branches
    print("\n--- Convergence: Joining Branches ---")
    # Create a cross-analysis by joining orders with both aggregations
    df_enriched = df_orders \
        .join(df_customer_agg, "customer", "left") \
        .join(df_product_agg, "product", "left") \
        .select(
            "order_id",
            "customer",
            "product",
            "total_amount",
            "order_count",
            "total_spent",
            "total_quantity",
            round("avg_price", 2).alias("avg_price")
        ) \
        .withColumn(
            "customer_contribution_pct",
            round((col("total_amount") / col("total_spent")) * 100, 2)
        )
    
    print("\nFinal Enriched DataFrame:")
    df_enriched.show()
    
    print("\n--- Execution Plan (showing diamond pattern) ---")
    df_enriched.explain(extended=True)
    
    return df_enriched

def complex_dag_pattern(spark):
    """
    Complex DAG Pattern: Multiple sources, branches, and merges
    
    Characteristics:
    - Multiple input sources
    - Multiple branching and merging points
    - Complex interdependencies
    - Pattern: Multiple sources with various transformations and joins
    
    Use Case: Enterprise data warehouse with multiple data sources
    """

        .otherwise(1.0)

    # Branch 2: Transaction summary

    # Branch 3: Customer enrichment (merge customers with tier analysis)
    print("\n--- Branch 3: Customer Enrichment ---")
    df_customer_enriched = df_customers.join(df_tier_analysis, "tier", "left")
    df_customer_enriched.show()
    
    # Complex Merge 1: Customers with transactions
    print("\n--- Complex Merge 1: Customers + Transactions ---")
    df_customer_transactions = df_customer_enriched.join(
        df_transaction_summary,
        "customer_id",
        "left"
```python
    ).fillna(0, subset=["transaction_count", "total_amount", "avg_amount"])
    df_customer_transactions.show()
    
    # Complex Merge 2: Add product category analysis
    print("\n--- Complex Merge 2: Adding Product Categories ---")
    # Simulate category assignment to transactions
    df_transactions_with_category = df_transactions.withColumn(
        "category_id",
        (col("transaction_id") % 3) + 1  # Simple assignment for demo
    )
    
    df_category_revenue = df_transactions_with_category \
        .filter(col("status") == "Completed") \
        .groupBy("category_id") \
        .agg(sum("amount").alias("category_revenue"))
    
    df_category_analysis = df_products.join(
        df_category_revenue,
        "category_id",
        "left"

        "commission_earned",
        col("category_revenue") * col("commission_rate")
    )
    df_category_analysis.show()
    
    # Final Complex Merge: Comprehensive customer analysis
    print("\n--- Final Complex Merge: Comprehensive Analysis ---")
    df_comprehensive = df_customer_transactions.join(
        df_transactions_with_category.select("customer_id", "category_id").distinct(),
        "customer_id",
        "left"

        df_products,
        "category_id",
        "left"
    ).select(
        "customer_id",
        "name",
        "tier",
        "tier_multiplier",
        "transaction_count",
        round("total_amount", 2).alias("total_spent"),
        round("avg_amount", 2).alias("avg_transaction"),
        "category_name",
        "commission_rate"
    ).withColumn(
        "adjusted_value",
        round(col("total_spent") * col("tier_multiplier"), 2)
    ).orderBy(desc("adjusted_value"))
    
    print("\nFinal Comprehensive Customer Analysis:")
    df_comprehensive.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Complex DAG Execution Plan ---")
    df_comprehensive.explain(extended=True)
    
    return {
        "tier_analysis": df_tier_analysis,
        "transaction_summary": df_transaction_summary,
        "category_analysis": df_category_analysis,
        "comprehensive": df_comprehensive
    }


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 5: OPTIMIZED DAG PATTERN
# ============================================================================
def optimized_dag_pattern(spark):
    """
    Optimized DAG Pattern: Demonstrates Catalyst optimizer improvements
    
    Characteristics:
    - Predicate pushdown
    - Column pruning
    - Constant folding
    - Join reordering
    - Broadcast joins
    
    Use Case: Performance-critical queries requiring optimization
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 5: OPTIMIZED DAG PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Create larger datasets for optimization demonstration
    from pyspark.sql.functions import expr
    
    # Large fact table
    print("\n--- Creating Sample Data ---")
    df_sales = spark.range(0, 10000).select(
        col("id").alias("sale_id"),
        (col("id") % 100).alias("customer_id"),
        (col("id") % 50).alias("product_id"),
        (col("id") % 10).alias("store_id"),
        (expr("rand() * 1000")).alias("amount"),
        expr("date_sub(current_date(), cast(rand() * 365 as int))").alias("sale_date")
    )
    
    # Dimension tables (small, suitable for broadcast)
    df_customers = spark.range(0, 100).select(
        col("id").alias("customer_id"),
        concat(lit("Customer_"), col("id")).alias("customer_name"),
        when(col("id") % 3 == 0, "Gold")
        .when(col("id") % 3 == 1, "Silver")
        .otherwise("Bronze").alias("tier")
    )
    
    df_products = spark.range(0, 50).select(
        col("id").alias("product_id"),
        concat(lit("Product_"), col("id")).alias("product_name"),
        when(col("id") % 4 == 0, "Electronics")
        .when(col("id") % 4 == 1, "Clothing")
        .when(col("id") % 4 == 2, "Food")
        .otherwise("Other").alias("category")
    )
    
    df_stores = spark.range(0, 10).select(
        col("id").alias("store_id"),
        concat(lit("Store_"), col("id")).alias("store_name"),
        when(col("id") < 5, "North").otherwise("South").alias("region")
    )
    
    print(f"Sales records: {df_sales.count()}")
    print(f"Customers: {df_customers.count()}")
    print(f"Products: {df_products.count()}")
    print(f"Stores: {df_stores.count()}")
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 1: Predicate Pushdown
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 1: Predicate Pushdown")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Unoptimized: Filter after join
    print("\nUnoptimized Query (filter after join):")
    df_unoptimized = df_sales.join(df_customers, "customer_id") \
        .filter(col("tier") == "Gold") \
        .filter(col("amount") > 500)
    
    print("Unoptimized Plan:")
    df_unoptimized.explain()
    
    # Optimized: Filter before join (Catalyst does this automatically)
    print("\nOptimized Query (filter before join - Catalyst optimizes):")
    df_optimized = df_sales.filter(col("amount") > 500) \
        .join(df_customers.filter(col("tier") == "Gold"), "customer_id")
    
    print("Optimized Plan:")
    df_optimized.explain()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 2: Column Pruning
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 2: Column Pruning")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Unoptimized: Select all columns then filter
    print("\nUnoptimized Query (selecting unnecessary columns):")
    df_unpruned = df_sales.join(df_customers, "customer_id") \
        .join(df_products, "product_id") \
        .select("sale_id", "amount", "customer_name")
    
    print("Unpruned Plan:")
    df_unpruned.explain()
    
    # Optimized: Select only needed columns early
    print("\nOptimized Query (column pruning):")
    df_pruned = df_sales.select("sale_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "amount") \
        .join(df_customers.select("customer_id", "customer_name"), "customer_id") \
        .select("sale_id", "amount", "customer_name")
    
    print("Pruned Plan:")
    df_pruned.explain()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 3: Broadcast Join
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 3: Broadcast Join")
    print("-"*80)
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Regular join
    print("\nRegular Join:")
    df_regular_join = df_sales.join(df_customers, "customer_id")
    print("Regular Join Plan:")
    df_regular_join.explain()
    
    # Broadcast join (for small dimension tables)
    print("\nBroadcast Join:")
    df_broadcast_join = df_sales.join(broadcast(df_customers), "customer_id")
    print("Broadcast Join Plan:")
    df_broadcast_join.explain()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 4: Caching/Persistence
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 4: Caching for Reuse")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Cache frequently used intermediate results
    df_filtered_sales = df_sales.filter(col("amount") > 500).cache()
    df_filtered_sales.count()  # Materialize cache
    
    print("\nCached DataFrame - First Use:")
    result1 = df_filtered_sales.groupBy("customer_id").count()
    result1.show(5)
    
    print("\nCached DataFrame - Second Use (from cache):")
    result2 = df_filtered_sales.groupBy("product_id").agg(sum("amount"))
    result2.show(5)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 5: Partition Pruning
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 5: Partition Pruning")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Repartition by date for partition pruning
    df_partitioned = df_sales.repartition(10, "sale_date")
    
    # Query with partition filter
    print("\nQuery with partition pruning:")
    df_partition_pruned = df_partitioned.filter(
        col("sale_date") >= "2024-01-01"
    ).groupBy("store_id").agg(
        sum("amount").alias("total_sales")
    )
    
    print("Partition Pruned Plan:")
    df_partition_pruned.explain()
    df_partition_pruned.show()
    
    # ========================================================================
    # OPTIMIZATION 6: Aggregate Pushdown
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("OPTIMIZATION 6: Aggregate Pushdown")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Aggregation before join (more efficient)
    print("\nOptimized: Aggregate before join:")
    df_sales_agg = df_sales.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
        sum("amount").alias("total_spent"),
        count("*").alias("purchase_count")
    )
    
    df_customer_summary = df_sales_agg.join(
        broadcast(df_customers),
        "customer_id"
    ).select(
        "customer_name",
        "tier",
        round("total_spent", 2).alias("total_spent"),
        "purchase_count"
    ).orderBy(desc("total_spent"))
    
    print("\nCustomer Summary (Optimized):")
    df_customer_summary.show(10)
    
    print("\nOptimized Execution Plan:")
    df_customer_summary.explain(extended=True)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # COMPREHENSIVE OPTIMIZED QUERY
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "-"*80)
    print("COMPREHENSIVE OPTIMIZED QUERY")
    print("-"*80)
    
    # Combine multiple optimization techniques
    df_comprehensive_optimized = df_sales \
        .filter(col("amount") > 100) \
        .select("sale_id", "customer_id", "product_id", "store_id", "amount", "sale_date") \
        .join(broadcast(df_customers.select("customer_id", "customer_name", "tier")), "customer_id") \
        .join(broadcast(df_products.select("product_id", "category")), "product_id") \
        .join(broadcast(df_stores.select("store_id", "region")), "store_id") \
        .groupBy("tier", "category", "region") \
        .agg(
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            sum("amount").alias("total_revenue"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_transaction"),
            min("amount").alias("min_transaction"),
            max("amount").alias("max_transaction")
        ) \
        .withColumn("avg_transaction", round(col("avg_transaction"), 2)) \
        .withColumn("total_revenue", round(col("total_revenue"), 2)) \
        .orderBy(desc("total_revenue"))
    
    print("\nComprehensive Optimized Results:")
    df_comprehensive_optimized.show(20, truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- Final Optimized Execution Plan ---")
    df_comprehensive_optimized.explain(mode="formatted")
    
    # Cleanup cache
    df_filtered_sales.unpersist()
    
    return {
        "predicate_pushdown": df_optimized,
        "column_pruning": df_pruned,
        "broadcast_join": df_broadcast_join,
        "customer_summary": df_customer_summary,
        "comprehensive": df_comprehensive_optimized
    }


# ============================================================================
# BONUS: DAG VISUALIZATION AND COMPARISON
# ============================================================================
def compare_dag_patterns(spark):
    """
    Compare different DAG patterns and their characteristics
    """
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("DAG PATTERN COMPARISON")
    print("="*80)
    
    comparison_data = [
        ("Linear", "Sequential", "Low", "Simple ETL", "A->B->C->D"),
        ("Tree", "Diverging", "Medium", "Multiple Reports", "A->(B,C,D)"),
        ("Diamond", "Diverge+Converge", "Medium", "Complex Aggregations", "A->(B,C)->D"),
        ("Complex", "Multi-source", "High", "Data Warehouse", "Multiple sources/joins"),
        ("Optimized", "Optimized", "Variable", "Performance Critical", "Catalyst optimizations")
    ]
    
    df_comparison = spark.createDataFrame(
        comparison_data,
        ["Pattern", "Flow_Type", "Complexity", "Use_Case", "Structure"]
    )
    
    print("\nDAG Pattern Comparison:")
    df_comparison.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Performance characteristics
    perf_data = [
        ("Linear", "Low", "Low", "Sequential", "Good"),
        ("Tree", "Medium", "Medium", "Parallel branches", "Excellent"),
        ("Diamond", "Medium", "High", "Some parallelization", "Good"),
        ("Complex", "High", "Very High", "Limited by dependencies", "Fair"),
        ("Optimized", "Variable", "Low", "Highly parallel", "Excellent")
    ]
    
    df_performance = spark.createDataFrame(
        perf_data,
        ["Pattern", "Memory_Usage", "Shuffle_Operations", "Parallelization", "Performance"]
    )
    
    print("\nPerformance Characteristics:")
    df_performance.show(truncate=False)

DAG PATTERN SELECTION GUIDE:
============================

1. LINEAR DAG PATTERN
   When to use:
   - Simple sequential transformations
   - Data cleaning pipelines
   - Single-path ETL processes
   
   Best Practices:
   - Keep transformations simple and focused
   - Use appropriate data types early
   - Apply filters as early as possible
   - Avoid unnecessary intermediate steps

2. TREE DAG PATTERN
   When to use:
   - Multiple independent reports from same source
   - Parallel processing of different metrics
   - Broadcasting single source to multiple consumers
   
   Best Practices:
   - Cache the root DataFrame if reused multiple times
   - Ensure branches are truly independent
   - Consider using foreachPartition for side effects
   - Monitor memory usage with multiple branches

3. DIAMOND DAG PATTERN
   When to use:
   - Aggregations requiring multiple perspectives
   - Feature engineering with different groupings
   - Reconciliation processes
   
   Best Practices:
   - Cache intermediate results if used multiple times
   - Use appropriate join types (inner, left, etc.)
   - Be aware of data skew in joins
   - Consider repartitioning before joins

4. COMPLEX DAG PATTERN
   When to use:
   - Enterprise data warehouses
   - Multi-source integrations
   - Complex business logic
   
   Best Practices:
   - Break down into manageable sub-queries
   - Use broadcast joins for small tables
   - Monitor shuffle operations
   - Consider using temporary views for readability
   - Profile and optimize bottlenecks

5. OPTIMIZED DAG PATTERN
   When to use:
   - Performance-critical applications
   - Large-scale data processing
   - Resource-constrained environments
   
   Best Practices:
   - Enable Adaptive Query Execution (AQE)
   - Use broadcast joins for small dimensions
   - Apply filters early (predicate pushdown)
   - Select only necessary columns (column pruning)
   - Cache reused DataFrames
   - Partition data appropriately
   - Monitor and tune shuffle partitions
   - Use appropriate file formats (Parquet, ORC)

GENERAL OPTIMIZATION TIPS:
==========================
✓ Use .explain() to understand query plans
✓ Monitor Spark UI for bottlenecks
✓ Avoid UDFs when possible (use built-in functions)
✓ Repartition data to balance workload
✓ Use appropriate storage levels for caching
✓ Minimize wide transformations (shuffles)
✓ Coalesce instead of repartition when reducing partitions
✓ Use DataFrame API over RDD API
✓ Enable cost-based optimizer (CBO)
✓ Collect statistics on tables

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID:
=========================
✗ Excessive shuffling
✗ Data skew in joins
✗ Small files problem
✗ Unnecessary caching
✗ Over-partitioning or under-partitioning
✗ Cartesian products
✗ Collecting large datasets to driver
✗ Using collect() instead of take() for sampling
