    metrics = sensors \\
        .withWatermark("timestamp", "10 seconds") \\
        .groupBy(window("timestamp", "5 seconds"), "sensor_id") \\

    metrics_query = metrics.writeStream \\
        .format("delta") \\
        .trigger(processingTime="5 seconds") \\
        .start()

    # Priority-based processing
    errors = logs.filter(col("level") == "ERROR")

def one_to_one_relationship():
    """
    One-to-One Relationship Pattern
    Example: User and UserProfile (each user has exactly one profile)
    """
    
    # Create Users table
    users_data = [
        (1, "john_doe", "john@example.com"),
        (2, "jane_smith", "jane@example.com"),
        (3, "bob_wilson", "bob@example.com"),
        (4, "alice_brown", "alice@example.com")
    ]
    users_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        users_data, 
        ["user_id", "username", "email"]
    )
    
    # Create UserProfiles table (one profile per user)
    profiles_data = [
        (1, 1, "John", "Doe", "New York", "555-0101"),
        (2, 2, "Jane", "Smith", "Los Angeles", "555-0102"),
        (3, 3, "Bob", "Wilson", "Chicago", "555-0103"),
        (4, 4, "Alice", "Brown", "Houston", "555-0104")
    ]
    profiles_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        profiles_data,
        ["profile_id", "user_id", "first_name", "last_name", "city", "phone"]
    )
    
    print("\nUsers Table:")
    users_df.show()
    
    print("User Profiles Table:")
    profiles_df.show()
    
    # Join operation for one-to-one relationship
    # Using inner join to get complete user information
    complete_user_info = users_df.join(
        profiles_df,
        users_df.user_id == profiles_df.user_id,
        "inner"
    ).select(
        users_df.user_id,
        users_df.username,
        users_df.email,
        profiles_df.first_name,
        profiles_df.last_name,
        profiles_df.city,
        profiles_df.phone
    )
    
    print("\nOne-to-One Join Result (Complete User Information):")
    complete_user_info.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Validation: Check for orphaned records
    print("\nValidation - Checking for orphaned profiles:")
    orphaned_profiles = profiles_df.join(
        users_df,
        profiles_df.user_id == users_df.user_id,
        "left_anti"
    )
    
    if orphaned_profiles.count() == 0:
        print("✓ No orphaned profiles found - One-to-One integrity maintained")
    else:
        print("✗ Orphaned profiles detected:")
        orphaned_profiles.show()
    
    return complete_user_info

        ["customer_id", "company_name", "email", "tier"]
    )
    
    # Create Orders table (multiple orders per customer)
    orders_data = [
        (1001, 101, "2024-01-15", 5000.00, "Completed"),
        (1002, 101, "2024-02-20", 7500.00, "Completed"),
        (1003, 101, "2024-03-10", 3200.00, "Pending"),
        (1004, 102, "2024-01-25", 2100.00, "Completed"),
        (1005, 102, "2024-03-05", 4300.00, "Shipped"),
        (1006, 103, "2024-02-14", 9800.00, "Completed"),
        (1007, 104, "2024-03-20", 1500.00, "Processing")
    ]
    orders_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        orders_data,
        ["order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "amount", "status"]
    )
    
    print("\nCustomers Table:")
    customers_df.show()
    
    print("Orders Table:")
    orders_df.show()
    
    # Method 1: Join with all orders expanded
    customer_orders = customers_df.join(
        orders_df,
        customers_df.customer_id == orders_df.customer_id,
        "left"
    ).select(
        customers_df.customer_id,
        customers_df.company_name,
        customers_df.tier,
        orders_df.order_id,
        orders_df.order_date,
        orders_df.amount,
        orders_df.status
    )
    
    print("\nOne-to-Many Join Result (All Customer Orders):")
    customer_orders.orderBy("customer_id", "order_date").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 2: Aggregated view (customer with order statistics)
    customer_order_summary = customers_df.join(
        orders_df,
        customers_df.customer_id == orders_df.customer_id,
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        customers_df.customer_id,
        customers_df.company_name,
        customers_df.tier
    ).agg(
        F.count(orders_df.order_id).alias("total_orders"),
        F.sum(orders_df.amount).alias("total_revenue"),
        F.avg(orders_df.amount).alias("avg_order_value"),
        F.collect_list(orders_df.order_id).alias("order_ids"),
        F.max(orders_df.order_date).alias("last_order_date")
    ).orderBy("total_revenue", ascending=False)
    
    print("\nCustomer Order Summary (Aggregated One-to-Many):")
    customer_order_summary.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 3: Nested structure (orders as array)
    customer_with_orders = customers_df.join(
        orders_df,
        customers_df.customer_id == orders_df.customer_id,
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        customers_df.customer_id,
        customers_df.company_name,
        customers_df.email,
        customers_df.tier
    ).agg(
        collect_list(
            struct(
                orders_df.order_id,
                orders_df.order_date,
                orders_df.amount,
                orders_df.status
            )
        ).alias("orders")
    )
    
    print("\nCustomer with Nested Orders (Structured One-to-Many):")
    customer_with_orders.show(truncate=False)
    
    return customer_orders, customer_order_summary

one_to_many_result, summary_result = one_to_many_relationship()

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("PATTERN 3: MANY-TO-MANY RELATIONSHIP")
print("=" * 80)
print("Description: Records in Table A can relate to multiple records in Table B and vice versa")
print("-" * 80)

def many_to_many_relationship():
    """
    Many-to-Many Relationship Pattern
    Example: Students and Courses (students enroll in multiple courses, 
             courses have multiple students)
    Uses a junction/bridge table
    """
    
    # Create Students table
    students_data = [
        (201, "Emma Watson", "Computer Science", 3),
        (202, "Liam Chen", "Data Science", 2),
        (203, "Olivia Martinez", "Computer Science", 4),
        (204, "Noah Johnson", "Information Systems", 1),
        (205, "Sophia Lee", "Data Science", 3)
    ]
    students_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        students_data,
        ["student_id", "student_name", "major", "year"]
    )
    
    # Create Courses table
    courses_data = [
        (301, "Database Systems", "CS", 3),
        (302, "Machine Learning", "DS", 4),
        (303, "Data Structures", "CS", 3),
        (304, "Big Data Analytics", "DS", 4),
        (305, "Web Development", "CS", 3)
    ]
    courses_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        courses_data,
        ["course_id", "course_name", "department", "credits"]
    )
    
    # Create Enrollments table (junction/bridge table)
    enrollments_data = [
        (201, 301, "2024-Spring", "A"),
        (201, 302, "2024-Spring", "B+"),
        (201, 303, "2024-Fall", "A-"),
        (202, 302, "2024-Spring", "A"),
        (202, 304, "2024-Spring", "A-"),
        (203, 301, "2024-Spring", "B"),
        (203, 303, "2024-Spring", "A"),
        (203, 305, "2024-Fall", "A-"),
        (204, 301, "2024-Spring", "B+"),
        (204, 303, "2024-Spring", "B"),
        (205, 302, "2024-Spring", "A"),
        (205, 304, "2024-Spring", "A+")
    ]
    enrollments_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        enrollments_data,
        ["student_id", "course_id", "semester", "grade"]
    )
    
    print("\nStudents Table:")
    students_df.show()
    
    print("Courses Table:")
    courses_df.show()
    
    print("Enrollments Table (Junction Table):")
    enrollments_df.show()
    
    # Method 1: Student perspective (students with their courses)
    student_courses = students_df.join(
        enrollments_df,
        students_df.student_id == enrollments_df.student_id,
        "left"
    ).join(
        courses_df,
        enrollments_df.course_id == courses_df.course_id,
        "left"
    ).select(
        students_df.student_id,
        students_df.student_name,
        students_df.major,
        courses_df.course_name,
        courses_df.department,
        enrollments_df.semester,
        enrollments_df.grade
    )
    
    print("\nMany-to-Many: Student-Course Enrollments:")
    student_courses.orderBy("student_id", "course_name").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 2: Course perspective (courses with their students)
    course_students = courses_df.join(
        enrollments_df,
        courses_df.course_id == enrollments_df.course_id,
        "left"
    ).join(
        students_df,
        enrollments_df.student_id == students_df.student_id,
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        courses_df.course_id,
        courses_df.course_name,
        courses_df.department
    ).agg(
        F.count(students_df.student_id).alias("enrolled_students"),
        collect_list(students_df.student_name).alias("student_names"),
        F.avg(
            when(col("grade") == "A+", 4.3)
            .when(col("grade") == "A", 4.0)
            .when(col("grade") == "A-", 3.7)
            .when(col("grade") == "B+", 3.3)
            .when(col("grade") == "B", 3.0)
            .otherwise(2.7)
        ).alias("avg_gpa")
    )
    
    print("\nMany-to-Many: Course Enrollment Summary:")
    course_students.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 3: Aggregated student view with nested courses
    student_course_list = students_df.join(
        enrollments_df,
        students_df.student_id == enrollments_df.student_id,
        "left"
    ).join(
        courses_df,
        enrollments_df.course_id == courses_df.course_id,
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        students_df.student_id,
        students_df.student_name,
        students_df.major
    ).agg(
        F.count(courses_df.course_id).alias("total_courses"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                courses_df.course_name,
                enrollments_df.semester,
                enrollments_df.grade
            )
        ).alias("courses")
    )
    
    print("\nMany-to-Many: Students with Course Lists:")
    student_course_list.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 4: Find students sharing courses (advanced M2M query)
    shared_courses = enrollments_df.alias("e1").join(
        enrollments_df.alias("e2"),
        (col("e1.course_id") == col("e2.course_id")) & 
        (col("e1.student_id") < col("e2.student_id"))
    ).join(
        students_df.alias("s1"),
        col("e1.student_id") == col("s1.student_id")
    ).join(
        students_df.alias("s2"),
        col("e2.student_id") == col("s2.student_id")
    ).
```python
    ).join(
        courses_df,
        col("e1.course_id") == courses_df.course_id
    ).select(
        col("s1.student_name").alias("student_1"),
        col("s2.student_name").alias("student_2"),
        courses_df.course_name,
        col("e1.semester")
    )
    
    print("\nMany-to-Many: Students Sharing Courses:")
    shared_courses.show(truncate=False)
    
    return student_courses, course_students, student_course_list

m2m_student_courses, m2m_course_students, m2m_student_list = many_to_many_relationship()

print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("PATTERN 4: SELF-REFERENTIAL RELATIONSHIP")
print("=" * 80)
print("Description: Records in a table relate to other records in the same table")
print("-" * 80)

def self_referential_relationship():
    """
    Self-Referential Relationship Pattern
    Example: Employee hierarchy (employees report to other employees)
    """
    
    # Create Employees table with manager reference
    employees_data = [
        (1, "Sarah Connor", "CEO", None, 250000),
        (2, "John Smith", "CTO", 1, 180000),
        (3, "Mary Johnson", "CFO", 1, 175000),
        (4, "David Lee", "VP Engineering", 2, 150000),
        (5, "Lisa Wang", "VP Product", 2, 145000),
        (6, "Mike Brown", "Senior Developer", 4, 120000),
        (7, "Anna Davis", "Senior Developer", 4, 118000),
        (8, "Tom Wilson", "Developer", 6, 95000),
        (9, "Emily Chen", "Developer", 6, 92000),
        (10, "Chris Taylor", "Product Manager", 5, 110000),
        (11, "Jessica Martinez", "Accountant", 3, 85000),
        (12, "Robert Garcia", "Junior Developer", 7, 75000)
    ]
    employees_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        employees_data,
        ["employee_id", "name", "position", "manager_id", "salary"]
    )
    
    print("\nEmployees Table (Self-Referential):")
    employees_df.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 1: Join employees with their managers (1 level)
    employees_with_managers = employees_df.alias("emp").join(
        employees_df.alias("mgr"),
        col("emp.manager_id") == col("mgr.employee_id"),
        "left"
    ).select(
        col("emp.employee_id"),
        col("emp.name").alias("employee_name"),
        col("emp.position"),
        col("emp.salary"),
        col("mgr.name").alias("manager_name"),
        col("mgr.position").alias("manager_position")
    )
    
    print("\nSelf-Referential: Employees with Their Managers:")
    employees_with_managers.orderBy("employee_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 2: Find all direct reports for each manager
    manager_reports = employees_df.alias("mgr").join(
        employees_df.alias("emp"),
        col("mgr.employee_id") == col("emp.manager_id"),
        "inner"
    ).groupBy(
        col("mgr.employee_id"),
        col("mgr.name").alias("manager_name"),
        col("mgr.position").alias("manager_position")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("emp.employee_id")).alias("direct_reports"),
        collect_list(col("emp.name")).alias("report_names"),
        F.sum(col("emp.salary")).alias("team_salary_total")
    ).orderBy("direct_reports", ascending=False)
    
    print("\nSelf-Referential: Managers with Direct Reports:")
    manager_reports.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 3: Multi-level hierarchy (2 levels deep)
    two_level_hierarchy = employees_df.alias("emp").join(
        employees_df.alias("mgr1"),
        col("emp.manager_id") == col("mgr1.employee_id"),
        "left"
    ).join(
        employees_df.alias("mgr2"),
        col("mgr1.manager_id") == col("mgr2.employee_id"),
        "left"
    ).select(
        col("emp.employee_id"),
        col("emp.name").alias("employee"),
        col("emp.position").alias("emp_position"),
        col("mgr1.name").alias("direct_manager"),
        col("mgr2.name").alias("skip_level_manager")
    )
    
    print("\nSelf-Referential: Two-Level Management Hierarchy:")
    two_level_hierarchy.orderBy("employee_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 4: Calculate organization depth/level
    # Level 1: CEO (no manager)
    level_1 = employees_df.filter(col("manager_id").isNull()).withColumn("level", lit(1))
    
    # Level 2: Reports to CEO
    level_2 = employees_df.alias("e").join(
        level_1.alias("l1"),
        col("e.manager_id") == col("l1.employee_id")
    ).select(
        col("e.employee_id"),
        col("e.name"),
        col("e.position"),
        col("e.manager_id"),
        col("e.salary"),
        lit(2).alias("level")
    )
    
    # Level 3: Reports to Level 2
    level_3 = employees_df.alias("e").join(
        level_2.alias("l2"),
        col("e.manager_id") == col("l2.employee_id")
    ).select(
        col("e.employee_id"),
        col("e.name"),
        col("e.position"),
        col("e.manager_id"),
        col("e.salary"),
        lit(3).alias("level")
    )
    
    # Level 4: Reports to Level 3
    level_4 = employees_df.alias("e").join(
        level_3.alias("l3"),
        col("e.manager_id") == col("l3.employee_id")
    ).select(
        col("e.employee_id"),
        col("e.name"),
        col("e.position"),
        col("e.manager_id"),
        col("e.salary"),
        lit(4).alias("level")
    )
    
    # Union all levels
    org_hierarchy = level_1.unionAll(level_2).unionAll(level_3).unionAll(level_4)
    
    print("\nSelf-Referential: Organizational Hierarchy by Level:")
    org_hierarchy.orderBy("level", "employee_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 5: Find employees without direct reports (leaf nodes)
    leaf_employees = employees_df.alias("e1").join(
        employees_df.alias("e2"),
        col("e1.employee_id") == col("e2.manager_id"),
        "left_anti"
    ).select(
        col("e1.employee_id"),
        col("e1.name"),
        col("e1.position"),
        col("e1.salary")
    )
    
    print("\nSelf-Referential: Leaf Employees (No Direct Reports):")
    leaf_employees.show(truncate=False)
    
    return employees_with_managers, manager_reports, org_hierarchy

self_ref_emp_mgr, self_ref_reports, self_ref_hierarchy = self_referential_relationship()

# PATTERN 5: HIERARCHICAL RELATIONSHIP PATTERN
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("PATTERN 5: HIERARCHICAL RELATIONSHIP")
print("=" * 80)
print("Description: Multi-level parent-child relationships forming a tree structure")
print("-" * 80)

def hierarchical_relationship():
    """
    Hierarchical Relationship Pattern
    Example: Product categories with subcategories (tree structure)
    """
    
    # Create Categories table with parent-child hierarchy
    categories_data = [
        (1, "Electronics", None, 1),
        (2, "Computers", 1, 2),
        (3, "Mobile Devices", 1, 2),
        (4, "Home & Garden", None, 1),
        (5, "Laptops", 2, 3),
        (6, "Desktops", 2, 3),
        (7, "Smartphones", 3, 3),
        (8, "Tablets", 3, 3),
        (9, "Gaming Laptops", 5, 4),
        (10, "Business Laptops", 5, 4),
        (11, "Furniture", 4, 2),
        (12, "Garden Tools", 4, 2),
        (13, "Office Chairs", 11, 3),
        (14, "Desks", 11, 3),
        (15, "Android Phones", 7, 4),
        (16, "iPhones", 7, 4)
    ]
    categories_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        categories_data,
        ["category_id", "category_name", "parent_id", "level"]
    )
    
    print("\nCategories Table (Hierarchical):")
    categories_df.orderBy("category_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 1: Categories with immediate parent
    categories_with_parent = categories_df.alias("child").join(
        categories_df.alias("parent"),
        col("child.parent_id") == col("parent.category_id"),
        "left"
    ).select(
        col("child.category_id"),
        col("child.category_name"),
        col("child.level"),
        col("parent.category_name").alias("parent_category"),
        col("parent.level").alias("parent_level")
    )
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Categories with Parent:")
    categories_with_parent.orderBy("category_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 2: Build full path (breadcrumb) for each category
    # Level 1 (root)
    level_1_path = categories_df.filter(col("parent_id").isNull()).select(
        col("category_id"),
        col("category_name"),
        col("category_name").alias("full_path"),
        col("level")
    )
    
    # Level 2
    level_2_path = categories_df.alias("c").filter(col("level") == 2).join(
        level_1_path.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        concat_ws(" > ", col("p.full_path"), col("c.category_name")).alias("full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    )
    
    # Level 3
    level_2_for_join = categories_df.alias("c").filter(col("level") == 2).join(
        level_1_path.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        concat_ws(" > ", col("p.full_path"), col("c.category_name")).alias("full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    )
    
    level_3_path = categories_df.alias("c").filter(col("level") == 3).join(
        level_2_for_join.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        concat_ws(" > ", col("p.full_path"), col("c.category_name")).alias("full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    )
    
    # Level 4
    level_3_for_join = categories_df.alias("c").filter(col("level") == 3).join(
        level_2_for_join.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        concat_ws(" > ", col("p.full_path"), col("c.category_name")).alias("full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    )
    
    level_4_path = categories_df.alias("c").filter(col("level") == 4).join(
        level_3_for_join.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        concat_ws(" > ", col("p.full_path"), col("c.category_name")).alias("full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    )
    
    # Union all levels
    category_paths = level_1_path.unionAll(level_2_path).unionAll(level_3_path).unionAll(level_4_path)
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Category Full Paths (Breadcrumbs):")
    category_paths.orderBy("level", "category_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 3: Find all descendants for a given category
    electronics_id = 1
    
    # Direct children (level 2)
    direct_children = categories_df.filter(col("parent_id") == electronics_id)
    
    # Grandchildren (level 3)
    grandchildren = categories_df.alias("c").join(
        direct_children.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(col("c.*"))
    
    # Great-grandchildren (level 4)
    great_grandchildren = categories_df.alias("c").join(
        grandchildren.alias("p"),
        col("c.parent_id") == col("p.category_id")
    ).select(col("c.*"))
    
    # All descendants
    all_descendants = direct_children.unionAll(grandchildren).unionAll(great_grandchildren)
    
    print(f"\nHierarchical: All Descendants of 'Electronics' (ID={electronics_id}):")
    all_descendants.orderBy("level", "category_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 4: Count children at each level
    children_count = categories_df.alias("parent").join(
        categories_df.alias("child"),
        col("parent.category_id") == col("child.parent_id"),
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        col("parent.category_id"),
        col("parent.category_name"),
        col("parent.level")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("child.category_id")).alias("direct_children"),
        collect_list(col("child.category_name")).alias("children_names")
    ).filter(col("direct_children") > 0).orderBy("level", "category_id")
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Categories with Children Count:")
    children_count.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 5: Create product hierarchy with sample products
    products_data = [
```python
        (1001, "Dell XPS 15", 9, 1299.99),
        (1002, "MacBook Pro", 10, 1999.99),
        (1003, "HP Pavilion", 10, 899.99),
        (1004, "iPhone 14", 16, 999.99),
        (1005, "Samsung Galaxy S23", 15, 899.99),
        (1006, "iPad Pro", 8, 1099.99),
        (1007, "Gaming Desktop", 6, 1499.99),
        (1008, "Office Chair Pro", 13, 299.99),
        (1009, "Standing Desk", 14, 499.99)
    ]
    products_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        products_data,
        ["product_id", "product_name", "category_id", "price"]
    )
    
    # Join products with full category hierarchy
    products_with_hierarchy = products_df.alias("p").join(
        category_paths.alias("c"),
        col("p.category_id") == col("c.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("p.product_id"),
        col("p.product_name"),
        col("p.price"),
        col("c.category_name").alias("category"),
        col("c.full_path").alias("category_hierarchy"),
        col("c.level").alias("category_level")
    )
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Products with Full Category Hierarchy:")
    products_with_hierarchy.orderBy("category_hierarchy").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 6: Aggregate sales by hierarchy level
    # Simulate some sales data
    sales_data = [
        (1001, 5, 6499.95),
        (1002, 3, 5999.97),
        (1003, 8, 7199.92),
        (1004, 12, 11999.88),
        (1005, 10, 8999.90),
        (1006, 4, 4399.96),
        (1007, 2, 2999.98),
        (1008, 15, 4499.85),
        (1009, 6, 2999.94)
    ]
    sales_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        sales_data,
        ["product_id", "quantity_sold", "total_sales"]
    )
    
    # Aggregate sales by category hierarchy
    sales_by_category = sales_df.alias("s").join(
        products_df.alias("p"),
        col("s.product_id") == col("p.product_id")
    ).join(
        category_paths.alias("c"),
        col("p.category_id") == col("c.category_id")
    ).groupBy(
        col("c.category_id"),
        col("c.category_name"),
        col("c.full_path"),
        col("c.level")
    ).agg(
        F.sum(col("s.quantity_sold")).alias("total_quantity"),
        F.sum(col("s.total_sales")).alias("total_revenue"),
        F.count(col("s.product_id")).alias("products_sold")
    ).orderBy("level", "total_revenue", ascending=[True, False])
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Sales Aggregated by Category Hierarchy:")
    sales_by_category.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 7: Roll-up sales to parent categories
    # Get all category relationships
    cat_relationships = categories_df.alias("child").join(
        categories_df.alias("parent"),
        col("child.parent_id") == col("parent.category_id"),
        "left"
    ).select(
        col("child.category_id").alias("child_id"),
        col("child.category_name").alias("child_name"),
        col("parent.category_id").alias("parent_id"),
        col("parent.category_name").alias("parent_name")
    )
    
    # Calculate sales at each level and roll up
    # Level 4 sales (leaf categories)
    level_4_sales = sales_by_category.filter(col("level") == 4)
    
    # Roll up to level 3
    level_3_rollup = level_4_sales.alias("l4").join(
        cat_relationships.alias("cr"),
        col("l4.category_id") == col("cr.child_id")
    ).groupBy(
        col("cr.parent_id").alias("category_id"),
        col("cr.parent_name").alias("category_name")
    ).agg(
        F.sum(col("l4.total_quantity")).alias("total_quantity"),
        F.sum(col("l4.total_revenue")).alias("total_revenue"),
        F.sum(col("l4.products_sold")).alias("products_sold")
    )
    
    # Add direct level 3 sales
    level_3_direct = sales_by_category.filter(col("level") == 3)
    level_3_combined = level_3_direct.select(
        "category_id", "category_name", "total_quantity", "total_revenue", "products_sold"
    ).unionAll(
        level_3_rollup.select(
            "category_id", "category_name", "total_quantity", "total_revenue", "products_sold"
        )
    ).groupBy("category_id", "category_name").agg(
        F.sum("total_quantity").alias("total_quantity"),
        F.sum("total_revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
        F.sum("products_sold").alias("products_sold")
    )
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Sales Rolled Up to Level 3 Categories:")
    level_3_combined.orderBy("total_revenue", ascending=False).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 8: Find leaf nodes (categories with no children)
    leaf_categories = categories_df.alias("c1").join(
        categories_df.alias("c2"),
        col("c1.category_id") == col("c2.parent_id"),
        "left_anti"
    ).select(
        col("c1.category_id"),
        col("c1.category_name"),
        col("c1.level")
    ).orderBy("level", "category_id")
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Leaf Categories (No Children):")
    leaf_categories.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 9: Find root nodes (categories with no parent)
    root_categories = categories_df.filter(col("parent_id").isNull())
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Root Categories (No Parent):")
    root_categories.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Method 10: Calculate depth of each subtree
    subtree_depth = categories_df.alias("root").join(
        categories_df.alias("all_cats"),
        col("all_cats.category_id") >= col("root.category_id")  # Simple approach for demo
    ).groupBy(
        col("root.category_id"),
        col("root.category_name")
    ).agg(
        F.max(col("all_cats.level")).alias("max_depth_in_tree")
    ).join(
        categories_df.alias("c"),
        col("root.category_id") == col("c.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("root.category_id"),
        col("root.category_name"),
        col("c.level").alias("category_level"),
        (col("max_depth_in_tree") - col("c.level")).alias("subtree_depth")
    ).orderBy("category_id")
    
    print("\nHierarchical: Subtree Depth for Each Category:")
    subtree_depth.show(truncate=False)
    
    return category_paths, products_with_hierarchy, sales_by_category

hier_paths, hier_products, hier_sales = hierarchical_relationship()

def advanced_relationship_patterns():
    """
    Advanced examples combining multiple relationship patterns
    """
    
    print("\n--- EXAMPLE 1: Combining One-to-Many with Many-to-Many ---")
    
    # Authors (one author, many books)
    authors_data = [
        (1, "J.K. Rowling", "British"),
        (2, "George R.R. Martin", "American"),
        (3, "Brandon Sanderson", "American")
    ]
    authors_df = spark.createDataFrame(authors_data, ["author_id", "author_name", "nationality"])
    
    # Books (many books, many genres)
    books_data = [
        (101, "Harry Potter", 1, 1997),
        (102, "Game of Thrones", 2, 1996),
        (103, "Mistborn", 3, 2006),
        (104, "The Way of Kings", 3, 2010)
    ]
    books_df = spark.createDataFrame(books_data, ["book_id", "book_title", "author_id", "year"])
    
    # Genres
    genres_data = [
        (1, "Fantasy"),
        (2, "Young Adult"),
        (3, "Epic Fantasy"),
        (4, "Adventure")
    ]
    genres_df = spark.createDataFrame(genres_data, ["genre_id", "genre_name"])
    
    # Book-Genre mapping (many-to-many)
    book_genres_data = [
        (101, 1), (101, 2), (101, 4),
        (102, 1), (102, 3),
        (103, 1), (103, 3),
        (104, 1), (104, 3), (104, 4)
    ]
    book_genres_df = spark.createDataFrame(book_genres_data, ["book_id", "genre_id"])
    
    # Complex join: Authors -> Books -> Genres
    author_books_genres = authors_df.join(
        books_df,
        authors_df.author_id == books_df.author_id
    ).join(
        book_genres_df,
        books_df.book_id == book_genres_df.book_id
    ).join(
        genres_df,
        book_genres_df.genre_id == genres_df.genre_id
    ).groupBy(
        authors_df.author_id,
        authors_df.author_name,
        books_df.book_id,
        books_df.book_title,
        books_df.year
    ).agg(
        collect_list(genres_df.genre_name).alias("genres")
    ).orderBy("author_id", "year")
    
    print("\nAuthors with Books and Genres:")
    author_books_genres.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- EXAMPLE 2: Self-Referential with Aggregation ---")
    
    # Social network - users following users
    users_data = [
        (1, "Alice", 150),
        (2, "Bob", 200),
        (3, "Charlie", 180),
        (4, "Diana", 220),
        (5, "Eve", 190)
    ]
    users_df = spark.createDataFrame(users_data, ["user_id", "username", "reputation"])
    
    # Followers relationship (self-referential many-to-many)
    follows_data = [
        (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4),
        (2, 1), (2, 3),
        (3, 1), (3, 4), (3, 5),
        (4, 2), (4, 3),
        (5, 1), (5, 2), (5, 3), (5, 4)
    ]
    follows_df = spark.createDataFrame(follows_data, ["follower_id", "following_id"])
    
    # Calculate follower and following counts
    follower_stats = users_df.alias("u").join(
        follows_df.alias("followers"),
        col("u.user_id") == col("followers.following_id"),
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        col("u.user_id"),
        col("u.username"),
        col("u.reputation")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("followers.follower_id")).alias("follower_count")
    )
    
    following_stats = users_df.alias("u").join(
        follows_df.alias("following"),
        col("u.user_id") == col("following.follower_id"),
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        col("u.user_id")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("following.following_id")).alias("following_count")
    )
    
    user_network_stats = follower_stats.join(
        following_stats,
        follower_stats.user_id == following_stats.user_id
    ).select(
        follower_stats.user_id,
        follower_stats.username,
        follower_stats.reputation,
        follower_stats.follower_count,
        following_stats.following_count,
        (follower_stats.follower_count - following_stats.following_count).alias("net_followers")
    ).orderBy("follower_count", ascending=False)
    
    print("\nSocial Network Statistics:")
    user_network_stats.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Find mutual follows
    mutual_follows = follows_df.alias("f1").join(
        follows_df.alias("f2"),
        (col("f1.follower_id") == col("f2.following_id")) &
        (col("f1.following_id") == col("f2.follower_id"))
    ).join(
        users_df.alias("u1"),
        col("f1.follower_id") == col("u1.user_id")
    ).join(
        users_df.alias("u2"),
        col("f1.following_id") == col("u2.user_id")
    ).select(
        col("u1.username").alias("user_1"),
        col("u2.username").alias("user_2")
    ).filter(col("user_1") < col("user_2"))  # Avoid duplicates
    
    print("\nMutual Follows (Bidirectional Relationships):")
    mutual_follows.show(truncate=False)
    
    print("\n--- EXAMPLE 3: Hierarchical with Temporal Dimension ---")
    
    # Organization structure with effective dates
    org_structure_data = [
        (1, "Company", None, "2020-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (2, "Engineering", 1, "2020-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (3, "Sales", 1, "2020-01-01", "2023-12-31", False),
        (4, "Marketing", 1, "2020-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (5, "Backend Team", 2, "2020-06-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (6, "Frontend Team", 2, "2020-06-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (7, "DevOps Team", 2, "2021-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (8, "Sales - East", 3, "2020-01-01", "2023-12-31", False),
        (9, "Sales - West", 3, "2020-01-01", "2
```python
023-12-31", False),
        (10, "Revenue", 1, "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (11, "Sales - North", 10, "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True),
        (12, "Sales - South", 10, "2024-01-01", "9999-12-31", True)
    ]
    org_structure_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        org_structure_data,
        ["dept_id", "dept_name", "parent_dept_id", "effective_from", "effective_to", "is_active"]
    )
    
    # Current active organization structure
    active_org = org_structure_df.filter(col("is_active") == True)
    
    print("\nCurrent Active Organization Structure:")
    active_org.orderBy("dept_id").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Historical view - show organizational changes
    org_changes = org_structure_df.groupBy("dept_name").agg(
        F.count("*").alias("num_versions"),
        F.min("effective_from").alias("first_created"),
        F.max("effective_to").alias("last_active"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                col("dept_id"),
                col("parent_dept_id"),
                col("effective_from"),
                col("effective_to"),
                col("is_active")
            )
        ).alias("history")
    ).filter(col("num_versions") > 1)
    
    print("\nDepartments with Structural Changes:")
    org_changes.show(truncate=False)
    
    return author_books_genres, user_network_stats, active_org

def demonstrate_optimization_techniques():
    """
    Demonstrate performance optimization techniques for relationship patterns
    """
    
    print("\n--- TECHNIQUE 1: Broadcast Joins for Small Dimension Tables ---")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    
    # Large fact table
    large_transactions = spark.range(0, 10000).select(
        col("id").alias("transaction_id"),
        (col("id") % 100 + 1).alias("customer_id"),
        (F.rand() * 1000).alias("amount")
    )
    
    # Small dimension table
    small_customers = spark.range(1, 101).select(
        col("id").alias("customer_id"),
        concat_ws("_", lit("Customer"), col("id")).alias("customer_name")
    )
    
    # Without broadcast (regular join)
    print("\nRegular Join (may cause shuffle):")
    regular_join = large_transactions.join(
        small_customers,
        "customer_id"
    )
    print(f"Partitions: {regular_join.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    
    # With broadcast (optimized for small tables)
    print("\nBroadcast Join (optimized for small dimension):")
    broadcast_join = large_transactions.join(
        broadcast(small_customers),
        "customer_id"
    )
    print(f"Partitions: {broadcast_join.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    print("Note: Broadcast join avoids shuffle for small dimension tables")
    
    print("\n--- TECHNIQUE 2: Partition Pruning for Hierarchical Data ---")
    
    # Partitioned hierarchical data
    partitioned_categories = categories_df.repartition(4, "level")
    
    print(f"\nOriginal partitions: {categories_df.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    print(f"Repartitioned by level: {partitioned_categories.rdd.getNumPartitions()}")
    print("Benefit: Queries filtering by level will only scan relevant partitions")
    
    print("\n--- TECHNIQUE 3: Caching for Repeated Self-Joins ---")
    
    # When doing multiple self-joins (common in hierarchical queries)
    employees_cached = employees_df.cache()
    
    print("\nCaching strategy for self-referential patterns:")
    print("- Cache the base table when performing multiple self-joins")
    print("- Reduces repeated scans of the same data")
    print("- Particularly useful for recursive hierarchy traversal")
    
    # Clean up cache
    employees_cached.unpersist()
    
    print("\n--- TECHNIQUE 4: Denormalization for Read-Heavy Workloads ---")
    
    # Instead of joining every time, pre-compute and store
    denormalized_customer_orders = customers_df.join(
        orders_df,
        "customer_id",
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        customers_df.customer_id,
        customers_df.company_name,
        customers_df.email,
        customers_df.tier
    ).agg(
        F.count(orders_df.order_id).alias("total_orders"),
        F.sum(orders_df.amount).alias("lifetime_value"),
        F.max(orders_df.order_date).alias("last_order_date"),
        collect_list(
            struct(
                orders_df.order_id,
                orders_df.order_date,
                orders_df.amount,
                orders_df.status
            )
        ).alias("orders")
    )
    
    print("\nDenormalized Customer-Order View:")
    denormalized_customer_orders.show(2, truncate=False)
    print("Benefit: Single table read instead of join for common queries")
    
    print("\n--- TECHNIQUE 5: Incremental Processing for Large Hierarchies ---")
    
    print("\nFor large hierarchies, process level by level:")
    print("1. Process root nodes first")
    print("2. Join with children iteratively")
    print("3. Use checkpointing for very deep hierarchies")
    print("4. Consider materialized path pattern for frequent traversals")
    
    # Example: Materialized path pattern
    categories_with_path = category_paths.select(
        col("category_id"),
        col("category_name"),
        col("full_path"),
        col("level")
    )
    
    print("\nMaterialized Path Pattern:")
    categories_with_path.show(5, truncate=False)
    print("Benefit: Single table scan for ancestor/descendant queries")

demonstrate_optimization_techniques()

def data_quality_checks():
    """
    Demonstrate data quality validation for different relationship patterns
    """
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 1: Referential Integrity ---")
    
    # Check for orphaned records (foreign key violations)
    orphaned_orders = orders_df.join(
        customers_df,
        orders_df.customer_id == customers_df.customer_id,
        "left_anti"
    )
    
    print(f"\nOrphaned orders (no matching customer): {orphaned_orders.count()}")
    
    # Check for missing relationships
    customers_without_orders = customers_df.join(
        orders_df,
        customers_df.customer_id == orders_df.customer_id,
        "left_anti"
    )
    
    print(f"Customers without orders: {customers_without_orders.count()}")
    if customers_without_orders.count() > 0:
        customers_without_orders.show()
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 2: Circular References in Hierarchies ---")
    
    # Check for circular references in self-referential data
    # An employee cannot be their own ancestor
    circular_check = employees_df.alias("e1").join(
        employees_df.alias("e2"),
        col("e1.employee_id") == col("e2.manager_id")
    ).join(
        employees_df.alias("e3"),
        col("e2.employee_id") == col("e3.manager_id")
    ).filter(
        col("e3.employee_id") == col("e1.employee_id")
    )
    
    print(f"\nCircular references detected: {circular_check.count()}")
    if circular_check.count() > 0:
        print("WARNING: Circular reference found!")
        circular_check.show()
    else:
        print("✓ No circular references in employee hierarchy")
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 3: Duplicate Relationships in Many-to-Many ---")
    
    # Check for duplicate enrollments
    duplicate_enrollments = enrollments_df.groupBy(
        "student_id", "course_id", "semester"
    ).agg(
        F.count("*").alias("count")
    ).filter(col("count") > 1)
    
    print(f"\nDuplicate enrollments: {duplicate_enrollments.count()}")
    if duplicate_enrollments.count() > 0:
        print("WARNING: Duplicate enrollments found!")
        duplicate_enrollments.show()
    else:
        print("✓ No duplicate enrollments")
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 4: Hierarchy Depth Validation ---")
    
    # Check if hierarchy exceeds maximum allowed depth
    max_allowed_depth = 5
    
    depth_check = org_hierarchy.agg(
        F.max("level").alias("max_depth")
    ).collect()[0]["max_depth"]
    
    print(f"\nMaximum hierarchy depth: {depth_check}")
    print(f"Allowed maximum depth: {max_allowed_depth}")
    
    if depth_check <= max_allowed_depth:
        print("✓ Hierarchy depth within acceptable limits")
    else:
        print("WARNING: Hierarchy exceeds maximum allowed depth!")
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 5: Relationship Cardinality Validation ---")
    
    # For one-to-one: ensure no duplicates on either side
    user_profile_counts = profiles_df.groupBy("user_id").agg(
        F.count("*").alias("profile_count")
    ).filter(col("profile_count") > 1)
    
    print(f"\nUsers with multiple profiles (should be 0): {user_profile_counts.count()}")
    if user_profile_counts.count() > 0:
        print("WARNING: One-to-One relationship violated!")
        user_profile_counts.show()
    else:
        print("✓ One-to-One relationship integrity maintained")
    
    print("\n--- CHECK 6: Null Foreign Key Check ---")
    
    # Check for null foreign keys where they shouldn't be
    null_fk_check = orders_df.filter(col("customer_id").isNull())
    
    print(f"\nOrders with null customer_id: {null_fk_check.count()}")
    if null_fk_check.count() > 0:
        print("WARNING: Null foreign keys found!")
        null_fk_check.show()
    else:
        print("✓ No null foreign keys in orders")

data_quality_checks()

    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("RELATIONSHIP DIAGRAMS (ASCII)")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    one_to_one_diagram = """
    ONE-TO-ONE RELATIONSHIP
    ═══════════════════════
    
    ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐
    │   Users      │         │  User Profiles   │
    ├──────────────┤         ├──────────────────┤
    │ user_id (PK) │────1:1──│ user_id (FK)     │
    │ username     │         │ first_name       │
    │ email        │         │ last_name        │
    └──────────────┘         │ city             │
                             │ phone            │
                             └──────────────────┘
    """
    
    one_to_many_diagram = """
    ONE-TO-MANY RELATIONSHIP
    ════════════════════════
    
    ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐
    │   Customers      │         │     Orders       │
    ├──────────────────┤         ├──────────────────┤
    │ customer_id (PK) │────1:N──│ customer_id (FK) │
    │ company_name     │         │ order_id (PK)    │
    │ email            │         │ order_date       │
    │ tier             │         │ amount           │
    └──────────────────┘         │ status           │
                                 └──────────────────┘
    """
    
    many_to_many_diagram = """
    MANY-TO-MANY RELATIONSHIP
    ═════════════════════════
    
    ┌──────────────┐      ┌─────────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐
    │  Students    │      │  Enrollments    │      │   Courses    │
    ├──────────────┤      ├─────────────────┤      ├──────────────┤
    │student_id(PK)│──N:1─│student_id (FK)  │─1:N──│course_id(PK) │
    │ name         │      │course_id (FK)   │      │ course_name  │
    │ major        │      │ semester        │      │ department   │
    │ year         │      │ grade           │      │ credits      │
    └──────────────┘      └─────────────────┘      └──────────────┘
                          (Junction Table)
    """
    
    self_referential_diagram = """
    SELF-REFERENTIAL RELATIONSHIP
    ═════════════════════════════
    
    ┌──────────────────────┐
    │     Employees        │◄───┐
    ├──────────────────────┤    │
    │ employee_id (PK)     │    │
    │ name                 │    │
    │ position             │    │
    │ manager_id (FK) ─────┼────┘
    │ salary               │  (Self-reference)
    └──────────────────────┘
    
    Example:
    Sarah (CEO) → manager_id: NULL
       ├─→ John (CTO) → manager_id: Sarah's ID
       │      ├─→ David (VP) → manager_id: John's ID
       │      └─→ Lisa (VP) → manager_id: John's ID
       └─→ Mary (CFO) → manager_id: Sarah's ID
    """
    
    hierarchical_diagram = """
    HIERARCHICAL RELATIONSHIP
    ═════════════════════════
    
    ┌──────────────────────┐
    │    Categories        │◄───┐
    ├──────────────────────┤    │
    │ category_id (PK)     │    │
    │ category_name        │    │
    │ parent_id (FK) ──────┼────┘
    │ level                │  (Parent-Child)
    └──────────────────────┘
    
    Tree Structure:
    
    Electronics (L1)
    ├── Computers (L2)
    │   ├── Laptops (L3)
    │   │   ├── Gaming Laptops (L4)
    │   │   └── Business Laptops (L4)
    │   └── Desktops (L3)
    └── Mobile Devices (L2)
        ├── Smartphones (L3)
        │   ├── Android Phones (L4)
        │   └── iPhones (L4)
        └── Tablets (L3)
    """
    
    print(one_to_one_diagram)
    print(one_to_many_diagram)
    print(many_to_many_diagram)
    print(self_referential_diagram)
    print(hierarchical_diagram)


def generate_sample_queries():
    """
    Generate sample SQL queries for each relationship pattern
    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("SAMPLE SQL QUERIES FOR RELATIONSHIP PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    queries = {
        "One-to-One": [
            """
            -- Get complete user information
            SELECT u.user_id, u.username, u.email,
                   p.first_name, p.last_name, p.city, p.phone
            FROM users u
            INNER JOIN user_profiles p ON u.user_id = p.user_id;
            """,
            """
            -- Find users without profiles
            SELECT u.user_id, u.username
            FROM users u
            LEFT JOIN user_profiles p ON u.user_id = p.user_id
            WHERE p.profile_id IS NULL;
            """
        ],
        "One-to-Many": [
            """
            -- Get all customer orders
            SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name,
                   o.order_id, o.order_date, o.amount
            FROM customers c
            LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
            ORDER BY c.customer_id, o.order_date;
            """,
            """
            -- Customer order summary
            SELECT c.customer_id, c.company_name,
                   COUNT(o.order_id) as total_orders,
                   SUM(o.amount) as total_revenue,
                   AVG(o.amount) as avg_order_value
            FROM customers c
            LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
            GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.company_name;
            """
        ],
        "Many-to-Many": [
            """
            -- Student course enrollments
            SELECT s.student_name, c.course_name, 
                   e.semester, e.grade
            FROM students s
            JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id
            JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id
            ORDER BY s.student_name, c.course_name;
            """,
            """
            -- Courses with enrollment count
            SELECT c.course_id, c.course_name,
                   COUNT(e.student_id) as enrolled_students
            FROM courses c
            LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id
            GROUP BY c.course_id, c.course_name
            ORDER BY enrolled_students DESC;
            """
        ],
        "Self-Referential": [
            """
            -- Employees with their managers
            SELECT e.employee_id, e.name as employee_name,
                   m.name as manager_name
            FROM employees e
            LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id;
            """,
            """
            -- Manager with direct report count
            SELECT m.employee_id, m.name as manager_name,
                   COUNT(e.employee_id) as direct_reports
            FROM employees m
            JOIN employees e ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
            GROUP BY m.employee_id, m.name
            ORDER BY direct_reports DESC;
            """
        ],
        "Hierarchical": [
            """
            -- Category hierarchy with parent
            SELECT c.category_id, c.category_name,
                   p.category_name as parent_category,
                   c.level
            FROM categories c
            LEFT JOIN categories p ON c.parent_id = p.category_id
            ORDER BY c.level, c.category_id;
            """,
            """
            -- All descendants of a category (2 levels)
            SELECT c1.category_name as level_1,
                   c2.category_name as level_2,
                   c3.category_name as level_3
            FROM categories c1
            LEFT JOIN categories c2 ON c1.category_id = c2.parent_id
            LEFT JOIN categories c3 ON c2.category_id = c3.parent_id
            WHERE c1.parent_id IS NULL
            ORDER BY c1.category_name, c2.category_name, c3.category_name;
            """
        ]
    }
    
    for pattern, query_list in queries.items():
        print(f"\n{'='*80}")
        print(f"{pattern} QUERIES")
        print('='*80)
        for i, query in enumerate(query_list, 1):
            print(f"\nQuery {i}:{query}")


def performance_comparison():
    """
    Compare performance of different join strategies
    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("PERFORMANCE COMPARISON")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    import time
    
    # Create larger datasets for meaningful comparison
    large_customers = spark.range(0, 1000).select(
        col("id").alias("customer_id"),
        concat_ws("_", lit("Customer"), col("id")).alias("company_name")
    )
    
    large_orders = spark.range(0, 50000).select(
        col("id").alias("order_id"),
        (col("id") % 1000).alias("customer_id"),
        (F.rand() * 1000).alias("amount")
    )
    
    print("\nDataset sizes:")
    print(f"Customers: {large_customers.count():,}")
    print(f"Orders: {large_orders.count():,}")
    
    # Test 1: Regular join
    print("\n--- Test 1: Regular Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    regular_result = large_customers.join(large_orders, "customer_id")
    regular_count = regular_result.count()
    regular_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"Time: {regular_time:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"Result count: {regular_count:,}")
    
    # Test 2: Broadcast join
    print("\n--- Test 2: Broadcast Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
    broadcast_result = large_orders.join(broadcast(large_customers), "customer_id")
    broadcast_count = broadcast_result.count()
    broadcast_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"Time: {broadcast_time:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"Result count: {broadcast_count:,}")
    
    # Test 3: Aggregated join
    print("\n--- Test 3: Pre-Aggregated Join ---")
    start_time = time.time()
    aggregated_orders = large_orders.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
        F.count("*").alias("order_count"),
        F.sum("amount").alias("total_amount")
    )
    agg_result = large_customers.join(aggregated_orders, "customer_id")
    agg_count = agg_result.count()
    agg_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"Time: {agg_time:.2f} seconds")
    print(f"Result count: {agg_count:,}")
    
    print("\n--- Performance Summary ---")
    print(f"Regular Join:      {regular_time:.2f}s")
    print(f"Broadcast Join:    {broadcast_time:.2f}s ({((regular_time-broadcast_time)/regular_time*100):.1f}% faster)")
    print(f"Aggregated Join:   {agg_time:.2f}s ({((regular_time-agg_time)/regular_time*100):.1f}% faster)")

def run_unit_tests():
    """
    Unit tests for relationship pattern implementations
    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("RUNNING UNIT TESTS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    test_results = []
    
    # Test 1: One-to-One relationship integrity
    print("\n[TEST 1] One-to-One Relationship Integrity")
    try:
        duplicate_profiles = profiles_df.groupBy("user_id").count().filter(col("count") > 1)
        assert duplicate_profiles.count() == 0, "Duplicate profiles found!"
        print("✓ PASSED: No duplicate profiles")
        test_results.append(("One-to-One Integrity", "PASSED"))
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"✗ FAILED: {str(e)}")
        test_results.append(("One-to-One Integrity", "FAILED"))
    
    # Test 2: Referential integrity for One-to-Many
    print("\n[TEST 2] One-to-Many Referential Integrity")
    try:
        orphaned = orders_df.join(
            customers_df,
            orders_df.customer_id == customers_df.customer_id,
            "left_anti"
        )
        assert orphaned.count() == 0, "Orphaned orders found!"
        print("✓ PASSED: All orders have valid customers")
        test_results.append(("One-to-Many Integrity", "PASSED"))
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"✗ FAILED: {str(e)}")
        test_results.append(("One-to-Many Integrity", "FAILED"))
    
    # Test 3: Many-to-Many junction table integrity
    print("\n[TEST 3] Many-to-Many Junction Table Integrity")
    try:
        invalid_students = enrollments_df.join(
            students_df,
            enrollments_df.student_id == students_df.student_id,
            "left_anti"
        )
        invalid_courses = enrollments_df.join(
            courses_df,
            enrollments_df.course_id == courses_df.course_id,
            "left_anti"
        )
        assert invalid_students.count() == 0, "Invalid student references!"
        assert invalid_courses.count() == 0, "Invalid course references!"
        print("✓ PASSED: All enrollments have valid references")
        test_results.append(("Many-to-Many Integrity", "PASSED"))
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"✗ FAILED: {str(e)}")
        test_results.append(("Many-to-Many Integrity", "FAILED"))
    
    # Test 4: Self-referential no circular references
    print("\n[TEST 4] Self-Referential Circular Reference Check")
    try:
        # Simple check: employee cannot be their own manager
        self_managed = employees_df.filter(col("employee_id") == col("manager_id"))
        assert self_managed.count() == 0, "Circular reference: self-management!"
        print("✓ PASSED: No direct circular references")
        test_results.append(("Self-Referential Integrity", "PASSED"))
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"✗ FAILED: {str(e)}")
        test_results.append(("Self-Referential Integrity", "FAILED"))
    
    # Test 5: Hierarchical depth consistency
    print("\n[TEST 5] Hierarchical Level Consistency")
    try:
        # Check if level values are consistent with parent-child relationships
        level_check = categories_df.alias("child").join(
            categories_df.alias("parent"),
            col("child.parent_id") == col("parent.category_id"),
            "inner"
        ).filter(
            col("child.level") != col("parent.level") + 1
        )
        assert level_check.count() == 0, "Inconsistent hierarchy levels!"
        print("✓ PASSED: Hierarchy levels are consistent")
        test_results.append(("Hierarchical Consistency", "PASSED"))
    except AssertionError as e:
        print(f"✗ FAILED: {str(e)}")
        test_results.append(("Hierarchical Consistency", "FAILED"))
    
    # Test Summary
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("TEST SUMMARY")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    passed = sum(1 for _, result in test_results if result == "PASSED")
    total = len(test_results)
    
    for test_name, result in test_results:
        status_symbol = "✓" if result == "PASSED" else "✗"
        print(f"{status_symbol} {test_name}: {result}")
    
    print(f"\n{'='*80}")
    print(f"Total: {passed}/{total} tests passed ({(passed/total*100):.1f}%)")
    print(f"{'='*80}")
    
    return all(result == "PASSED" for _, result in test_results)

def advanced_query_patterns():
    """
    Demonstrate advanced query patterns combining multiple relationships
    """
    
    print("\n" + "=" * 80)
    print("ADVANCED QUERY PATTERNS")
    print("=" * 80)
    
    # Pattern 1: Recursive aggregation up the hierarchy
    print("\n--- PATTERN 1: Recursive Hierarchical Aggregation ---")
    print("Calculate total sales rolled up through category hierarchy")
    
    # Simulated sales at leaf categories
    leaf_sales = spark.createDataFrame([
        (9, 5000),   # Gaming Laptops
        (10, 3000),  # Business Laptops
        (15, 8000),  # Android Phones
        (16, 12000), # iPhones
        (13, 2000),  # Office Chairs
        (14, 1500)   # Desks
    ], ["category_id", "sales_amount"])
    
    # Join with category hierarchy and aggregate
    hierarchical_sales = leaf_sales.alias("s").join(
        category_paths.alias("c"),
        col("s.category_id") == col("c.category_id")
    ).select(
        col("c.full_path"),
        col("c.level"),
        col("s.sales_amount")
    )
    
    print("\nSales by Category Path:")
    hierarchical_sales.orderBy("full_path").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 2: Find relationship gaps
    print("\n--- PATTERN 2: Identify Relationship Gaps ---")
    print("Find customers who haven't ordered in specific time period")
    
    from pyspark.sql.functions import datediff, current_date, to_date
    
    # Add date conversion
    orders_with_dates = orders_df.withColumn(
        "order_date_parsed",
        to_date(col("order_date"), "yyyy-MM-dd")
    )
    
    # Find last order date per customer
    last_orders = orders_with_dates.groupBy("customer_id").agg(
        F.max("order_date_parsed").alias("last_order_date")
    )
    
    # Customers with no recent orders (more than 30 days)
    inactive_customers = customers_df.join(
        last_orders,
        "customer_id",
        "left"
    ).withColumn(
        "days_since_order",
        datediff(current_date(), col("last_order_date"))
    ).filter(
        (col("days_since_order") > 30) | col("last_order_date").isNull()
    )
    
    print("\nInactive Customers (No orders in 30+ days):")
    inactive_customers.select(
        "customer_id", "company_name", "last_order_date", "days_since_order"
    ).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 3: Cross-hierarchy comparisons
    print("\n--- PATTERN 3: Cross-Hierarchy Peer Comparison ---")
    print("Compare employees at the same level")
    
    # Group employees by level and compare
    from pyspark.sql.window import Window
    
    level_window = Window.partitionBy("level")
    
    employee_comparison = org_hierarchy.withColumn(
        "avg_salary_at_level",
        F.avg("salary").over(level_window)
    ).withColumn(
        "salary_vs_peers",
        ((col("salary") - col("avg_salary_at_level")) / col("avg_salary_at_level") * 100)
    ).select(
        "employee_id",
        "name",
        "position",
        "level",
        "salary",
        "avg_salary_at_level",
        F.round("salary_vs_peers", 2).alias("salary_vs_peers_pct")
    )
    
    print("\nEmployee Salary Comparison Within Hierarchy Level:")
    employee_comparison.orderBy("level", "salary", ascending=[True, False]).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 4: Multi-hop relationship traversal
    print("\n--- PATTERN 4: Multi-Hop Relationship Traversal ---")
    print("Find students who share multiple courses (strong connections)")
    
    # Count shared courses between students
    student_connections = enrollments_df.alias("e1").join(
        enrollments_df.alias("e2"),
        (col("e1.course_id") == col("e2.course_id")) &
        (col("e1.student_id") < col("e2.student_id"))
    ).groupBy(
        col("e1.student_id").alias("student_1_id"),
        col("e2.student_id").alias("student_2_id")
    ).agg(
        F.count("*").alias("shared_courses"),
        collect_list(col("e1.course_id")).alias("course_ids")
    ).join(
        students_df.alias("s1"),
        col("student_1_id") == col("s1.student_id")
    ).join(
        students_df.alias("s2"),
        col("student_2_id") == col("s2.student_id")
    ).select(
        col("s1.student_name").alias("student_1"),
        col("s2.student_name").alias("student_2"),
        col("shared_courses"),
        col("course_ids")
    ).filter(col("shared_courses") >= 2)  # Strong connections
    
    print("\nStudent Pairs with Multiple Shared Courses:")
    student_connections.orderBy("shared_courses", ascending=False).show(truncate=False)
    
    # Pattern 5: Temporal relationship analysis
    print("\n--- PATTERN 5: Temporal Relationship Analysis ---")
    print("Analyze relationship changes over time")
    
    # Customer lifetime value progression
    customer_progression = orders_with_dates.join(
        customers_df,
        "customer_id"
    ).withColumn(
        "order_number",
        F.row_number().over(
            Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("order_date_parsed")
        )
    ).withColumn(
        "cumulative_revenue",
        F.sum("amount").over(
            Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy("order_date_parsed")
            .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)
        )
    ).select(
        "customer_id",
        "company_name",
        "order_date_parsed",
        "order_number",
        "amount",
        F.round("cumulative_revenue", 2).alias("cumulative_revenue")
    )
    
    print("\nCustomer Lifetime Value Progression:")
    customer_progression.orderBy("customer_id", "order_number").show(truncate=False)

    # Use Case 4: Social Network Analysis
    print("\n--- USE CASE 4: Social Network Influence Score ---")
    print("Using self-referential follower relationships")
    
    # Calculate influence metrics
    influence_metrics = follows_df.alias("f").join(
        users_df.alias("u"),
        col("f.following_id") == col("u.user_id")
    ).groupBy(
        col("u.user_id"),
        col("u.username"),
        col("u.reputation")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("f.follower_id")).alias("follower_count")
    ).withColumn(
        "influence_score",
        (col("follower_count") * 0.6 + col("reputation") * 0.4)
    ).orderBy("influence_score", ascending=False)
    
    print("\nUser Influence Rankings:")
    influence_metrics.select(
        "username",
        "follower_count",
        "reputation",
        F.round("influence_score", 2).alias("influence_score")
    ).show()
    
    # Use Case 5: Supply Chain Hierarchy
    print("\n--- USE CASE 5: Supply Chain Bill of Materials ---")
    print("Using hierarchical part-subpart relationships")
    
    # Bill of Materials (BOM)
    bom_data = [
        (1, "Laptop", None, 1),
        (2, "Motherboard", 1, 2),
        (3, "Screen", 1, 2),
        (4, "Battery", 1, 2),
        (5, "CPU", 2, 3),
        (6, "RAM", 2, 3),
        (7, "GPU", 2, 3),
        (8, "LCD Panel", 3, 3),
        (9, "Backlight", 3, 3)
    ]
    bom_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        bom_data,
        ["part_id", "part_name", "parent_part_id", "level"]
    )
    
    # Calculate total parts needed (explosion)
    parts_explosion = bom_df.alias("p1").join(
        bom_df.alias("p2"),
        col("p1.part_id") == col("p2.parent_part_id"),
        "left"
    ).groupBy(
        col("p1.part_id"),
        col("p1.part_name"),
        col("p1.level")
    ).agg(
        F.count(col("p2.part_id")).alias("direct_subparts")
    ).orderBy("level", "part_id")
    
    print("\nBill of Materials - Parts Breakdown:")
    parts_explosion.show(truncate=False)

def generate_documentation():
    """
    Generate comprehensive documentation for the relationship patterns
    """
    
    documentation = """
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                 COMPREHENSIVE RELATIONSHIP PATTERNS GUIDE                  ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

TABLE OF CONTENTS
═════════════════
1. Introduction to Relationship Patterns
2. Pattern Implementations
3. Performance Considerations
4. Best Practices
5. Common Pitfalls
6. Troubleshooting Guide

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. INTRODUCTION TO RELATIONSHIP PATTERNS
═════════════════════════════════════════

Relationship patterns define how data entities are connected in a data model.
Understanding these patterns is crucial for:
- Efficient data modeling
- Optimized query performance
- Maintaining data integrity
- Scalable system design

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2. PATTERN IMPLEMENTATIONS
═══════════════════════════

2.1 ONE-TO-ONE RELATIONSHIP
───────────────────────────

Definition: Each record in Table A relates to exactly one record in Table B

When to Use:
✓ Splitting large tables for performance
✓ Separating sensitive data
✓ Optional extended attributes

PySpark Implementation:
```python
# Inner join for complete records
result = table_a.join(table_b, table_a.id == table_b.foreign_id, "inner")

# Left join to keep all records from table_a
result = table_a.join(table_b, table_a.id == table_b.foreign_id, "left")
```

Validation Checks:
- Ensure no duplicate foreign keys in table_b
- Check for orphaned records
- Verify cardinality constraints

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.2 ONE-TO-MANY RELATIONSHIP
────────────────────────────

Definition: Each record in Table A can relate to multiple records in Table B

When to Use:
✓ Parent-child relationships (customer-orders)
✓ Master-detail scenarios
✓ Aggregation requirements

PySpark Implementation:
```python
# Expanded view (all child records)
result = parent.join(child, parent.id == child.parent_id, "left")

# Aggregated view (summary statistics)
result = parent.join(child, "parent_id", "left") \
    .groupBy(parent.columns) \
    .agg(count(child.id).alias("child_count"))

# Nested structure (array of children)
result = parent.join(child, "parent_id", "left") \
    .groupBy(parent.columns) \
    .agg(collect_list(struct(child.columns)).alias("children"))
```

Performance Tips:
- Use broadcast join for small parent tables
- Consider pre-aggregation for read-heavy workloads
- Partition child table by parent_id for large datasets

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.3 MANY-TO-MANY RELATIONSHIP
──────────────────────────────

Definition: Records in Table A relate to multiple records in Table B and vice versa

When to Use:
✓ Complex associations (students-courses)
✓ Tagging systems
✓ Permission matrices

PySpark Implementation:
```python
# Complete relationship view
result = table_a \
    .join(junction_table, table_a.id == junction_table.a_id) \
    .join(table_b, junction_table.b_id == table_b.id)

# Aggregated from A perspective
result = table_a \
    .join(junction_table, "a_id", "left") \
    .join(table_b, "b_id", "left") \
    .groupBy(table_a.columns) \
    .agg(collect_list(table_b.name).alias("related_items"))
```

Junction Table Design:
- Composite primary key (a_id, b_id)
- Optional attributes (timestamp, status)
- Indexes on both foreign keys

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.4 SELF-REFERENTIAL RELATIONSHIP
──────────────────────────────────

Definition: Records in a table relate to other records in the same table

When to Use:
✓ Hierarchical data (employee-manager)
✓ Social networks (follower-following)
✓ Linked structures

PySpark Implementation:
```python
# Single level relationship
result = table.alias("child") \
    .join(table.alias("parent"), 
          col("child.parent_id") == col("parent.id"), 
          "left")

# Multi-level traversal
level_1 = table.filter(col("parent_id").isNull())
level_2 = table.join(level_1, table.parent_id == level_1.id)
# Continue for additional levels...
```

Special Considerations:
- Prevent circular references
- Limit recursion depth
- Cache base table for multiple self-joins

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

2.5 HIERARCHICAL RELATIONSHIP
──────────────────────────────

Definition: Multi-level parent-child relationships forming tree structures

When to Use:
✓ Category taxonomies
✓ Organizational structures
✓ File systems

PySpark Implementation:
```python
# Build full paths iteratively
def build_hierarchy(df, max_depth):
    result = df.filter(col("parent_id").isNull()) \
        .withColumn("path", col("name"))
    
    for level in range(2, max_depth + 1):
        next_level = df.alias("c") \
            .join(result.alias("p"), 
                  col("c.parent_id") == col("p.id")) \
            .select(col("c.*"), 
                    concat_ws(" > ", col("p.path"), col("c.name")).alias("path"))
        result = result.union(next_level)
    
    return result
```

Optimization Strategies:
- Materialized path pattern for frequent queries
- Nested set model for read-heavy scenarios
- Closure table for flexible traversal

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

3. PERFORMANCE CONSIDERATIONS
══════════════════════════════

3.1 Join Strategies
───────────────────

Broadcast Join:
- Use for: Small dimension tables (< 10MB)
- Benefit: Eliminates shuffle
- Code: broadcast(small_table)

Sort-Merge Join:
- Use for: Large tables of similar size
- Benefit: Efficient for sorted data
- Requires: Data partitioned by join key

Shuffle Hash Join:
- Use for: One large, one medium table
- Benefit: Better than sort-merge for skewed data

3.2 Partitioning Strategies
────────────────────────────

For One-to-Many:
- Partition child table by parent_id
- Co-locate related records

For Hierarchical:
- Partition by level for level-based queries
- Consider range partitioning for temporal hierarchies

3.3 Caching Guidelines
──────────────────────

Cache when:
✓ Table used in multiple operations
✓ Performing iterative algorithms
✓ Base table for self-joins

Don't cache when:
✗ Data used only once
✗ Very large datasets (memory constraints)
✗ Rapidly changing data

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

4. BEST PRACTICES
═════════════════

Data Modeling:
□ Define clear primary and foreign keys
□ Document relationship cardinality
□ Use appropriate data types
□ Implement referential integrity checks

Query Optimization:
□ Select only required columns
□ Filter early in the pipeline
□ Use appropriate join types
□ Leverage partitioning

Code Quality:
□ Use meaningful aliases
□ Comment complex joins
□ Validate assumptions with assertions
□ Handle null values explicitly

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

5. COMMON PITFALLS
══════════════════

❌ Cartesian Products
Problem: Joining without proper conditions
Solution: Always specify join conditions

❌ Data Skew
Problem: Uneven distribution causing slow partitions
Solution: Salting, broadcast joins, or repartitioning

❌ Memory Issues
Problem: Collecting large datasets to driver
Solution: Use DataFrame operations, avoid collect()

❌ Circular Dependencies
Problem: Self-referential cycles
Solution: Validate data, implement cycle detection

❌ Missing NULL Handling
Problem: Unexpected results with null foreign keys
Solution: Use coalesce(), explicit null checks

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

6. TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE
════════════════════════

Issue: Slow Join Performance
Diagnosis:
- Check explain() output
- Look for shuffle operations
- Identify data skew

Solutions:
1. Use broadcast for small tables
2. Repartition by join key
3. Enable adaptive query execution

Issue: Out of Memory Errors
Diagnosis:
- Check partition sizes
- Monitor driver/executor memory
- Identify large shuffles

Solutions:
1. Increase executor memory
2. Repartition to smaller chunks
3. Use incremental processing

Issue: Incorrect Results
Diagnosis:
- Verify join conditions
- Check for duplicate keys
- Validate null handling

Solutions:
1. Add data quality checks
2. Use appropriate join type
3. Handle nulls explicitly

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

For more information and examples, refer to:
- Apache Spark SQL Documentation
- PySpark API Reference
- This implementation guide

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
"""
    
    print(documentation)
