class ElasticityBestPractices:
    """
    Collection of best practices for elasticity patterns
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def print_best_practices():
        """Print comprehensive best practices guide"""
        practices = """
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                  ELASTICITY BEST PRACTICES                           ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

1. GENERAL PRINCIPLES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Monitor Before Scaling
     • Establish baseline metrics before implementing elasticity
     • Understand your workload patterns
     • Identify bottlenecks (CPU, Memory, I/O, Network)
   
   ✓ Start Conservative
     • Begin with manual scaling to understand behavior
     • Gradually move to auto-scaling
     • Use predictive scaling only when patterns are established
   
   ✓ Set Appropriate Thresholds
     • Avoid aggressive thresholds that cause thrashing
     • Include cooldown periods between scaling actions
     • Consider both scale-out and scale-in thresholds
   
   ✓ Test Thoroughly
     • Test scaling behavior under various loads
     • Simulate failure scenarios
     • Validate cost implications


2. HORIZONTAL SCALING BEST PRACTICES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Data Partitioning
     • Ensure data is properly partitioned for parallelism
     • Avoid data skew across partitions
     • Use appropriate number of partitions (2-3x total cores)
   
   ✓ Shuffle Operations
     • Minimize shuffle operations
     • Use broadcast joins for small datasets
     • Configure shuffle partitions appropriately
   
   ✓ Resource Configuration
     • Balance executor memory and cores
     • Consider memory overhead (10-15%)
     • Monitor executor failures
   
   Example Configuration:
     spark.executor.instances = 10
     spark.executor.cores = 4
     spark.executor.memory = 8g
     spark.executor.memoryOverhead = 1g


3. VERTICAL SCALING BEST PRACTICES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Memory Management
     • Monitor heap usage and GC behavior
     • Increase memory for memory-intensive operations
     • Consider off-heap memory for caching
   
   ✓ CPU Allocation
     • Match cores to parallelism requirements
     • Avoid over-subscription of CPU
     • Monitor CPU utilization patterns
   
   ✓ When to Use
     • Single-threaded bottlenecks
     • Large object processing
     • Memory-intensive aggregations
   
   Warning: Vertical scaling has hardware limits!


4. AUTO-SCALING BEST PRACTICES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Threshold Configuration
     • CPU threshold: 70-80% for scale-out
     • Memory threshold: 75-85% for scale-out
     • Scale-in thresholds: 20-30% lower than scale-out
   
   ✓ Timing Parameters
     • Check interval: 10-30 seconds
     • Cooldown period: 30-60 seconds
     • Stabilization time: 2-5 minutes
   
   ✓ Limits
     • Set minimum executors (prevent complete scale-in)
     • Set maximum executors (cost control)
     • Monitor scaling frequency
   
   Example:
     Min Executors: 2
     Max Executors: 20
     Scale-out at: CPU > 80% OR Memory > 85%
     Scale-in at: CPU < 30% AND Memory < 40%
     Cooldown: 60 seconds


5. PREDICTIVE SCALING BEST PRACTICES
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Data Collection
     • Collect metrics for at least 2-4 weeks
     • Include time-based features (hour, day, etc.)
     • Track workload characteristics
   
   ✓ Model Selection
     • Start with simple models (linear regression)
     • Consider time-series models for seasonal patterns
     • Validate predictions regularly
   
   ✓ Prediction Window
     • Predict 5-10 minutes ahead
     • Allow time for resources to provision
     • Account for startup time
   
   ✓ Fallback Strategy
     • Always have auto-scaling as fallback
     • Handle prediction failures gracefully
     • Monitor prediction accuracy


6. COST OPTIMIZATION
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Right-Sizing
     • Don't over-provision resources
     • Use appropriate instance types
     • Consider spot/preemptible instances
   
   ✓ Scheduling
     • Scale down during off-peak hours
     • Use predictive scaling for known patterns
     • Implement aggressive scale-in policies
   
   ✓ Monitoring
     • Track cost per job/query
     • Monitor resource utilization
     • Identify optimization opportunities


7. PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION
   ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   
   ✓ Caching Strategy
     • Cache frequently accessed data
     • Use appropriate storage levels
     • Monitor cache hit rates
   
   ✓ Parallelism
     • Optimize partition count
     • Avoid small files problem
     • Balance parallelism with overhead
   
   ✓ Code Optimization
     • Use efficient transformations
     • Minimize data movement
     • Leverage predicate pushdown


8. MONITORING AND ALERTING

    @staticmethod
    def get_troubleshooting_guide():
        """Return troubleshooting guide for common issues"""
        guide = """
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              ELASTICITY TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE                        ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

ISSUE 1: Scaling Thrashing (Constant Scale-Out/Scale-In)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Frequent scaling events
  • Unstable executor count
  • Poor performance

Solutions:
  1. Increase cooldown period (60-120 seconds)
  
```python
  1. Increase cooldown period (60-120 seconds)
  2. Widen threshold gap between scale-out and scale-in
  3. Add hysteresis to prevent rapid changes
  4. Use moving average for metrics instead of instant values

Example Fix:
  scale_out_threshold = 80%
  scale_in_threshold = 30%  # At least 50% difference
  cooldown_period = 90s


ISSUE 2: Out of Memory Errors Despite Scaling
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • OOM errors even with many executors
  • Task failures
  • Slow garbage collection

Solutions:
  1. Switch to vertical scaling (increase executor memory)
  2. Increase spark.executor.memoryOverhead
  3. Optimize data structures and caching
  4. Reduce partition size
  5. Use disk spillover for large datasets

Example Fix:
  spark.executor.memory = 8g
  spark.executor.memoryOverhead = 2g
  spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 400


ISSUE 3: Slow Scale-Out Response
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Jobs timeout before resources arrive
  • Performance degradation during spikes
  • Delayed scaling actions

Solutions:
  1. Implement predictive scaling
  2. Reduce check interval
  3. Pre-warm executors during known peak times
  4. Use faster instance types
  5. Keep minimum executors higher

Example Fix:
  spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors = 5  # Higher baseline
  check_interval = 5s  # More frequent checks
  Enable predictive scaling for known patterns


ISSUE 4: Executors Not Scaling In
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Executors remain active despite low load
  • High costs during off-peak
  • Idle resources

Solutions:
  1. Check executor idle timeout settings
  2. Verify cached data isn't preventing scale-in
  3. Reduce cachedExecutorIdleTimeout
  4. Manually unpersist unused DataFrames
  5. Check for long-running tasks

Example Fix:
  spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout = 60s
  spark.dynamicAllocation.cachedExecutorIdleTimeout = 120s
  df.unpersist()  # Release cached data


ISSUE 5: Data Skew Preventing Effective Scaling
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Some tasks take much longer than others
  • Uneven resource utilization
  • Stragglers despite scaling

Solutions:
  1. Repartition data with better key distribution
  2. Use salting technique for skewed keys
  3. Increase parallelism
  4. Use adaptive query execution
  5. Filter data earlier in pipeline

Example Fix:
  # Add salt to skewed keys
  df_salted = df.withColumn("salt", (rand() * 10).cast("int"))
  df_repartitioned = df_salted.repartition(200, "key", "salt")


ISSUE 6: Network Bottlenecks with Horizontal Scaling
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • High shuffle read/write times
  • Network saturation
  • Scaling doesn't improve performance

Solutions:
  1. Reduce shuffle operations
  2. Use broadcast joins for small tables
  3. Optimize partition count
  4. Increase network bandwidth
  5. Co-locate data and compute

Example Fix:
  # Use broadcast join
  from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
  result = large_df.join(broadcast(small_df), "key")
  
  # Reduce shuffle partitions
  spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "100")


ISSUE 7: Predictive Model Inaccuracy
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Poor scaling decisions
  • Over/under provisioning
  • Frequent prediction errors

Solutions:
  1. Collect more historical data
  2. Add more relevant features
  3. Retrain model more frequently
  4. Use ensemble methods
  5. Implement fallback to auto-scaling

Example Fix:
  # Add more features
  features = [hour, day_of_week, recent_avg_load, 
              trend, seasonality]
  
  # Retrain regularly
  if iteration % 100 == 0:
      retrain_model()
  
  # Fallback mechanism
  if prediction_confidence < 0.7:
      use_auto_scaling()


ISSUE 8: High Costs Despite Optimization
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Unexpectedly high cloud bills
  • Resources not scaling down
  • Inefficient resource usage

Solutions:
  1. Audit scaling policies
  2. Implement aggressive scale-in
  3. Use spot/preemptible instances
  4. Schedule scale-down during off-peak
  5. Set strict maximum limits

Example Fix:
  # Aggressive scale-in
  scale_in_threshold = 20%  # Lower threshold
  executorIdleTimeout = 30s  # Faster timeout
  
  # Use spot instances
  spark.executor.instances.spot = 80%  # 80% spot
  
  # Scheduled scaling
  if hour < 6 or hour > 20:  # Off-peak
      scale_to_minimum()


ISSUE 9: Executor Startup Time Too Long
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Delayed job execution
  • Timeout errors
  • Poor user experience

Solutions:
  1. Use container pools
  2. Pre-warm executors
  3. Optimize Docker image size
  4. Use faster storage for dependencies
  5. Cache application JARs

Example Fix:
  # Pre-warm executors
  spark.dynamicAllocation.minExecutors = 3
  
  # Use smaller images
  FROM spark:3.3-slim  # Smaller base image
  
  # Cache dependencies
  spark.yarn.archive = hdfs:///spark-libs.jar


ISSUE 10: Monitoring Gaps
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Symptoms:
  • Scaling issues not detected
  • No visibility into resource usage
  • Unable to diagnose problems

Solutions:
  1. Implement comprehensive metrics collection
  2. Set up real-time dashboards
  3. Configure alerting
  4. Enable Spark event logs
  5. Use APM tools

Example Fix:
  # Enable detailed metrics
  spark.metrics.conf.*.sink.console.class = ConsoleMetrics
  spark.eventLog.enabled = true
  spark.eventLog.dir = hdfs:///spark-logs
  
  # Set up alerts
  if cpu_usage > 90% for 5 minutes:
      alert("High CPU usage")
  
  if scaling_events > 10 per hour:
      alert("Scaling thrashing detected")

╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
        """
        
        print(guide)

# DOCUMENTATION GENERATOR
# ============================================================================

def generate_documentation():
    """Generate comprehensive documentation for all patterns"""
    doc = """
# PySpark Resource Elasticity Patterns - Complete Documentation

## Table of Contents
1. [Overview](#overview)
2. [Pattern Descriptions](#pattern-descriptions)
3. [Usage Examples](#usage-examples)
4. [Best Practices](#best-practices)
5. [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
6. [API Reference](#api-reference)

## Overview

This module provides comprehensive implementations of five resource elasticity
patterns for Apache Spark applications:

1. **Horizontal Elasticity Pattern** - Scale by adding/removing executors
2. **Vertical Elasticity Pattern** - Scale by adjusting resources per executor
3. **Auto-Scaling Elasticity Pattern** - Automatic scaling based on metrics
4. **Manual Scaling Pattern** - Explicit user-controlled scaling
5. **Predictive Scaling Pattern** - ML-based proactive scaling

## Pattern Descriptions

### 1. Horizontal Elasticity Pattern

**Purpose**: Distribute workload across multiple nodes by dynamically adjusting
the number of executors.

**When to Use**:
- Workload can be parallelized
- Need fault tolerance
- Variable concurrent users
- Cost optimization important

**Configuration**:
```python
horizontal = HorizontalElasticityPattern()
horizontal.scale_out(num_executors=3)  # Add 3 executors
horizontal.scale_in(num_executors=1)   # Remove 1 executor
```

### 2. Vertical Elasticity Pattern

**Purpose**: Adjust memory and CPU cores allocated to individual executors
without changing their count.

**When to Use**:
- Single-threaded operations
- Memory-intensive tasks
- Workload doesn't parallelize well
- Need to avoid network overhead

**Configuration**:
```python
vertical = VerticalElasticityPattern()
vertical.create_spark_session('large')  # 8g memory, 8 cores
vertical.scale_up()    # Upgrade to next tier
vertical.scale_down()  # Downgrade to previous tier
```

### 3. Auto-Scaling Elasticity Pattern

**Purpose**: Automatically adjust resources based on system metrics and
predefined thresholds.

**When to Use**:
- Variable workload over time
- Want hands-off management
- Cost optimization critical
- Can tolerate scaling lag

**Configuration**:
```python
auto_scaling = AutoScalingElasticityPattern()
auto_scaling.config['cpu_threshold_high'] = 80
auto_scaling.config['memory_threshold_high'] = 85
auto_scaling.start_monitoring()
```

### 4. Manual Scaling Pattern

**Purpose**: Provide explicit control over resource allocation for predictable
workloads.

**When to Use**:
- Predictable, stable workload
- Need fine-grained control
- Testing/benchmarking scenarios
- Compliance requires oversight

**Configuration**:
```python
manual = ManualScalingPattern()
manual.scale_to(num_executors=8, executor_memory='4g', executor_cores=4)
manual.add_executors(2)
manual.remove_executors(1)
```

### 5. Predictive Scaling Pattern

**Purpose**: Use machine learning to predict future resource requirements and
proactively scale resources.

**When to Use**:
- Workload has predictable patterns
- Can't tolerate scaling lag
- Historical data available
- Performance critical

**Configuration**:
```python
predictive = PredictiveScalingPattern()
predictive.collect_metrics(workload_size=100000)
predictive.train_prediction_model()
predicted_load = predictive.predict_future_load()
```

## Usage Examples

### Example 1: Simple Horizontal Scaling
```python
from elasticity_patterns import HorizontalElasticityPattern

# Create pattern instance
pattern = HorizontalElasticityPattern()

# Process data with scaling
pattern.process_with_horizontal_scaling(data_size=100000)

# Cleanup
pattern.spark.stop()
```

### Example 2: Auto-Scaling with Custom Thresholds
```python
from elasticity_patterns import AutoScalingElasticityPattern

# Create and configure
auto = AutoScalingElasticityPattern()
auto.config['cpu_threshold_high'] = 75
auto.config['cooldown_period'] = 45

# Run with monitoring
auto.simulate_workload(duration=120)
```

### Example 3: Predictive Scaling for Batch Jobs
```python
from elasticity_patterns import PredictiveScalingPattern

# Initialize
predictive = PredictiveScalingPattern()

# Collect historical data
for i in range(30):
    predictive.collect_metrics(workload_size=50000 + i*1000)

# Train model
predictive.train_prediction_model()

# Use predictions for scaling
predictive.simulate_workload_pattern(duration=90)
```

## API Reference

### HorizontalElasticityPattern

**Methods**:
- `__init__(app_name: str)` - Initialize pattern
- `scale_out(num_executors: int) -> bool` - Add executors
- `scale_in(num_executors: int) -> bool` - Remove executors
- `get_current_executors() -> int` - Get executor count
- `process_with_horizontal_scaling(data_size: int)` - Demo processing

### VerticalElasticityPattern

**Methods**:
- `__init__(app_name: str)` - Initialize pattern
- `create_spark_session(config_level: str)` - Create with config
- `scale_up() -> bool` - Upgrade resource tier
- `scale_down() -> bool` - Downgrade resource tier
- `benchmark_configuration(data_size: int) -> float` - Benchmark

### AutoScalingElasticityPattern

**Methods**:
- `__init__(app_name: str)` - Initialize pattern
- `get_system_metrics() -> Dict` - Collect current metrics
- `should_scale_out(metrics: Dict) -> bool` - Check scale-out condition
- `should_scale_in(metrics: Dict) -> bool` - Check scale-in condition
- `start_monitoring()` - Start background monitoring
- `stop_monitoring()` - Stop monitoring
- `simulate_workload(duration: int)` - Run simulation

### ManualScalingPattern

**Methods**:
- `__init__(app_name: str)` - Initialize pattern
- `get_cluster_status() -> Dict` - Get cluster info
- `scale_to(num_executors, executor_memory, executor_cores) -> bool` - Scale to config
- `add_executors(count: int) -> bool` - Add executors
- `remove_executors(count: int) -> bool` - Remove executors
- `benchmark_current_config(data_size: int) -> Dict` - Benchmark
- `print_scaling_history()` - Show scaling history

### PredictiveScalingPattern

**Methods**:
- `__init__(app_name: str)` - Initialize pattern
- `collect_metrics(workload_size: int) -> Dict` - Collect metrics
- `train_prediction_model() -> bool` - Train ML model
- `predict_future_load() -> float` - Predict load
- `make_scaling_decision(predicted_load: float) -> str` - Decide action
- `simulate_workload_pattern(duration: int)` - Run simulation

## Performance Tuning

### Optimization Tips

1. **Partition Tuning**
   ```python
   # Rule of thumb: 2-3 partitions per CPU core
   num_partitions = num_executors * executor_cores * 2
   df.repartition(num_partitions)
   ```

2. **Memory Optimization**
   ```python
   # Set appropriate memory overhead
   spark.executor.memoryOverhead = executor_memory * 0.10
   
   # Use efficient storage levels
   df.persist(StorageLevel.MEMORY_AND_DISK)
   ```

3. **Shuffle Optimization**
   ```python
   # Adjust shuffle partitions
   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")
   
   # Use broadcast for small tables
   from pyspark.sql.functions import broadcast
   result = large_df.join(broadcast(small_df), "key")
   ```

1. **Resource Utilization**
   - CPU percentage
   - Memory percentage
   - Disk I/O
   - Network throughput

2. **Performance Metrics**
   - Job execution time
   - Task duration
   - Shuffle read/write
   - GC time

3. **Scaling Metrics**
   - Scaling events frequency
   - Time to scale
   - Resource efficiency
   - Cost per job

        print("""
Resource elasticity is the ability to dynamically adjust computational

# PySpark Data Constraint Validation Patterns

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.types import *
from typing import List, Dict, Tuple, Optional
from datetime import datetime
import logging

# Configure logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class DataConstraintValidator:
    """
    A comprehensive class for validating various data constraints in PySpark DataFrames.
    Implements multiple validation patterns for data quality assurance.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        """
        Initialize the validator with a SparkSession.
        
        Args:
            spark: Active SparkSession instance
        """
        self.spark = spark
        self.validation_results = []
    
    def get_validation_summary(self) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get a summary of all validation results.
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing validation summary
        """
        if not self.validation_results:
            return self.spark.createDataFrame([], 
                StructType([
                    StructField("validation_type", StringType()),
                    StructField("table_name", StringType()),
                    StructField("column_name", StringType()),
                    StructField("is_valid", BooleanType()),
                    StructField("violation_count", LongType()),
                    StructField("timestamp", TimestampType())
                ]))
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(self.validation_results)


class PrimaryKeyValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Pattern 1: Primary Key Validation Pattern
    Validates that specified columns form a valid primary key (unique and not null).
    """
    
    def validate_primary_key(
        self, 
        df: DataFrame, 
        pk_columns: List[str],
        table_name: str = "unknown"
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate primary key constraints on specified columns.
        
        A valid primary key must:
        1. Not contain null values in any PK column
        2. Be unique across all rows
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            pk_columns: List of column names forming the primary key
            table_name: Name of the table for reporting
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results and violation details
        """
        logger.info(f"Validating primary key for table '{table_name}' on columns: {pk_columns}")
        
        # Validate input
        for col in pk_columns:
            if col not in df.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"Column '{col}' not found in DataFrame")
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        
        # Check for null values in PK columns
        null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in pk_columns])
        null_violations = df.filter(null_check_expr)
        null_count = null_violations.count()
        
        # Check for duplicate values
        duplicate_check = df.groupBy(pk_columns).count().filter("count > 1")
        duplicate_count = duplicate_check.count()
        duplicate_rows = duplicate_check.agg(F.sum("count").alias("total_duplicate_rows")).collect()[0][0] or 0
        
        # Check for uniqueness (distinct count should equal total count for non-null rows)
        non_null_df = df.filter(" AND ".join([f"{col} IS NOT NULL" for col in pk_columns]))
        distinct_count = non_null_df.select(pk_columns).distinct().count()
        non_null_count = non_null_df.count()
        
        is_valid = (null_count == 0) and (duplicate_count == 0)
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "PRIMARY_KEY",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "pk_columns": pk_columns,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_rows": total_rows,
            "null_violations": null_count,
            "duplicate_key_groups": duplicate_count,
            "duplicate_rows": duplicate_rows - duplicate_count if duplicate_rows else 0,
            "distinct_keys": distinct_count,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "null_violation_df": null_violations if null_count > 0 else None,
            "duplicate_violation_df": duplicate_check if duplicate_count > 0 else None
        }
        
        # Store result
        self.validation_results.append({
            "validation_type": "PRIMARY_KEY",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "column_name": ",".join(pk_columns),
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "violation_count": null_count + duplicate_rows,
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        })
        
        logger.info(f"Primary key validation completed. Valid: {is_valid}")
        return result
    
    def get_pk_violations(
        self, 
        df: DataFrame, 
        pk_columns: List[str],
        violation_type: str = "all"
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get detailed primary key violations.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            pk_columns: Primary key columns
            violation_type: Type of violation ('null', 'duplicate', 'all')
            
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing violation details
        """
        violations = []
        
        if violation_type in ["null", "all"]:
            null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in pk_columns])
            null_violations = df.filter(null_check_expr).withColumn(
                "violation_type", F.lit("NULL_IN_PK")
            )
            violations.append(null_violations)
        
        if violation_type in ["duplicate", "all"]:
            # Add row number to identify duplicates
            window_spec = Window.partitionBy(pk_columns).orderBy(F.monotonically_increasing_id())
            duplicate_violations = df.withColumn("row_num", F.row_number().over(window_spec)) \
                .filter("row_num > 1") \
                .withColumn("violation_type", F.lit("DUPLICATE_PK")) \
                .drop("row_num")
            violations.append(duplicate_violations)
        
        if violations:
            return violations[0].unionByName(violations[1]) if len(violations) > 1 else violations[0]
        else:
            return self.spark.createDataFrame([], df.schema)


class ForeignKeyValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Pattern 2: Foreign Key Validation Pattern
    Validates referential integrity between parent and child tables.
    """
    
    def validate_foreign_key(
        self,
        child_df: DataFrame,
        parent_df: DataFrame,
        fk_columns: List[str],
        pk_columns: List[str],
        child_table_name: str = "child",
        parent_table_name: str = "parent",
        allow_null: bool = True
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate foreign key constraints between child and parent tables.
        
        Args:
            child_df: Child DataFrame containing foreign key
            parent_df: Parent DataFrame containing primary key
            fk_columns: Foreign key columns in child table
            pk_columns: Primary key columns in parent table
            child_table_name: Name of child table
            parent_table_name: Name of parent table
            allow_null: Whether NULL values are allowed in FK
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
        """
        logger.info(f"Validating foreign key from '{child_table_name}' to '{parent_table_name}'")
        
        # Validate column existence
        for col in fk_columns:
            if col not in child_df.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"FK column '{col}' not found in child DataFrame")
        for col in pk_columns:
            if col not in parent_df.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"PK column '{col}' not found in parent DataFrame")
        
        total_child_rows = child_df.count()
        
        # Handle null values in FK
        if allow_null:
            # Exclude rows where all FK columns are NULL
            null_check_expr = " AND ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in fk_columns])
            child_df_non_null = child_df.filter(f"NOT ({null_check_expr})")
            null_fk_count = total_child_rows - child_df_non_null.count()
        else:
            child_df_non_null = child_df
            # Check for null violations
            null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in fk_columns])
            null_fk_count = child_df.filter(null_check_expr).count()
        
        # Perform left anti join to find orphaned records
        # Rename columns to avoid conflicts
        join_conditions = [
            child_df_non_null[fk_col] == parent_df[pk_col] 
            for fk_col, pk_col in zip(fk_columns, pk_columns)
        ]
        
        orphaned_records = child_df_non_null.join(
            parent_df.select(pk_columns),
            on=[fk_columns[i] == pk_columns[i] for i in range(len(fk_columns))],
            how="left_anti"
        )
        
        orphaned_count = orphaned_records.count()
        is_valid = (orphaned_count == 0) and (not allow_null or null_fk_count >= 0)
        
        if not allow_null:
            is_valid = is_valid and (null_fk_count == 0)
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "FOREIGN_KEY",
            "child_table": child_table_name,
            "parent_table": parent_table_name,
            "fk_columns": fk_columns,
            "pk_columns": pk_columns,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_child_rows": total_child_rows,
            "orphaned_records": orphaned_count,
            "null_fk_records": null_fk_count if not allow_null else 0,
            "allow_null": allow_null,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "orphaned_records_df": orphaned_records if orphaned_count > 0 else None
        }
        
        # Store result
        self.validation_results.append({
            "validation_type": "FOREIGN_KEY",
            "table_name": f"{child_table_name}->{parent_table_name}",
            "column_name": ",".join(fk_columns),
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "violation_count": orphaned_count + (null_fk_count if not allow_null else 0),
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        })
        
        logger.info(f"Foreign key validation completed. Valid: {is_valid}")
        return result
    
    def get_fk_violations(
        self,
        child_df: DataFrame,
        parent_df: DataFrame,
        fk_columns: List[str],
        pk_columns: List[str]
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get detailed foreign key violations (orphaned records).
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing orphaned records
        """
        orphaned_records = child_df.join(
            parent_df.select(pk_columns),
            on=[fk_columns[i] == pk_columns[i] for i in range(len(fk_columns))],
            how="left_anti"
        ).withColumn("violation_type", F.lit("ORPHANED_RECORD"))
        
        return orphaned_records


class UniqueKeyValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Pattern 3: Unique Key Validation Pattern
    Validates uniqueness constraints on specified columns (allows NULLs).
    """
    
    def validate_unique_key(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        unique_columns: List[str],
        table_name: str = "unknown",
        null_handling: str = "ignore"  # 'ignore', 'consider', 'separate'
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate unique key constraints.
        
        Unlike primary keys, unique keys:
        1. Allow NULL values
        2. Ensure uniqueness among non-NULL values
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            unique_columns: Columns that should be unique
            table_name: Name of the table
            null_handling: How to handle NULLs
                - 'ignore': NULLs are not considered in uniqueness check
                - 'consider': Each NULL is considered unique
                - 'separate': Report NULL statistics separately
                
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
        """
        logger.info(f"Validating unique key for table '{table_name}' on columns: {unique_columns}")
        
        # Validate input
        for col in unique_columns:
            if col not in df.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"Column '{col}' not found in DataFrame")
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        
        # Count NULL rows
        null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in unique_columns])
        null_count = df.filter(null_check_expr).count()
        
        # Check uniqueness based on null_handling strategy
        if null_handling == "ignore":
            # Only check uniqueness for non-NULL values
            non_null_df = df.filter(" AND ".join([f"{col} IS NOT NULL" for col in unique_columns]))
            duplicate_check = non_null_df.groupBy(unique_columns).count().filter("count > 1")
            
        elif null_handling == "consider":
            # Treat each NULL combination as unique (standard SQL behavior)
            # Create a composite key that makes NULLs unique
            df_with_key = df
            for col in unique_columns:
                df_with_key = df_with_key.withColumn(
                    f"{col}_unique",
                    F.when(F.col(col).isNull(), F.monotonically_increasing_id()).otherwise(F.col(col))
                )
            unique_cols_modified = [f"{col}_unique" for col in unique_columns]
            duplicate_check = df_with_key.groupBy(unique_cols_modified).count().filter("count > 1")
            
        else:  # separate
            # Check uniqueness only for non-NULL values
            non_null_df = df.filter(" AND ".join([f"{col} IS NOT NULL" for col in unique_columns]))
            duplicate_check = non_null_df.groupBy(unique_columns).count().filter("count > 1")
        
        duplicate_count = duplicate_check.count()
        duplicate_rows = duplicate_check.agg(F.sum("count").alias("total_duplicate_rows")).collect()[0][0] or 0
        
        is_valid = (duplicate_count == 0)
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "UNIQUE_KEY",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "unique_columns": unique_columns,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_rows": total_rows,
            "null_count": null_count,
            "duplicate_key_groups": duplicate_count,
            "duplicate_rows": duplicate_rows - duplicate_count if duplicate_rows else 0,
            "null_handling": null_handling,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "duplicate_violation_df": duplicate_check if duplicate_count > 0 else None
        }
        
        # Store result
        self.validation_results.append({
            "validation_type": "UNIQUE_KEY",
            "table_name": table_name
```python
            "column_name": ",".join(unique_columns),
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "violation_count": duplicate_rows - duplicate_count if duplicate_rows else 0,
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        })
        
        logger.info(f"Unique key validation completed. Valid: {is_valid}")
        return result
    
    def get_unique_violations(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        unique_columns: List[str],
        include_all_duplicates: bool = True
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get detailed unique key violations.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            unique_columns: Columns with unique constraint
            include_all_duplicates: If True, include all rows of duplicate groups
                                   If False, include only excess duplicates
                                   
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing duplicate records
        """
        # Filter out NULL values for unique key check
        non_null_df = df.filter(" AND ".join([f"{col} IS NOT NULL" for col in unique_columns]))
        
        # Find duplicate groups
        duplicate_groups = non_null_df.groupBy(unique_columns).count().filter("count > 1")
        
        # Join back to get full records
        violations = non_null_df.join(
            duplicate_groups.select(unique_columns),
            on=unique_columns,
            how="inner"
        )
        
        if not include_all_duplicates:
            # Keep only excess duplicates (n-1 for each group)
            window_spec = Window.partitionBy(unique_columns).orderBy(F.monotonically_increasing_id())
            violations = violations.withColumn("row_num", F.row_number().over(window_spec)) \
                .filter("row_num > 1") \
                .drop("row_num")
        
        return violations.withColumn("violation_type", F.lit("DUPLICATE_UNIQUE_KEY"))


class CheckConstraintValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Pattern 4: Check Constraint Validation Pattern
    Validates business rules and data constraints using custom conditions.
    """
    
    def validate_check_constraint(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        constraint_name: str,
        constraint_condition: str,
        table_name: str = "unknown",
        constraint_description: str = None
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate check constraints using SQL-like conditions.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            constraint_name: Name of the constraint
            constraint_condition: SQL condition that should be TRUE for valid rows
            table_name: Name of the table
            constraint_description: Human-readable description of constraint
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
            
        Example:
            validate_check_constraint(
                df, 
                "salary_positive", 
                "salary > 0 AND salary < 1000000",
                "employees"
            )
        """
        logger.info(f"Validating check constraint '{constraint_name}' for table '{table_name}'")
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        
        # Find violations (rows where constraint is FALSE or NULL)
        # Valid rows are those where the constraint is TRUE
        violations = df.filter(f"NOT ({constraint_condition})")
        violation_count = violations.count()
        
        is_valid = (violation_count == 0)
        
        # Calculate pass rate
        pass_rate = ((total_rows - violation_count) / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "CHECK_CONSTRAINT",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "constraint_name": constraint_name,
            "constraint_condition": constraint_condition,
            "constraint_description": constraint_description,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_rows": total_rows,
            "violation_count": violation_count,
            "valid_count": total_rows - violation_count,
            "pass_rate_percent": round(pass_rate, 2),
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "violation_df": violations if violation_count > 0 else None
        }
        
        # Store result
        self.validation_results.append({
            "validation_type": "CHECK_CONSTRAINT",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "column_name": constraint_name,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "violation_count": violation_count,
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        })
        
        logger.info(f"Check constraint validation completed. Valid: {is_valid}, Pass rate: {pass_rate:.2f}%")
        return result
    
    def validate_multiple_constraints(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        constraints: List[Dict[str, str]],
        table_name: str = "unknown"
    ) -> List[Dict]:
        """
        Validate multiple check constraints at once.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            constraints: List of constraint dictionaries with keys:
                        'name', 'condition', 'description'
            table_name: Name of the table
            
        Returns:
            List of validation result dictionaries
        """
        results = []
        for constraint in constraints:
            result = self.validate_check_constraint(
                df,
                constraint.get('name'),
                constraint.get('condition'),
                table_name,
                constraint.get('description')
            )
            results.append(result)
        
        return results
    
    def get_check_violations(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        constraint_condition: str,
        constraint_name: str
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get detailed check constraint violations.
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing violating records
        """
        violations = df.filter(f"NOT ({constraint_condition})") \
            .withColumn("violation_type", F.lit(f"CHECK_CONSTRAINT_{constraint_name}")) \
            .withColumn("constraint_condition", F.lit(constraint_condition))
        
        return violations
    
    def validate_range_constraint(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        column_name: str,
        min_value: Optional[float] = None,
        max_value: Optional[float] = None,
        table_name: str = "unknown",
        include_min: bool = True,
        include_max: bool = True
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate range constraints on numeric columns.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            column_name: Column to validate
            min_value: Minimum allowed value
            max_value: Maximum allowed value
            table_name: Name of the table
            include_min: Whether min_value is inclusive
            include_max: Whether max_value is inclusive
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
        """
        conditions = []
        
        if min_value is not None:
            op = ">=" if include_min else ">"
            conditions.append(f"{column_name} {op} {min_value}")
        
        if max_value is not None:
            op = "<=" if include_max else "<"
            conditions.append(f"{column_name} {op} {max_value}")
        
        constraint_condition = " AND ".join(conditions) if conditions else "TRUE"
        constraint_name = f"{column_name}_range_check"
        
        min_str = f"[{min_value}" if include_min else f"({min_value}"
        max_str = f"{max_value}]" if include_max else f"{max_value})"
        description = f"{column_name} must be in range {min_str}, {max_str}"
        
        return self.validate_check_constraint(
            df,
            constraint_name,
            constraint_condition,
            table_name,
            description
        )
    
    def validate_enum_constraint(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        column_name: str,
        allowed_values: List,
        table_name: str = "unknown",
        case_sensitive: bool = True
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate that column values are within allowed set.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            column_name: Column to validate
            allowed_values: List of allowed values
            table_name: Name of the table
            case_sensitive: Whether comparison is case-sensitive (for strings)
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
        """
        if not case_sensitive and all(isinstance(v, str) for v in allowed_values):
            # Convert to uppercase for comparison
            allowed_values_upper = [v.upper() for v in allowed_values]
            allowed_str = "', '".join(allowed_values_upper)
            constraint_condition = f"UPPER({column_name}) IN ('{allowed_str}')"
        else:
            # Handle different data types
            if all(isinstance(v, str) for v in allowed_values):
                allowed_str = "', '".join(allowed_values)
                constraint_condition = f"{column_name} IN ('{allowed_str}')"
            else:
                allowed_str = ", ".join(str(v) for v in allowed_values)
                constraint_condition = f"{column_name} IN ({allowed_str})"
        
        constraint_name = f"{column_name}_enum_check"
        description = f"{column_name} must be one of: {allowed_values}"
        
        return self.validate_check_constraint(
            df,
            constraint_name,
            constraint_condition,
            table_name,
            description
        )


class NotNullValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Pattern 5: Not Null Validation Pattern
    Validates that specified columns do not contain NULL values.
    """
    
    def validate_not_null(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        columns: List[str],
        table_name: str = "unknown"
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate NOT NULL constraints on specified columns.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            columns: List of columns that should not be NULL
            table_name: Name of the table
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing validation results
        """
        logger.info(f"Validating NOT NULL constraint for table '{table_name}' on columns: {columns}")
        
        # Validate input
        for col in columns:
            if col not in df.columns:
                raise ValueError(f"Column '{col}' not found in DataFrame")
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        
        # Check each column for NULL values
        column_results = {}
        total_violations = 0
        
        for col in columns:
            null_count = df.filter(F.col(col).isNull()).count()
            column_results[col] = {
                "null_count": null_count,
                "null_percentage": (null_count / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0,
                "is_valid": null_count == 0
            }
            total_violations += null_count
        
        # Find rows with any NULL in specified columns
        null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in columns])
        rows_with_nulls = df.filter(null_check_expr)
        rows_with_null_count = rows_with_nulls.count()
        
        is_valid = all(result["is_valid"] for result in column_results.values())
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "NOT_NULL",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "columns": columns,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_rows": total_rows,
            "rows_with_nulls": rows_with_null_count,
            "total_null_values": total_violations,
            "column_details": column_results,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "violation_df": rows_with_nulls if rows_with_null_count > 0 else None
        }
        
        # Store result for each column
        for col, col_result in column_results.items():
            self.validation_results.append({
                "validation_type": "NOT_NULL",
                "table_name": table_name,
                "column_name": col,
                "is_valid": col_result["is_valid"],
                "violation_count": col_result["null_count"],
                "timestamp": datetime.now()
            })
        
        logger.info(f"NOT NULL validation completed. Valid: {is_valid}")
        return result
    
    def validate_not_null_single_column(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        column_name: str,
        table_name: str = "unknown"
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate NOT NULL constraint on a single column with detailed statistics.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            column_name: Column to validate
            table_name: Name of the table
            
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing detailed validation results
        """
        if column_name not in df.columns:
            raise ValueError(f"Column '{column_name}' not found in DataFrame")
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        null_count = df.filter(F.col(column_name).isNull()).count()
        non_null_count = total_rows - null_count
        
        is_valid = (null_count == 0)
        null_percentage = (null_count / total_rows * 100) if total_rows > 0 else 0
        
        result = {
            "validation_type": "NOT_NULL",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "column_name": column_name,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "total_rows": total_rows,
            "null_count": null_count,
            "non_null_count": non_null_count,
            "null_percentage": round(null_percentage, 2),
            "completeness_percentage": round(100 - null_percentage, 2),
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        }
        
        # Store result
        self.validation_results.append({
            "validation_type": "NOT_NULL",
            "table_name": table_name,
            "column_name": column_name,
            "is_valid": is_valid,
            "violation_count": null_count,
            "timestamp": datetime.now()
        })
        
        return result
    
    def get_null_violations(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        columns: List[str],
        include_null_pattern: bool = True
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get detailed NULL violations with pattern analysis.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            columns: Columns to check for NULLs
            include_null_pattern: If True, add column showing which columns are NULL
            
        Returns:
            DataFrame containing rows with NULL values
        """
        null_check_expr = " OR ".join([f"{col} IS NULL" for col in columns])
        violations = df.filter(null_check_expr)
        
        if include_null_pattern:
            # Add columns indicating which fields are NULL
            for col in columns:
                violations = violations.withColumn(
                    f"{col}_is_null",
                    F.when(F.col(col).isNull(), True).otherwise(False)
                )
        
        violations = violations.withColumn("violation_type", F.lit("NULL_VALUE"))
        
        return violations
    
    def get_null_summary(
        self,

    ) -> DataFrame:
        """

        Returns:
            DataFrame with NULL statistics per column
        """
        if columns is None:
            columns = df.columns
        
        total_rows = df.count()
        
        summary_data = []
        for col in columns:

class CompositeValidator(DataConstraintValidator):
    """
    Composite validator that combines all validation patterns.
    Provides comprehensive data quality validation.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        super().__init__(spark)
        self.pk_validator = PrimaryKeyValidator(spark)
        self.fk_validator = ForeignKeyValidator(spark)
        self.uk_validator = UniqueKeyValidator(spark)
        self.check_validator = CheckConstraintValidator(spark)
        self.nn_validator = NotNullValidator(spark)
    
    def validate_all_constraints(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        table_name: str,
        constraints_config: Dict
    ) -> Dict:
        """
        Validate all configured constraints on a DataFrame.
        
        Args:
            df: Input DataFrame
            table_name: Name of the table
            constraints_config: Dictionary containing constraint configurations
                {
                    "primary_key": ["col1", "col2"],
                    "not_null": ["col1", "col3"],
                    "unique_keys": [["col4"], ["col5", "col6"]],
                    "check_constraints": [
                        {"name": "check1", "condition": "col7 > 0"}
                    ]
                }
        
        Returns:
            Dictionary containing all validation results
        """
        logger.info(f"Starting comprehensive validation for table '{table_name}'")
        
        all_results = {
            "table_name": table_name,
            "timestamp": datetime.now(),
            "validations": {}
        }
        
        # Validate Primary Key
        if "primary_key" in constraints_config:
            pk_result = self.pk_validator.validate_primary_key(
                df, 
                constraints_config["primary_key"],
                table_name
            )
            all_results["validations"]["primary_key"] = pk_result
        
        # Validate NOT NULL constraints
        if "not_null" in constraints_config:
            nn_result = self.nn_validator.validate_not_null(
                df,
                constraints_config["not_null"],
                table_name
            )
            all_results["validations"]["not_null"] = nn_result
        
        # Validate Unique Keys
        if "unique_keys" in constraints_config:
            uk_results = []
            for idx, uk_cols in enumerate(constraints_config["unique_keys"]):
                uk_result = self.uk_validator.validate_unique_key(
                    df,
                    uk_cols,
                    f"{table_name}_uk_{idx}"
                )
                uk_results.append(uk_result)
            all_results["validations"]["unique_keys"] = uk_results
        
        # Validate Check Constraints
        if "check_constraints" in constraints_config:
            check_results = self.check_validator.validate_multiple_constraints(
                df,
                constraints_config["check_constraints"],
                table_name
            )
            all_results["validations"]["check_constraints"] = check_results
        
        # Calculate overall validity
        all_valid = True
        total_violations = 0
        
        for validation_type, results in all_results["validations"].items():
            if isinstance(results, list):
                for result in results:
                    all_valid = all_valid and result.get("is_valid", True)
                    total_violations += result.get("violation_count", 0)
            else:
                all_valid = all_valid and results.get("is_valid", True)
                total_violations += results.get("violation_count", 0)
        
        all_results["overall_valid"] = all_valid
        all_results["total_violations"] = total_violations
        
        logger.info(f"Comprehensive validation completed. Overall valid: {all_valid}")
        return all_results
    
    def get_consolidated_violations(
        self,
        df: DataFrame,
        constraints_config: Dict
    ) -> DataFrame:
        """
        Get all violations consolidated into a single DataFrame.
        
        Returns:
            DataFrame with all violations and their types
        """
        violations_list = []
        
        # Primary Key violations
        if "primary_key" in constraints_config:
            pk_violations = self.pk_validator.get_pk_violations(
                df,
                constraints_config["primary_key"]
            )
            if pk_violations.count() > 0:
                violations_list.append(pk_violations)
        
        # NOT NULL violations
        if "not_null" in constraints_config:
            nn_violations = self.nn_validator.get_null_violations(
                df,
                constraints_config["not_null"]
            )
            if nn_violations.count() > 0:
                violations_list.append(nn_violations)
        
        # Unique Key violations
        if "unique_keys" in constraints_config:
            for uk_cols in constraints_config["unique_keys"]:
                uk_violations = self.uk_validator.get_unique_violations(
                    df,
                    uk_cols
                )
                if uk_violations.count() > 0:
                    violations_list.append(uk_violations)
        
        # Check Constraint violations
        if "check_constraints" in constraints_config:
            for constraint in constraints_config["check_constraints"]:
                check_violations = self.check_validator.get_check_violations(
                    df,
                    constraint["condition"],
                    constraint["name"]
                )
                if check_violations.count() > 0:
                    violations_list.append(check_violations)
        
        # Union all violations
        if violations_list:
            consolidated = violations_list[0]
            for violation_df in violations_list[1:]:
                consolidated = consolidated.unionByName(violation_df, allowMissingColumns=True)
            return consolidated
        else:
            return self.spark.createDataFrame([], df.schema)

def create_sample_data(spark: SparkSession) -> Tuple[DataFrame, DataFrame, DataFrame]:
    """
    Create sample data for demonstrating all validation patterns.
    
    Returns:
        Tuple of (employees_df, departments_df, projects_df)
    """
    # Departments table (parent)
    departments_data = [
        (1, "Engineering", "ENG"),
        (2, "Sales", "SAL"),
        (3, "Marketing", "MKT"),
        (4, "HR", "HR"),
        (5, "Finance", "FIN")
    ]
    departments_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        departments_data,
        ["dept_id", "dept_name", "dept_code"]
    )
    
    # Employees table (child) - with intentional violations
    employees_data = [
        (1, "John Doe", 1, 75000.0, "ACTIVE", "john@example.com"),
        (2, "Jane Smith", 2, 85000.0, "ACTIVE", "jane@example.com"),
        (3, "Bob Johnson", 1, 65000.0, "ACTIVE", "bob@example.com"),
        (4, "Alice Williams", 3, 70000.0, "INACTIVE", "alice@example.com"),
        (5, "Charlie Brown", None, 60000.0, "ACTIVE", "charlie@example.com"),  # NULL FK
        (6, "David Lee", 99, 80000.0, "ACTIVE", "david@example.com"),  # Invalid FK
        (7, "Eve Davis", 2, -5000.0, "ACTIVE", "eve@example.com"),  # Negative salary
        (8, "Frank Miller", 1, 75000.0, "PENDING", "frank@example.com"),  # Invalid status
        (None, "Ghost Employee", 1, 50000.0, "ACTIVE", "ghost@example.com"),  # NULL PK
        (10, None, 2, 70000.0, "ACTIVE", "noname@example.com"),  # NULL name
        (11, "Grace Hopper", 4, 90000.0, "ACTIVE", "grace@example.com"),
        (12, "Henry Ford", 5, 95000.0, "ACTIVE", "henry@example.com"),
        (13, "Iris West", 1, 72000.0, "ACTIVE", "iris@example.com"),
        (2, "Duplicate Jane", 2, 88000.0, "ACTIVE", "jane2@example.com"),  # Duplicate PK
        (14, "Jack Ryan", 1, 78000.0, "ACTIVE", "jack@example.com"),
        (15, "Kate Bishop", 2, 82000.0, "ACTIVE", "kate@example.com"),
        (16, "Liam Neeson", 3, 79000.0, "ACTIVE", "kate@example.com"),  # Duplicate email (UK violation)
    ]
    employees_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        employees_data,
        ["emp_id", "emp_name", "dept_id", "salary", "status", "email"]
    )
    
    # Projects table - for additional unique key examples
    projects_data = [
        (1, "Project Alpha", "PRJ001", 1),
        (2, "Project Beta", "PRJ002", 2),
        (3, "Project Gamma", "PRJ003", 1),
        (4, "Project Delta", "PRJ002", 3),  # Duplicate project_code (UK violation)
        (5, "Project Epsilon", "PRJ005", 2),
        (6, "Project Zeta", None, 1),  # NULL project_code
    ]
    projects_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        projects_data,
        ["project_id", "project_name", "project_code", "dept_id"]
    )
    
    return employees_df, departments_df, projects_df


def demonstrate_primary_key_validation(spark: SparkSession):
    """Demonstrate Primary Key Validation Pattern"""
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 1: PRIMARY KEY VALIDATION")
    print("="*80)
    
    employees_df, departments_df, projects_df = create_sample_data(spark)
    
    pk_validator = PrimaryKeyValidator(spark)
    
    # Validate employees primary key
    print("\n--- Validating Employees Primary Key (emp_id) ---")
    result = pk_validator.validate_primary_key(
        employees_df,
        ["emp_id"],
        "employees"
    )
    
    print(f"Is Valid: {result['is_valid']}")
    print(f"Total Rows: {result['total_rows']}")
    print(f"NULL Violations: {result['null_violations']}")
    print(f"Duplicate Key Groups: {result['duplicate_key_groups']}")
    print(f"Duplicate Rows: {result['duplicate_rows']}")
    
    # Show violations
    if not result['is_valid']:
        print("\n--- Primary Key Violations ---")
        violations = pk_validator.get_pk_violations(employees_df, ["emp_id"])
        violations.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Validate departments primary key (should be valid)
    print("\n--- Validating Departments Primary Key (dept_id) ---")
    result_dept = pk_validator.validate_primary_key(
        departments_df,
        ["dept_id"],
        "departments"
    )
    print(f"Is Valid: {result_dept['is_valid']}")
    print(f"Total Rows: {result_dept['total_rows']}")
    
    # Composite primary key example
    print("\n--- Composite Primary Key Example ---")
    composite_data = [
        (1, "A", "Data1"),
        (1, "B", "Data2"),
        (2, "A", "Data3"),
        (1, "A", "Data4"),  # Duplicate
    ]
    composite_df = spark.createDataFrame(composite_data, ["key1", "key2", "value"])
    
    result_composite = pk_validator.validate_primary_key(
        composite_df,
        ["key1", "key2"],
        "composite_table"
    )
    print(f"Is Valid: {result_composite['is_valid']}")
    if not result_composite['is_valid']:
        print("Violations:")
        pk_validator.get_pk_violations(composite_df, ["key1", "key2"]).show()

def demonstrate_check_constraint_validation(spark: SparkSession):
    """Demonstrate Check Constraint Validation Pattern"""
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 4: CHECK CONSTRAINT VALIDATION")
    print("="*80)
    
    employees_df, departments_df, projects_df = create_sample_data(spark)
    
    check_validator = CheckConstraintValidator(spark)
    
    # Validate salary range
    print("\n--- Validating Salary Range (0 < salary <= 100000) ---")
    result_salary = check_validator.validate_check_constraint(
        employees_df,
        "salary_positive",
        "salary > 0 AND salary <= 100000",
        "employees",
        "Salary must be positive and not exceed 100,000"
    )
    
    print(f"Is Valid: {result_salary['is_valid']}")
    print(f"Total Rows: {result_salary['total_rows']}")
    print(f"Violations: {result_salary['violation_count']}")
    print(f"Pass Rate: {result_salary['pass_rate_percent']}%")
    
    if result_salary['violation_count'] > 0:
        print("\n--- Salary Violations ---")
        violations = check_validator.get_check_violations(
            employees_df,
            "salary > 0 AND salary <= 100000",
            "salary_positive"
        )
        violations.select("emp_id", "emp_name", "salary").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Validate status enum
    print("\n--- Validating Status Enum (ACTIVE, INACTIVE) ---")
    result_status = check_validator.validate_enum_constraint(
        employees_df,
        "status",
        ["ACTIVE", "INACTIVE"],
        "employees",
        case_sensitive=True
    )
    
    print(f"Is Valid: {result_status['is_valid']}")
    print(f"Violations: {result_status['violation_count']}")
    print(f"Pass Rate: {result_status['pass_rate_percent']}%")
    
    if result_status['violation_count'] > 0:
        print("\n--- Status Violations ---")
        violations = check_validator.get_check_violations(
            employees_df,
            result_status['constraint_condition'],
            "status_enum"
        )
        violations.select("emp_id", "emp_name", "status").show(truncate=False)
    
    # Validate using range constraint helper
    print("\n--- Validating Salary Range Using Helper Method ---")
    result_range = check_validator.validate_range_constraint(
        employees_df,
        "salary",
        min_value=0.0,
        max_value=200000.0,
        table_name="employees",
        include_min=False,
        include_max=True
    )
    
    print(f"Is Valid: {result_range['is_valid']}")
    print(f"Constraint: {result_range['constraint_description']}")
    print(f"Violations: {result_range['violation_count']}")
    
    # Multiple constraints validation
    print("\n--- Validating Multiple Constraints ---")
    constraints = [
        {
            "name": "salary_positive",
            "condition": "salary > 0",
            "description": "Salary must be positive"
        },
        {
            "name": "valid_status",
            "condition": "status IN ('ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE')",
            "description": "Status must be ACTIVE or INACTIVE"
        },
        {
            "name": "name_not_empty",
            "condition": "emp_name IS NOT NULL AND LENGTH(emp_name) > 0",
            "description": "Employee name must not be empty"
        }
    ]
    
    results = check_validator.validate_multiple_constraints(
        employees_df,
        constraints,
        "employees"
    )
    
    for result in results:
        print(f"\n{result['constraint_name']}: Valid={result['is_valid']}, "
              f"Violations={result['violation_count']}, "
              f"Pass Rate={result['pass_rate_percent']}%")

def demonstrate_advanced_scenarios(spark: SparkSession):
    """Demonstrate advanced validation scenarios and edge cases"""
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("ADVANCED VALIDATION SCENARIOS")
    print("="*80)
    
    # Scenario 1: Cascading Validations
    print("\n--- Scenario 1: Cascading Validations ---")
    print("Validate parent table first, then child table with FK")
    
    # Create parent table with violations
    parent_data = [
        (1, "Parent1"),
        (2, "Parent2"),
        (2, "Parent2_Duplicate"),  # Duplicate PK
        (None, "Parent_Null"),     # NULL PK
    ]
    parent_df = spark.createDataFrame(parent_data, ["parent_id", "parent_name"])
    
    # Create child table
    child_data = [
        (101, 1, "Child1"),
        (102, 2, "Child2"),
        (103, 3, "Child3"),  # Orphaned - parent doesn't exist
        (104, 1, "Child4"),
    ]
    child_df = spark.createDataFrame(child_data, ["child_id", "parent_id", "child_name"])
    
    composite_validator = CompositeValidator(spark)
    
    # Validate parent first
    parent_constraints = {
        "primary_key": ["parent_id"],
        "not_null": ["parent_id", "parent_name"]
    }
    parent_result = composite_validator.validate_all_constraints(
        parent_df, "parent_table", parent_constraints
    )
    print(f"Parent Table Valid: {parent_result['overall_valid']}")
    
    # Only validate FK if parent is valid
    if parent_result['overall_valid']:
        print("Parent is valid, proceeding with FK validation...")
    else:
        print("WARNING: Parent table has violations. FK validation may be unreliable.")
    
    fk_validator = ForeignKeyValidator(spark)
    fk_result = fk_validator.validate_foreign_key(
        child_df, parent_df, ["parent_id"], ["parent_id"],
        "child_table", "parent_table"
    )
    print(f"FK Valid: {fk_result['is_valid']}, Orphaned: {fk_result['orphaned_records']}")
    
    # Scenario 2: Conditional Constraints
    print("\n--- Scenario 2: Conditional Constraints ---")
    print("Validate constraints that depend on other column values")
    
    employee_data = [
        (1, "John", "FULL_TIME", 80000, 40),
        (2, "Jane", "PART_TIME", 40000, 20),
        (3, "Bob", "FULL_TIME", 75000, 35),   # Hours < 40 for full-time (violation)
        (4, "Alice", "PART_TIME", 50000, 45), # Hours > 40 for part-time (violation)
        (5, "Charlie", "CONTRACT", 60000, 30),
    ]
    emp_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        employee_data,
        ["emp_id", "name", "emp_type", "salary", "hours_per_week"]
    )
    
    check_validator = CheckConstraintValidator(spark)
    
    # Conditional constraint: Full-time employees must work 40 hours
    result1 = check_validator.validate_check_constraint(
        emp_df,
        "fulltime_hours",
        "(emp_type != 'FULL_TIME') OR (emp_type = 'FULL_TIME' AND hours_per_week = 40)",
        "employees",
        "Full-time employees must work exactly 40 hours per week"
    )
    print(f"Full-time hours constraint: Valid={result1['is_valid']}, "
          f"Violations={result1['violation_count']}")
    
    # Conditional constraint: Part-time employees must work <= 35 hours
    result2 = check_validator.validate_check_constraint(
        emp_df,
        "parttime_hours",
        "(emp_type != 'PART_TIME') OR (emp_type = 'PART_TIME' AND hours_per_week <= 35)",
        "employees",
        "Part-time employees must work 35 hours or less per week"
    )
    print(f"Part-time hours constraint: Valid={result2['is_valid']}, "
          f"Violations={result2['violation_count']}")
    
    if result2['violation_count'] > 0:
        violations = check_validator.get_check_violations(
            emp_df,
            "(emp_type != 'PART_TIME') OR (emp_type = 'PART_TIME' AND hours_per_week <= 35)",
            "parttime_hours"
        )
        violations.select("emp_id", "name", "emp_type", "hours_per_week").show()
    
    # Scenario 3: Multi-column Uniqueness with Partial Keys
    print("\n--- Scenario 3: Multi-column Uniqueness with Partial Keys ---")
    
    order_data = [
        (1, "2024-01-01", "CUST001", "PROD001", 100),
        (2, "2024-01-01", "CUST001", "PROD002", 200),
        (3, "2024-01-02", "CUST001", "PROD001", 150),
        (4, "2024-01-01", "CUST001", "PROD001", 120),  # Duplicate: same date, customer, product
        (5, "2024-01-03", "CUST002", "PROD001", 300),
    ]
    orders_df = spark.createDataFrame(
        order_data,
        ["order_id", "order_date", "customer_id", "product_id", "amount"]
    )
    
    uk_validator = UniqueKeyValidator(spark)
    
    # Validate that combination of date, customer, product is unique
    result_uk = uk_validator.validate_unique_key(
        orders_df,
        ["order_date", "customer_id", "product_id"],
        "orders"
    )
    print(f"Composite UK Valid: {result_uk['is_valid']}, "
          f"Duplicate Groups: {result_uk['duplicate_key_groups']}")
    
    if not result_uk['is_valid']:
        violations = uk_validator.get_unique_violations(
            orders_df,
            ["order_date", "customer_id", "product_id"]
        )
        violations.select("order_id", "order_date", "customer_id", "product_id").show()
    
    # Scenario 4: Data Quality Scoring
    print("\n--- Scenario 4: Data Quality Scoring ---")
    
    def calculate_data_quality_score(validation_results: Dict) -> float:
        """Calculate overall data quality score based on validation results"""
        total_checks = 0
        passed_checks = 0
        
        for validation_type, results in validation_results.get('validations', {}).items():
            if isinstance(results, list):
                for result in results:
                    total_checks += 1
                    if result.get('is_valid', False):
                        passed_checks += 1
            else:
                total_checks += 1
                if results.get('is_valid', False):
                    passed_checks += 1
        
        return (passed_checks / total_checks * 100) if total_checks > 0 else 0
    
    employees_df, departments_df, projects_df = create_sample_data(spark)
    
    employees_constraints = {
        "primary_key": ["emp_id"],
        "not_null": ["emp_id", "emp_name"],
        "unique_keys": [["email"]],
        "check_constraints": [
            {"name": "salary_positive", "condition": "salary > 0"}
        ]
    }
    
    result = composite_validator.validate_all_constraints(
        employees_df, "employees", employees_constraints
    )
    
    quality_score = calculate_data_quality_score(result)
    print(f"Data Quality Score: {quality_score:.2f}%")
    print(f"Total Violations: {result['total_violations']}")
    print(f"Overall Valid: {result['overall_valid']}")
    
    # Scenario 5: Incremental Validation (New vs Existing Data)
    print("\n--- Scenario 5: Incremental Validation ---")
    
    # Existing data (assumed valid)
    existing_data = [
        (1, "Existing1", "existing1@example.com"),
        (2, "Existing2", "existing2@example.com"),
    ]
    existing_df = spark.createDataFrame(existing_data, ["id", "name", "email"])
    
    # New data to validate
    new_data = [
        (3, "New1", "new1@example.com"),
        (4, "New2", "existing1@example.com"),  # Duplicate email with existing
        (1, "New3", "new3@example.com"),       # Duplicate ID with existing
    ]
    new_df = spark.createDataFrame(new_data, ["id", "name", "email"])
    
    # Combine for validation
    combined_df = existing_df.unionByName(new_df)
    
    pk_validator = PrimaryKeyValidator(spark)
    pk_result = pk_validator.validate_primary_key(combined_df, ["id"], "combined")
    
    uk_validator = UniqueKeyValidator(spark)
    uk_result = uk_validator.validate_unique_key(combined_df, ["email"], "combined")
    
    print(f"PK Valid: {pk_result['is_valid']}, Duplicates: {pk_result['duplicate_rows']}")
    print(f"UK Valid: {uk_result['is_valid']}, Duplicates: {uk_result['duplicate_rows']}")
    
    # Identify which new records cause violations
    if not pk_result['is_valid'] or not uk_result['is_valid']:
        print("\nNew records causing violations:")
        violations = pk_validator.get_pk_violations(combined_df, ["id"])
        new_violations = violations.join(new_df, ["id"], "inner")
        new_violations.show()
